title: Windows ML CLI's CORS wildcard gives websites localhost RCE
summary: The winml-cli project's local API server exposes every WinML CLI command over unauthenticated HTTP, and while it correctly binds to localhost, it also sets allow_origins to a wildcard — so any website the victim's browser visits can call the endpoint. Combined with the build/config commands' `trust_remote_code` flag, an attacker-hosted malicious model repository reaches `AutoConfig.from_pretrained(..., trust_remote_code=True)`, achieving remote code execution as the server user just by getting the victim to load a malicious webpage.
takeaway: Binding a local tooling server to localhost is not a security boundary by itself if it also sets a wildcard CORS policy — the loopback bind stops remote network attackers, but a wildcard `allow_origins` reopens the exact same access to any website the victim's browser visits, and that combined with an unsandboxed `trust_remote_code` model-loading path is enough for drive-by RCE.

lessons.point: The server binds to localhost by default (blocking remote attackers) but also sets allow_origins to a wildcard, which erases the security boundary the loopback bind was supposed to provide, since the victim's own browser can now be used as a proxy by any website it visits.
lessons.excerpt: serve/cli_api.py exposes every winml CLI command over HTTP with no authentication. That's defensible on its own - it binds 127.0.0.1 by default, so the audience is this machine. But it also sets allow_origins=["*"] (cli_api.py:150, duplicated at app.py:219), and the victim's browser is a local process: the wildcard lets any website call the endpoint and read the reply, erasing the boundary the loopback bind draws.

lessons.point: The trust_remote_code flag, passed unfiltered from a JSON request body, causes transformers to import and execute Python code from an attacker-named model repository at config-load time — the malicious payload runs on import, before any explicit "run this model" step.
lessons.excerpt: build and config both accept --trust-remote-code, and a JSON true becomes that flag unfiltered. An attacker-named model repo reaches AutoConfig.from_pretrained(..., trust_remote_code=True) (_autoconfig.py:191), where transformers imports Python from that repo - RCE as the server user from any page the victim loads. The payload runs on import, so the command's exit_code: 1 is irrelevant.

actionable.title: Never combine a wildcard CORS policy with a localhost-bound tool server
actionable.detail: For any local developer-tooling HTTP server (ML CLIs, dev servers, IDE helper daemons): never set allow_origins to a wildcard even when bound to localhost — a browser visiting any website can still reach it. Separately, treat trust_remote_code as equivalent to arbitrary code execution and never accept it from an unauthenticated or CORS-reachable endpoint.

prior_art: Localhost-bound service + wildcard CORS drive-by attacks are a documented pattern (cf. 'localhost-CORS-bypass' research on local AI servers); trust_remote_code RCE via transformers/AutoConfig is a long-known HF-ecosystem issue.
verify_note: Both lessons match the advisory and PoC exactly; taking the lower novelty score (50 vs 70) since this combines two already-known bug classes.

title: The Framing Gap: reframed indirect prompt-injection exfiltration defeats surface-level defenses
summary: Overt injection to exfiltrate a secret is refused (gpt-4o 0%), but reframing the identical leak as a mandatory 'integrity signature', config field, or look-alike trusted host drives success to 100%. The reusable asset is the template, not the mechanism, and the root cause is instruction/data confusion rather than defeated alignment. Only payload-blind controls - destination allow-lists and a planner/reader capability split - close the gap; SecAlign fine-tuning, channel separation, and output-normalizing guards do not.

lessons.point: Attacks the model refuses when overt succeed fully when reframed as benign-sounding requirements - alignment does not recognize the semantics.
lessons.excerpt: reframing the identical leak as a mandatory integrity signature, config field, or look-alike "trusted" host drives gpt-4o 0% to 100%

lessons.point: The reusable attack asset is a template, so paraphrase and field-swap make injection cheap to scale.
lessons.excerpt: the reusable asset is the template, not the mechanism

lessons.point: Only payload-blind architectural controls - destination allow-lists and planner/reader capability isolation - reliably stop exfiltration.
lessons.excerpt: What closes the gap is payload-blind checks: a destination allow-list (0%, when destinations are closed) and a capability-isolating planner/reader split (0%).

lessons.point: Fine-tuning defenses, channel separation, and output normalization all fail against reframing or held-out encodings like ROT13.
lessons.excerpt: an output-normalizing guard loses to a held-out encoding (ROT13, 100%)

takeaway: Don't rely on the acting model to recognize injection; constrain where data can go and isolate the capability that can send it.

actionable.title: Enforce destination allow-lists and planner/reader separation
actionable.detail: For agents that hold secrets and read untrusted content, gate all outbound actions to a closed destination allow-list and split the reader (untrusted parsing) from the planner/actor (privileged sending) so untrusted text can never directly choose an exfiltration destination; do not depend on fine-tuning, channel tags, or output filters.

prior_art: SecAlign (CCS 2025), channel-separation and output-normalization defenses, AgentDojo-style injection benchmarks; contribution is the framing-gap characterization and payload-blind mitigations.
threat: Indirect prompt-injection exfiltration of a held secret via semantically reframed leak requests.
conditions: Tool-using LLM agent holds a secret and processes attacker-controlled web content with an open outbound channel.
mitigations: Closed destination allow-lists and capability-isolating planner/reader split; surface-level model defenses are inadequate.

title: Safety Does Not Compose: Non-Decaying Loop State for Autonomous LLM Agents
summary: Autonomous agents run as loops but their safety monitors are scoped to a single trajectory and reset each iteration, so attacks whose evidence is fragmented across iterations are invisible - the authors prove a trajectory-scoped monitor's true-positive rate equals its false-positive rate. A decaying risk score doesn't help because a patient adversary's cooling-off wait is constant. LoopHarness maintains persistent, non-decaying loop-level safety state and bounds unauthorized irreversible actions by a constant independent of horizon N.

lessons.point: Single-trajectory safety monitors provably cannot detect attacks whose evidence spans multiple agent iterations.
lessons.excerpt: every trajectory-scoped monitor has a true-positive rate equal to its false-positive rate

lessons.point: A geometrically decaying risk score does not fix this because a patient attacker only needs a constant cooling-off wait.
lessons.excerpt: the cooling-off period a patient adversary must wait is a constant that does not grow with the horizon N

lessons.point: Persistent, non-decaying loop-level safety state can bound unauthorized irreversible actions by a constant independent of horizon.
lessons.excerpt: it bounds the expected number of unauthorized irreversible actions by a constant in N

takeaway: Agent safety must accumulate state across the whole loop; per-trajectory monitors that reset each iteration are blind to slow, fragmented attacks.

actionable.title: Give agent monitors persistent cross-iteration memory
actionable.detail: For long-running autonomous loops, keep a non-decaying safety state across iterations, mediate irreversible commits through an arbiter, and back critical limits with a model-free rule so a colluding verifier cannot lift them; test with an outer-state attack suite whose evidence only appears across multiple iterations.

prior_art: Trajectory-scoped agent monitors and Agent-SafetyBench; contribution is the impossibility separation and non-decaying loop-level state (LoopHarness).
threat: Patient adversary spreads attack evidence across many iterations to stay under per-trajectory monitor thresholds.
conditions: Autonomous agent runs unattended loops with safety state reset at each new trajectory.
mitigations: Persistent non-decaying loop-level safety state with mediated commits and a model-free action bound.

title: SEAL cuts jailbreak success on Mixture-of-Experts models with a shared expert anchor
summary: A CCS 2026 paper identifies that Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLM safety is structurally vulnerable because it hinges on which sparse experts get activated per token, and adversaries can subvert routing via jailbreak prompts, malicious fine-tuning, or pruning safety-critical neurons — defenses that only harden the router can still be bypassed since routing is nondeterministic. SEAL instead trains a plug-and-play adapter on the always-activated shared-expert component (which holds a small proportion of safety-critical neurons) as a router-independent safety anchor, reducing attack success rate by up to 60% across six attack scenarios at a capability cost of at most 1.4%.
takeaway: Router-hardening defenses for MoE model safety can still be bypassed because routing itself is nondeterministic and manipulable — anchoring safety to the always-activated shared-expert component instead sidesteps that uncertainty entirely, since it's not subject to the same routing-path manipulation.

lessons.point: MoE safety is structurally tied to which sparse experts activate per token, and existing router-hardening defenses can still be bypassed because an adversary can manipulate or evade the routing trajectory itself, given its nondeterministic nature.
lessons.excerpt: MoE safety hinges on which experts are activated, and adversaries can subvert this selection through jailbreak prompts, malicious fine-tuning, and weight-level pruning of safety-critical neurons. Existing defenses primarily focus on hardening the router, but an adversary may still manipulate or bypass the routing trajectory due to the routing process's nondeterministic nature, thereby collapsing the defense.

lessons.point: SEAL anchors safety to the shared expert — a component that is always activated regardless of routing decisions and already holds a small proportion of safety-critical neurons — making it a router-independent defense point that sidesteps the routing-manipulation problem entirely.
lessons.excerpt: shared expert, an always-activated component containing a small proportion of safety-critical neurons, can overcome the uncertainty of sparsely activated routing path and serve as a router-independent anchor to enhance global safety alignment.

lessons.point: Across six attack scenarios combining three adversarial input types (harmful prompting, jailbreak, malicious fine-tuning) with and without neuron pruning, SEAL reduced attack success rate by up to 60% at a capability cost of at most 1.4% on a five-benchmark average.
lessons.excerpt: We evaluate SEAL and SEAL++ across six attack scenarios that combine three adversarial inputs (harmful prompting, jailbreak, malicious fine-tuning) with and without neuron pruning.

actionable.title: Evaluate MoE safety defenses for router-independence, not just router-hardening
actionable.detail: When evaluating or designing safety defenses for Mixture-of-Experts models, check whether the defense depends on the router behaving predictably — SEAL's approach shows anchoring to the always-activated shared-expert component avoids the routing-manipulation bypass that router-hardening-only defenses are vulnerable to.

prior_art: Router-hardening defenses for MoE jailbreaks (the paper's own contrasted baseline) and general dense-model safety-alignment/circuit-breaker techniques; MoE-specific shared-expert anchoring is this paper's distinct contribution.
verify_note: All three lessons are direct restatements of the arXiv abstract; taking lower novelty (65 vs 72) and relevance (40 vs 55, since this is training-time research for model builders, not an operational control for the ai-security defender audience).

title: SPA: Securing Persistent LLM Agents Across Queries with Plan-First Information-Flow Control
summary: Persistent LLM agents face threats beyond single tool calls: attacker data can alter control flow, poison tool arguments, or compromise later queries via reused state. SPA generates a full executable plan once per query in a declarative DSL, then applies dual-lattice information-flow control over confidentiality and integrity, storing results as labeled artifacts that expose only metadata to later planning. It reduces 'tool_knowledge' attack success to zero on AgentDojo and 0.2% on a new multi-query extension, at a security-utility cost.

lessons.point: Persistent agents need defenses that span planning, execution, and cross-query state, not just individual tool calls.
lessons.excerpt: attacker-controlled data can alter control flow, enter security-sensitive tool arguments, or compromise later queries

lessons.point: Storing results as labeled artifacts and exposing only metadata to later planning prevents re-injection of untrusted payloads across queries.
lessons.excerpt: SPA stores execution results as labeled artifacts and reveals only semantic metadata during later planning

lessons.point: Dual-lattice information-flow control can drive prompt-injection attack success to near zero, but strict integrity enforcement costs utility.
lessons.excerpt: revealing an important security-utility tradeoff introduced by strict integrity enforcement

takeaway: Plan-first execution plus information-flow labels that persist across queries can nearly eliminate tool-knowledge injection in stateful agents, at some utility cost.

actionable.title: Apply information-flow labels to agent state reuse
actionable.detail: For long-running agents, generate a complete plan up front, track confidentiality and integrity labels across data and control dependencies, and persist prior results as labeled artifacts exposing only metadata to the planner; evaluate delayed/multi-query attacks (e.g., AgentDojo-MQ) and budget for the utility tradeoff.

prior_art: AgentDojo benchmark and prior planning- or tool-level injection defenses; extends to cross-query persistence with dual-lattice IFC and AgentDojo-MQ.
threat: Indirect prompt injection and delayed attacks that corrupt control flow, tool arguments, or reused state in persistent agents.
conditions: Agent operates over untrusted web/document/tool inputs while reusing state across multiple queries.
mitigations: Plan-first declarative execution with dual-lattice information-flow control and label-preserving artifact persistence.

title: n8n agent workflow tool bypassed sub-workflow caller restrictions
summary: n8n's "this workflow can be called by" caller-restriction setting was enforced by the manual Execute Workflow node but silently not consulted when the same restricted workflow was attached to an AI Agent as a callable tool, letting any user who could build an agent invoke and read back results from workflows their owner had explicitly restricted.
takeaway: A permission check enforced on one invocation path (a manual node) is not automatically enforced on a newer invocation path (agent tool-calling) added later to the same underlying resource — every new way to reach a resource needs its own explicit authorization check, not an assumption that existing checks cover it.

lessons.point: The caller-restriction policy on a workflow was enforced by the manual Execute Workflow node, but was never checked when the same workflow was exposed to an AI Agent as a tool, so agent-based invocation silently bypassed an access control the workflow owner had explicitly configured.
lessons.excerpt: A workflow's "_This workflow can be called by_" setting was enforced by the Execute Workflow node but was not consulted when the same workflow was attached to an Agent as a tool. A user who could build an Agent could therefore call a workflow that its owner had restricted, and read back what it returned.

actionable.title: Re-verify every access-control check when a resource gains a new agent-tool invocation path
actionable.detail: When any internal workflow, function, or resource that already has an access-control check becomes callable as an agent tool, explicitly re-verify the check applies on that new code path — don't assume tool-calling reuses the same authorization logic as the original manual invocation.

prior_art: Classic broken-access-control/IDOR pattern (OWASP A01) where a check enforced on one code path is missing on a newer one, applied to a new agent-tool-calling interface.
verify_note: The lesson is an almost verbatim restatement of the GHSA advisory text; fully supported.

title: Scary object names make agent guardrails over-refuse legitimate actions
summary: Agent guardrails suffer over-safety: they refuse authorized, genuinely safe actions, blocking deployment. The authors build Cautious Bench, the first benchmark that makes over-safety the measured construct, codesigning each sample with a stated authorization policy and mechanically re-deriving labels. Measuring six guardrails, they find a 'name-superstition effect' - the same authorized action is over-refused more often when the object simply has a scary-looking name.

lessons.point: Over-safety (refusing authorized, safe actions) is a real deployment blocker and must be measured against a stated authorization policy.
lessons.excerpt: This over-safety blocks deployment when a guardrail refuses an authorized task.

lessons.point: Guardrail decisions are swayed by superficial cues - scary object names - rather than the actual authorization context.
lessons.excerpt: the guardrails read the surface label, not the authorization context

lessons.point: Reliable over-safety benchmarks need mechanically re-derived labels tied to policy, not per-sample annotator verdicts.
lessons.excerpt: each label is a mechanical consequence of the policy rather than an annotator's per-sample verdict

takeaway: Guardrails that key on scary-sounding surface labels will over-refuse legitimate work; evaluate over-safety with policy-derived benchmarks.

actionable.title: Test guardrails for name-superstition over-refusal
actionable.detail: Build benign/twin action pairs that differ only in object naming, define an explicit authorization policy, and measure whether your guardrail refuses authorized actions more often under alarming names; if so, condition decisions on authorization context rather than surface tokens.

prior_art: Prior over-refusal/exaggerated-safety studies (e.g., XSTest-style) for chat models; extends the construct to agent action guardrails with a policy-certified benchmark.
threat: Not an attack: usability/availability failure where guardrails block legitimate authorized agent actions.
conditions: Guardrail evaluates an authorized action whose object bears a threatening-sounding name.
mitigations: Authorization-context-aware guardrails and policy-derived over-safety benchmarking (Cautious Bench).

title: When AI infrastructure becomes the target: attacks on LiteLLM/RAGFlow/Kestra control points
summary: Microsoft details in-the-wild compromises of three AI workloads - a LiteLLM gateway, a RAGFlow deployment, and a Kestra orchestration environment - where attackers converged on credential theft, persistence, and cryptomining. For LiteLLM, code execution in the gateway process led to harvesting /proc/1/environ secrets and dumping virtual-key/model tables. The report frames AI gateways/retrieval/orchestration as a high-value control plane needing dedicated monitoring.

lessons.point: AI gateways, retrieval, and orchestration services concentrate credentials, data access and execution privileges, making them high-value targets.
lessons.excerpt: These systems concentrate credentials, data access, model connectivity, and execution privileges, making them some of the most powerful components in the AI stack.

lessons.point: Different AI workloads with different intrusion paths converge on the same objectives: credential theft, persistence, and compute monetization.
lessons.excerpt: attackers treated AI infrastructure as a control plane where credential theft, host compromise, and downstream data access can converge

lessons.point: Containerized gateways running as PID 1 leak their whole secret-bearing environment via /proc/1/environ once code execution is achieved.
lessons.excerpt: In containerized LiteLLM deployments where the gateway runs as PID 1, /proc/1/environ exposes the environment block for the gateway process.

lessons.point: Monitor AI workloads by their control-plane role, correlating app-origin shells with secret access and outbound callbacks.
lessons.excerpt: Defenders should monitor AI workloads according to their control-plane role, not only as isolated applications.

takeaway: Attackers are already treating AI gateways like LiteLLM as a credential-rich control plane, so these services need the same scrutiny as any critical enterprise infrastructure.

actionable.title: Inventory and harden exposed AI management surfaces
actionable.detail: Patch LiteLLM/RAGFlow/Kestra to fixed versions, remove internet exposure of AI gateways/orchestrators, restrict admin access, avoid running gateways as PID 1 with secrets in env, rotate provider and master keys, lock down the Docker socket, and alert on gateway-originated shell/interpreter execution plus secret access and outbound callbacks.

prior_art: Public LiteLLM CVE research; Embrace The Red's LiteLLM hijack post; general cryptomining intrusions
threat: Exploitation of exposed AI gateway/retrieval/orchestration services for credential theft, persistence, data access, and cryptomining.
conditions: Organizations exposing LiteLLM, RAGFlow, Kestra or similar AI infrastructure to the network, especially in default/containerized configs.
mitigations: Patch known CVEs, remove public exposure, least-privilege secrets, secure Docker socket, monitor control-plane-origin execution and secret access.

title: SkillShield: Prompt-Space Security Skills for LLM Coding Agents
summary: A coding agent runs shell commands and edits files with developer privileges, so malicious requests become real harmful actions; weight-level alignment isn't available to API-only deployers and monitors need extra classifiers. SkillShield synthesizes security 'skills' offline from known attacks or recorded failures and injects them into the system prompt for the whole tool-use loop, needing no runtime classification. On RedCode it cuts harmful-generation severity from 3.37 to 0.58 and matches Llama Guard 3 without a separate 8B classifier, at a 0.14% benign refusal rate.

lessons.point: Coding agents are high-risk because malicious prompts become privileged file and shell actions.
lessons.excerpt: allowing malicious requests to translate directly into harmful actions

lessons.point: System-prompt security skills can approximate a guardrail classifier's protection without a separate model on the trajectory.
lessons.excerpt: comparable to Llama Guard 3's 42.7% without its separate 8B classifier

lessons.point: Prompt-space defenses can be tuned to strong protection with very low benign over-refusal.
lessons.excerpt: SkillShield yields a mean safety-refusal rate of 0.14%

takeaway: API-only deployers can harden coding agents with offline-synthesized, always-on system-prompt security skills instead of extra runtime classifiers.

actionable.title: Provision system-prompt security skills for coding agents
actionable.detail: Synthesize security policy 'skills' offline from known attack classes and recorded agent failures, inject them at session start so they persist through the tool-use loop, and pick a provisioning scope to fit the prompt budget; measure execution attack success on RedCode and benign refusal rate to tune the tradeoff.

prior_art: Weight-level alignment, input filters, execution-boundary monitors, and Llama Guard 3; contribution is a classifier-free prompt-space skill defense evaluated on RedCode.
threat: Malicious or jailbroken requests driving a privileged coding agent to perform harmful actions.
conditions: API-only coding-agent deployment without access to model weights or an auxiliary guard model.
mitigations: Offline-synthesized security skills injected into the system prompt and active across the tool-use loop.

title: Five Primitives for Governing Autonomous AI Agents at Runtime
summary: Enterprise access-control models built for human users and long-lived services fail for agents that are ephemeral, act via model choice rather than fixed programs, and are discovered rather than provisioned. The authors argue agent governance is a runtime problem and derive five primitives - discovery, identity, governance, attestation, supply chain - mediating each action against policy before it takes effect and recording it in a verifiable hash-linked signed ledger.

lessons.point: Human/service access-control models fail for agents because agents are ephemeral, model-driven, and self-created via any API caller.
lessons.excerpt: agent principals are ephemeral, appearing and vanishing faster than provisioning

lessons.point: Agent governance is fundamentally a runtime enforcement problem, distinct from model alignment or build-time controls.
lessons.excerpt: governing such agents is a runtime problem -- not a model-alignment problem and not a build-time problem

lessons.point: Mediating each action against policy and recording it in a verifiable signed ledger enables third-party audit without trusting the vendor.
lessons.excerpt: recorded in a hash-linked signed ledger a third party can verify with the vendor out of the loop

lessons.point: Runtime mediation has real costs: critical-path latency, per-workload identity sidecars, and fail-closed denial during outages.
lessons.excerpt: fail-closed mediation converts availability incidents into denial

takeaway: Govern agents at runtime with per-action policy mediation, per-tenant action vocabularies, verifiable ledgers, and explicit availability tradeoffs.

actionable.title: Mediate agent actions at runtime against a per-tenant vocabulary
actionable.detail: Deploy an enforcement point that checks each agent action against policy before it takes effect, authorizes it against a per-tenant action vocabulary, and appends to a hash-linked signed ledger for independent audit; plan for critical-path latency, identity sidecars, and fail-closed behavior during incidents.

prior_art: IAM/RBAC for humans and services, workload identity (SPIFFE-style sidecars), and transparency-log designs; contribution is the agent-specific five-primitive runtime decomposition.
threat: Ungoverned autonomous agents taking unauthorized actions with no verifiable accountability.
conditions: Enterprise runs autonomous agents whose principals are ephemeral and dynamically created.
mitigations: Runtime action mediation, agent identity, per-tenant action vocabulary, attestation, and a verifiable signed ledger.

title: ChainDrop npm worm targeted Claude Code configs and stole OIDC tokens
summary: Unit 42's SDLC supply-chain roundup details the ChainDrop npm worm, which infected 400+ packages (including popular ones like keyv and cacheable-request) via a preinstall script, then read live process memory on GitHub Actions runners to steal OIDC tokens, backdoored local Claude Code/VS Code configs for persistence, and ran its C2 over Ethereum blockchain transactions.
takeaway: Supply-chain worms are now targeting AI coding-agent configuration files as a persistence vector, not just credentials — and using decentralized blockchain C2 to resist takedown, which existing npm-hardening advice (--ignore-scripts, cooldowns) doesn't fully address once it establishes IDE-level persistence.

lessons.point: ChainDrop's theft stage went beyond scraping files on disk — a hidden Python script read live process memory on GitHub Actions runners directly to steal temporary OIDC tokens and secrets.
lessons.excerpt: Rather than just scraping disk files, a hidden Python script directly read live process memory from GitHub Actions runners to steal temporary OpenID Connect (OIDC) tokens and secrets, alongside a massive sweep for local developer credentials.

lessons.point: The worm secured long-term persistence by modifying local developer tool configs, specifically calling out Claude Code and VS Code, and ran its C2 infrastructure dynamically over Ethereum blockchain transactions to resist takedown.
lessons.excerpt: ChainDrop secured long-term persistence by establishing cross-linked hooks directly inside developer tools like VS Code and Claude Code, while managing its entire command-and-control (C2) infrastructure dynamically through Ethereum blockchain transactions.

lessons.point: Unit 42's hardening recommendation acknowledges --ignore-scripts as one of several mitigations, alongside ephemeral CI/CD servers, dependency cooldowns, and SHA-pinning, rather than a standalone fix — consistent with the existing pool finding that install-time controls alone are insufficient against import-time or memory-resident payloads.
lessons.excerpt: organizations must lock down the developer environment by disabling lifecycle install scripts (--ignore-scripts), enforcing package cooldown periods, restricting CI/CD egress traffic, using ephemeral CI/CD servers and pinning dependencies down to exact commit SHAs.

actionable.title: Add IDE/agent config drift detection to endpoint monitoring
actionable.detail: Monitor for unauthorized writes to Claude Code, VS Code (tasks.json, settings.json), and similar coding-agent config files as a first-class persistence indicator, not just secrets/credentials scraping. Treat CI runner process memory as in-scope for OIDC token theft, not just disk and environment variables.

prior_art: Unit 42's own prior Shai-Hulud npm worm and Axios supply-chain writeups cover preinstall-script/credential-theft mechanics generally.
verify_note: All 3 lessons directly and accurately quoted from the Unit 42 SDLC roundup.

title: Diffusion LLMs as Targets and Adversaries: Mechanistic Safety Exploits
summary: The authors show diffusion-based LLMs inherit a sparse, mappable set of 'safety neurons' from their autoregressive predecessors, so pruning those neurons (self- or transfer-pruning from models like Qwen2.5) drives attack success rates from single digits to 70–86 percent. They then build SN-Guided Diffusion, an offline black-box jailbreak that steers denoising away from safety-triggering regions and transfers to Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite with only 20 generation episodes per prompt.
takeaway: Safety alignment in diffusion LLMs is sparse enough to be located by neuron mapping and cheaply bypassed — and the resulting attack transfers across families, including to a closed frontier model.

lessons.point: Diffusion LLMs inherit the same sparse safety neurons as their autoregressive predecessors, enabling transfer attacks by direct neuron mapping and pruning.
lessons.excerpt: DLLMs initialized from autoregressive predecessors inherit the same mechanistic safety footprint as their source models, enabling transfer attacks via direct safety neuron mapping and pruning.

lessons.point: Self- or transfer-pruning of these safety neurons lifts attack success rates dramatically on multiple DLLMs.
lessons.excerpt: Self-pruning increases attack success rates (ASR) from 2.6% to 73.8% on LLaDA and from 1.9% to 86.6% on Dream, while transfer pruning from Qwen2.5 increases ASR from 1.9% to 73.2% on Dream and from 7.0% to 86.3% on Fast-dLLM.

lessons.point: SN-Guided Diffusion is an offline black-box jailbreak whose transfer generalizes to proprietary autoregressive frontier models with very few queries.
lessons.excerpt: Our method achieves a transfer ASR of up to 77.1% on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, 86.9% on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and 74.3% against Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, while requiring only 20 generation episodes per prompt.

actionable.title: Add a diffusion-LLM neuron-pruning red-team scenario to jailbreak evals
actionable.detail: For any DLLM (LLaDA, Dream, Fast-dLLM, and derivatives) inheriting weights from an autoregressive predecessor, include a scenario where a red-team maps safety neurons from the predecessor and applies transfer pruning. Track ASR under 20-episode budgets against a fixed jailbreak set; treat cross-family transfer to closed models as an in-scope threat, not a theoretical one.

prior_art: Extends prior work on safety-neuron identification and pruning in autoregressive LLMs (Wei et al., 'Assessing the Brittleness of Safety Alignment via Pruning and Low-Rank Modifications') and mechanistic-interpretability-driven jailbreaks; novelty is showing the property transfers into diffusion LLMs and gives a cheap black-box jailbreak with cross-family reach.
threat: Sparse and inherited safety neurons in diffusion LLMs let attackers cheaply locate and disable alignment, then reuse the same guidance to jailbreak unrelated autoregressive and proprietary models with tens of queries.
conditions: Attacker needs (1) a source model or its safety-neuron map to seed the attack, (2) an offline pipeline to steer diffusion sampling with a safety-neuron loss, and (3) black-box query access to the target; results are demonstrated on LLaDA, Dream, Fast-dLLM, Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite.
mitigations: Do not treat sparse safety-neuron alignment as sufficient; combine mechanistic alignment with prompt-level classifiers and output filters; monitor for pruning-signature or SN-guided attack patterns; assume any DLLM derived from a known base model inherits its jailbreak surface and gate deployment accordingly.
verify_note: All three excerpts verbatim from fetched abstract. Related_claims chosen for content overlap on jailbreak transfer and durability of the injection/jailbreak surface — both exist in claims.json.

title: Cisco AI Defense mcp-scanner checks MCP tools, prompts, resources, and server instructions
summary: mcp-scanner is a Python CLI/SDK that scans MCP servers for security issues across four surfaces — tools, prompts, resources, and the server's `InitializeResult` instructions — using three interchangeable engines: YARA rules, an LLM-as-judge, and Cisco's inspect API. It adds pip-audit-based vulnerable-dependency scanning, VirusTotal hash lookups for bundled binaries, and Docker-sandboxed PyPI/npm package downloads for behavioral analysis. Scanning `InitializeResult` instructions is called out as its own subcommand because those instructions are a first-class prompt-injection surface.
takeaway: Treat every MCP surface — tools, prompts, resources, and server instructions — as a distinct attack surface with its own scanner; a single engine misses cases each of YARA, LLM-judge, and dataflow catches.

lessons.point: MCP `InitializeResult` server instructions are their own scan target, not incidental metadata: they are consumed by the model and can carry prompt injection, tool poisoning, or misleading guidance.
lessons.excerpt: Server instructions provide usage guidelines, security notes, and configuration details in the MCP `InitializeResult`. Scanning instructions helps detect prompt injection, tool poisoning, and misleading guidance.

lessons.point: Behavioral scanning that compares an MCP tool's docstring claim against its actual dataflow is the way to catch tool poisoning; string-match YARA rules are complementary but not sufficient.
lessons.excerpt: The Behavioral Analyzer performs advanced static analysis of MCP server source code to detect behavioral mismatches between docstring claims and actual implementation. It uses LLM-powered alignment checking combined with cross-file dataflow tracking.

lessons.point: Layered engines matter: the scanner combines three independent detectors so a defender is not betting on one signal.
lessons.excerpt: The MCP Scanner combines Cisco AI Defense inspect API, YARA rules and LLM-as-a-judge to detect malicious MCP tools.

actionable.title: Add MCP scanning to CI as a gate on any newly installed MCP server
actionable.detail: Wire `mcp-scanner --scan-known-configs --analyzers yara,llm --format raw` into pre-merge and pre-install checks. Include the `instructions`, `supplychain`, and `pypi-scan`/`npm-scan` subcommands so behavioral mismatches and bundled malware surface at admission time, not runtime.

prior_art: Complements ToolHive MCP SSRF and 'Agent skill security is a lifecycle problem' (SkillSec-Eval) entries in the pool: both frame skill/tool metadata as needing lifecycle scanning, and this is the concrete tool that operationalizes it.
threat: MCP tool descriptions, prompt templates, resource contents, and `InitializeResult` instructions all flow into the model context and can carry prompt injection or tool poisoning. Without dedicated scanning, a hostile or compromised MCP server gets admitted to an agent's tool set through normal `mcp add` flows, and behavioral mismatches between docstrings and implementations are invisible to human reviewers scanning READMEs.
conditions: An organization runs agents that connect to external or third-party MCP servers; scanning is not gated on admission; and human review is limited to the tool README rather than the tool's dataflow.
mitigations: Run mcp-scanner across all four MCP surfaces (tools, prompts, resources, instructions) at admission; add pip-audit and VirusTotal scans for bundled dependencies; keep pypi-scan/npm-scan sandboxed via Docker (default) and treat behavioral analyzer output as blocking for tools that mutate state.

title: BurpMCP-Ultra is a 150-tool MCP server with a scope gate
summary: BurpMCP-Ultra is a native Kotlin Burp Suite extension that exposes 150 Montoya-API tools through an embedded MCP server over token-secured local SSE. It ships with a scope gate that governs which offensive tools can issue live requests, plus host-header allowlisting, origin lockdown, and an append-only audit log. Every live-request tool is force-routed through operator-configured controls the agent cannot override.
takeaway: If you must expose an offensive toolkit via MCP, the operator-only scope gate and per-session token are load-bearing controls; loopback binding is not a trust boundary.

lessons.point: For MCP servers wrapping powerful local tooling, localhost is not a security boundary; the transport must add host-header, origin, and per-session token defenses.
lessons.excerpt: Binding to `127.0.0.1` is **not** a trust boundary, so the transport is hardened and offensive tools are governed by **operator-only** controls the agent cannot change.

lessons.point: Governance of destructive or scope-crossing tools should live in the operator's config layer, not in agent-visible tool metadata; the agent must not be able to escalate itself.
lessons.excerpt: `mcp_scope_mode` — `off` / `warn` / `enforce`. Every live-request tool passes through a central **scope gate** (`http_*`, `auth_diff`, `api_import_openapi`, `recon_*`, `graphql_probe`, `cors_probe`, `access_control_sweep`, `injection_probe`).

lessons.point: Query-string tokens do not survive MCP's SSE back-channel because the SDK's relative POST endpoint replaces the query per RFC 3986; the token must live in a header or a path segment.
lessons.excerpt: A `?token=…` query does **not** work for MCP: the SDK advertises its POST endpoint as the relative reference `?sessionId=…`, which per RFC 3986 §5.3 replaces the query (so the token is dropped and every message `401`s) while preserving the path.

lessons.point: Shipping 150 tools cuts against harness-design guidance that tool count degrades agent performance; the compensating design choice here is stable names and a `server.tools.size` surface for verification.
lessons.excerpt: **150 MCP tools** across 37 categories. Names are stable; the authoritative count is `server.tools.size`, surfaced in the Server tab.

actionable.title: Adopt the operator-only scope-gate pattern for offensive MCP servers
actionable.detail: For any MCP server exposing live-request tools, put a central scope gate the agent cannot override, force host-header/origin allowlisting, and prefer header or path-segment auth over query-string tokens (which the MCP SDK drops on the SSE back-channel).

prior_art: Complements ToolHive MCP SSRF and AWS API MCP fail-open advisories in the pool: both illustrate what happens when host-side MCP tooling lacks the localhost-hardening BurpMCP-Ultra ships as default.
threat: An MCP server that exposes offensive tooling on localhost can be reached by any process on the host (including a browser rendering a malicious page via DNS rebinding). Without host-header/origin/token defenses and an operator-only scope gate, an agent can be prompt-injected into running scans or exfiltrating captured credentials against out-of-scope targets.
conditions: A local MCP server binds to 127.0.0.1 and trusts the loopback interface as authenticated; the agent client accepts tool descriptions verbatim; and destructive controls are exposed as MCP tools rather than operator-only config.
mitigations: Use per-session bearer tokens delivered on Authorization or a first path segment; enforce Host and Origin allowlists; keep destructive tools (shutdown, config import) behind an operator-set `mcp_allow_destructive` flag; append-only audit log for scope-gated calls.

title: snyk/agent-scan
summary: Snyk Agent Scan is a CLI that inventories installed agent components (harnesses, MCP servers, skills) across Claude Code/Desktop, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Windsurf, Amp, Amazon Q, Kiro, OpenCode, Antigravity, and Codex, then scans each for prompt injection, tool poisoning, tool shadowing, toxic flows, malware payloads, credential handling, and hardcoded secrets. It ships with a technical report on emerging agent-skill ecosystem threats. A crucial caveat: scanning an MCP config actually STARTS the stdio servers to fetch tool descriptions, so scanning untrusted configs must happen in a sandbox and interactive runs prompt for per-server consent before execution.
takeaway: Any 'MCP scanner' that reads tool descriptions from stdio servers is executing third-party code as a side effect of scanning. Treat scan-time as install-time from a threat-model perspective, and never run these scanners against untrusted configs outside a disposable sandbox.

lessons.point: Scanning an MCP configuration executes the configured stdio server commands, so the scanner is itself an execution surface.
lessons.excerpt: When Agent Scan scans an MCP configuration file, it starts the stdio MCP servers by executing the commands and arguments specified in the config. This is necessary to retrieve tool descriptions and perform security analysis.

lessons.point: Interactive per-server consent is the default; --dangerously-run-mcp-servers is required to bypass it in CI, and that flag is only safe in trusted environments.
lessons.excerpt: By default, Agent Scan requires explicit user consent (y/n) before starting each stdio MCP server during interactive runs. This gives you control over what gets executed on your system.

lessons.point: The tool's issue taxonomy separates MCP-side risks (prompt injection, tool poisoning, tool shadowing, toxic flows) from skill-side risks (prompt injection, malware payloads, untrusted content, credential handling, hardcoded secrets), reflecting a two-surface threat model.
lessons.excerpt:
Detects [15+ distinct security risks](docs/issue-codes.md) across MCP servers and agent skills:
  - MCP: [Prompt Injection](docs/issue-codes.md#E001), [Tool Poisoning](docs/issue-codes.md#E001), [Tool Shadowing](docs/issue-codes.md#E002), [Toxic Flows](docs/issue-codes.md#ToxicFlows)
  - Skills: [Prompt Injection](docs/issue-codes.md#E004), [Malware Payloads](docs/issue-codes.md#E006), [Untrusted Content](docs/issue-codes.md#W011), [Credential Handling](docs/issue-codes.md#W007), [Hardcoded Secrets](docs/issue-codes.md#W008)

actionable.title: Run Snyk Agent Scan in a sandbox when scanning untrusted MCP configs
actionable.detail: Install and run `uvx snyk-agent-scan@latest` for a first-pass inventory of installed agents, MCP servers, and skills on developer machines. Never enable --dangerously-run-mcp-servers outside a disposable sandbox — scanning starts every stdio MCP server as configured.

prior_art: Overlaps with Invariant Labs' MCP-Scan and the Tool Poisoning Attacks taxonomy; extends the same idea to agent skills as a first-class surface.
threat: A hostile MCP server or skill file can inject instructions or exfiltrate secrets via tool descriptions the agent consumes as part of its system prompt. Scanning a hostile MCP config itself executes the attacker's command line to fetch those descriptions.
conditions: User installs a scanner and points it at a config referencing a hostile stdio MCP server. Scanner is run outside a sandbox, or the --dangerously-run-mcp-servers flag is used in a non-CI shell where consent is skipped.
mitigations: Run agent-component scanners inside a Docker container, VM, or disposable environment when evaluating untrusted or third-party MCP configs. Keep interactive consent enabled and review each server command and env before approving. Reserve --dangerously-run-mcp-servers for CI environments where every referenced command is already trusted. Version-pin and change-review MCP tool descriptions and skill bundles so metadata updates go through the same approval path as system-prompt changes.
verify_note: All three excerpts verified verbatim against data/_raw/snyk-agent-scan-f565968f99.txt (lines 41, 48, 98-100). Related claims exist in claims.json.

title: Omnigent meta-harness adds policy enforcement and sandboxing across coding-agent backends
summary: Omnigent is an open-source meta-harness (9,793 stars) that provides a common orchestration layer over Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Hermes, and custom agents, letting users swap or mix harnesses, run sessions in disposable cloud sandboxes (Modal, Daytona, E2B, CoreWeave, Kubernetes, and others), and enforce policies — approval gates for risky actions, spend caps, and tool restrictions — scoped to the whole server, a single agent, or one chat.
takeaway: The rapid adoption of a meta-harness abstraction layer (9.8k stars in roughly six months) signals that teams increasingly want harness-agnostic policy and sandboxing enforcement rather than trusting each individual coding agent's own built-in safety features — governance is being pulled into a separate orchestration layer above the agent itself.

lessons.point: Omnigent lets users enforce policies (approval gates, spend caps, tool restrictions) at three different scopes — the entire server, a single agent, or a single chat — rather than requiring policy to be configured per-underlying-harness.
lessons.excerpt:
to pause for your approval
  before risky actions, cap spend, or limit which tools an agent reaches.
  They apply to the whole server, one agent, or a single chat.

lessons.point: The project lets users mix multiple different coding-agent harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Hermes, Pi, custom YAML-defined agents) together in the same session, including having one agent review another's work.
lessons.excerpt:
Mix Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode,
  Hermes, Pi, and custom agents (defined in YAML) together in the same
  session. Ask one agent to review another's work, or split a task across
  agents that are each good at different things.

actionable.title: Evaluate a meta-harness policy layer instead of relying on each agent tool's built-in guardrails
