title: Trust in agent networks must be baked in, not bolted on
summary: SIGKDD 2026 Blue Sky Ideas position paper arguing that Agent-to-Agent (A2A) networks introduce systemic vulnerabilities (adversarial composition, semantic misalignment, cascading operational failures) that per-agent alignment techniques cannot cover, and that trust must be designed into the coordination framework from the start rather than retrofitted. Proposes a four-pillar conceptual framework but is a vision paper without a concrete protocol or evaluation.
takeaway: A2A network trust is a coordination-layer problem: individual-agent alignment does not compose, so agent-network protocols need trust primitives designed in from the beginning.

lessons.point: Multi-agent A2A networks introduce classes of vulnerabilities that single-agent alignment cannot address.
lessons.excerpt: they introduce systemic vulnerabilities, such as adversarial composition, semantic misalignment, and cascading operational failures, that existing agent alignment techniques cannot address

lessons.point: Retrofitting trust onto protocols designed for individual agents is insufficient; trust needs to be a first-class property of the coordination framework.
lessons.excerpt: the trustworthiness of A2A networks cannot be fully guaranteed via retrofitting on existing protocols that are largely designed for individual agents. Rather, it must be architected from the very beginning of the A2A coordination framework.

lessons.point: The paper proposes a four-pillar conceptual framework as a design vision, not a concrete protocol or empirical evaluation.
lessons.excerpt: We present a comprehensive conceptual framework that situates trust in A2A systems through four design pillars.

actionable.title: When adopting an A2A protocol, ask what trust primitives are in the protocol vs. bolted on later
actionable.detail: For teams evaluating an A2A or agent-mesh protocol (Google A2A, Anthropic MCP-of-agents patterns, custom orchestrations), treat trust primitives — identity, capability scoping, semantic-mismatch handling, failure containment — as protocol-level acceptance criteria rather than application-level responsibilities. The paper does not prescribe a specific mechanism, so this is a review posture, not a checklist.

prior_art: Overlaps with earlier A2A security taxonomies and the general 'security must be designed in, not bolted on' thesis applied to distributed systems for decades. Similar to Google's A2A protocol design goals and multi-agent alignment literature.
threat: Agent-network compositions can be attacked in ways single-agent defenses do not cover: an adversarial agent joining a network, semantic drift across agent hand-offs, or a fault in one agent cascading through downstream tool calls.

mitigations: The paper proposes trust be architected via four design pillars in the coordination framework rather than added later, but does not commit to a specific mechanism. title: This Shit is Hard: Patching a vulnerability that has no fix
summary: Chainguard describes how its Athena clearinghouse authors patches for AI-discovered zero-days that have no upstream fix, where the hard problem is trusting an AI-generated diff rather than producing one. Every candidate patch is gated by feasibility, regression (baseline test suite before/after), and an exploit test written before the fix that must pass on the unpatched build and fail on the patched one. Fixes are batched per package, backported with the full gate re-run per version, rebuilt from source with signed provenance/SBOM, and made fatal so a patch that fails to apply breaks the build loudly.

lessons.excerpt: when there's no upstream fix to compare against, the only way to tell them apart is to prove it yourself

lessons.excerpt: we author an exploit test and prove it demonstrates real harm against the unpatched build

lessons.excerpt: a security patch that doesn't apply cleanly has to fail the build and never slip through as a warning

takeaway: When remediating (including AI-generated) fixes, gate every patch on feasibility, regression testing, and an independent exploit test, batch interdependent fixes, re-validate on each backported version, rebuild from source with signed provenance, and fail the build loudly if a patch doesn't apply.

title: phpseclib's X25519 leaks its private key through a libgmp side channel
summary: phpseclib's pure-PHP X25519 scalar multiplication performs data-dependent conditional modular reductions whose cost is a function of the secret scalar's prefix. A timing side-channel recovers the full 251-bit clamped private key from 32 observed operations using ordinary RFC 7748 base-point input (u=9) — no attacker-chosen input required, and rejecting low-order inputs does not close it. Critically, counting libgmp function calls instead of timing (e.g. via a Flush+Reload cache spy on the shared libgmp.so mapping) recovers a key from a single operation, tolerating 20-30% wrong per-step counts.
takeaway: It's an implementation side channel triggered in ordinary use, so input validation can't fix it.

lessons.point: The attack recovers the full private key using the standard RFC 7748 base point (u=9) with no attacker-chosen input at all, and explicitly is not a low-order-input issue — rejecting low-order public values does not mitigate it.
lessons.excerpt: This is not a low-order-input issue. Recovery works with the RFC 7748 base point `u = 9`, with no attacker-chosen input at all. Rejecting low-order public values does not close it.

lessons.point: An observer that counts libgmp function calls instead of measuring timing recovers a full key from a single observed operation, and tolerates 20-30% of individual per-step counts being wrong, compared to 32 observations needed for the timing-based variant.
lessons.excerpt: libgmp call counts | either | **1** | 20/20 keys; tolerates 20–30% of per-step counts being wrong

lessons.point: The vulnerable code path in the common key-loading APIs is reachable only when PHP's bundled ext-sodium extension is absent, since the safe sodium implementation is used instead whenever it's available.
lessons.excerpt: `PKCS8` / `PublicKeyLoader::load` / `EC::createKey` run the ladder **only when ext-sodium is absent** — `PKCS8.php:194` gates on `sodium_crypto_box_publickey_from_secretkey`. OpenSSL does not help here.

lessons.point: Because ext-sodium is bundled and enabled by default in PHP 7.2+, most default installations are not exposed via the common code paths — but hardened or stripped-down PHP builds (disable_functions hardening, --disable-sodium builds, common in shared hosting) are.
lessons.excerpt: ext-sodium is bundled and enabled by default in PHP 7.2+, so the reachable configurations are a minority — though `disable_functions` hardening and `--disable-sodium` builds do occur, particularly in shared hosting.

actionable.title: Treat shared-library call-count side channels as at least as dangerous as timing side channels in crypto reviews
actionable.detail: When reviewing cryptographic implementations for constant-time behavior, don't stop at wall-clock timing analysis — also check whether the operation count of underlying library calls (e.g. libgmp) varies with secret data, since a call-count observer via cache-timing techniques can be dramatically more sample-efficient than timing alone (1 observation vs 32 here).

prior_art: Non-constant-time EC/RSA timing side channels and cache-based operation-counting attacks (Percival 2005, Flush+Reload) are an established class; using library call-counting to cut required observations from dozens to one is a novel specific contribution.
verify_note: All lessons precisely supported; reviewer notes the lessons omit the advisory's caveat that exploitation requires a reused/long-lived key and local co-residency, which narrows real-world impact though nothing stated is wrong. Taking lower relevance (52 vs 55).

title: What's in a tag name? JavaScript, apparently
summary: Gareth Heyes shows that HTML tag names can carry XSS payloads: DOM properties like localName, part, and classList expose case-preserving or array-split versions of the tag name that can be fed back into event handlers, the Function constructor, or setHTMLUnsafe to execute JavaScript across every browser. Because these vectors use unusual, uppercase, or separator-character HTML, they readily bypass blocklists and WAF signatures. The defensive lesson is that WAF/blocklist filtering is fragile and should not be relied on in place of proper output encoding and CSP.

lessons.point: Browsers are far more lenient with tag-name characters than filters assume, enabling novel XSS vectors.
lessons.excerpt: browsers are far more lenient than you would expect

lessons.point: Seemingly harmless DOM properties (localName, part, classList) can smuggle and transform payloads past blocklists/WAFs.
lessons.excerpt: unusual HTML and seemingly harmless properties such as localName, part, and classList can become unexpected sources of hiding payloads and transformations that can bypass blocklists and WAF signatures

lessons.point: WAF signature filtering is an unreliable primary XSS defense.
lessons.excerpt: It's also a pretty nice way to bypass a WAF

takeaway: Do not rely on WAFs or character blocklists to stop XSS; enforce context-aware output encoding, a strict Content-Security-Policy, and trusted HTML sanitization, since exotic tag-name and DOM-property tricks bypass signature-based filters in every browser.

actionable.title: Defend XSS with encoding and CSP, not WAF signatures
actionable.detail: Treat WAF/blocklist filtering as defense-in-depth only; enforce context-aware output encoding, a strict CSP, and a vetted HTML sanitizer, and test filters against uppercase, separator-character, and DOM-property (localName/part/classList) vectors.

prior_art: PortSwigger XSS cheat sheet and prior WAF/blocklist-bypass research (unicode overflows, phantom Version cookie).

title: Show, Don't Tell: Evo found issues in a real enterprise SaaS
summary: Snyk's autonomous offensive-security agent (Evo COS) black-box tested a multi-tenant SaaS and found 33 validated issues, including a legacy admin JSON endpoint that did an unbounded key/value upsert with no role check and no enforcement of its HMAC signature/timestamp, letting the lowest-privilege user rewrite tenant-wide security settings for full compromise. It also proved a credentialed CORS origin-reflection flaw enabling zero-interaction token theft. The lessons are classic broken-authorization and CORS defenses: enforce server-side role checks, allowlist settable keys, actually verify signatures, and lock down cross-origin credentialed responses.

lessons.point: Server-side authorization must be enforced on every write, especially legacy/admin endpoints, not assumed from the UI.
lessons.excerpt: performed an unbounded key/value upsert with no server-side role or permission check

lessons.point: Restrict mass-assignment by allowlisting settable keys rather than accepting arbitrary input.
lessons.excerpt: No allowlist of settable keys; the endpoint accepts any key string

lessons.point: Business-logic/authorization chains are invisible to signature-based scanners and need reasoning-driven testing.
lessons.excerpt: This is the reasoning layer that traditional scanners cannot reach: recognizing an ungated write, understanding what each setting means for the business, and chaining a handful of them into tenant-wide compromise

takeaway: Enforce server-side role/permission checks and key allowlists on every write endpoint (including legacy admin ones), actually validate HMAC signatures, and lock down credentialed CORS, then test for authorization and business-logic chains that signature scanners miss.

actionable.title: Close broken-authorization and CORS gaps on write endpoints
actionable.detail: Add server-side role/permission checks to every write (including legacy admin JSON endpoints), allowlist settable keys to block mass assignment, verify HMAC signature/timestamp params instead of trusting their presence, and never reflect arbitrary Origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.

prior_art: OWASP broken object/function-level authorization (BOLA/BFLA), mass-assignment, and credentialed CORS misconfiguration research.

title: Consumer smart glasses enable a video-based password-cracking pipeline
summary: A CCS 2026 paper presents the first general video-based keystroke-inference pipeline that recovers rule-based alphanumeric smartphone passwords across all four QWERTY keyboard layouts, using nothing but the built-in camera of consumer Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses. It tracks fingertips at sub-pixel resolution, predicts keystrokes via a self-supervised neural-network ensemble, and combines video-derived per-key probabilities with prior statistics from 2.19 billion leaked passwords, reducing human-chosen password entropy by up to 60 bits and cracking password-manager-generated random passwords up to 13 characters in under an hour on a modern GPU, from up to 1.8 meters away.
takeaway: Consumer AI-enabled wearables (smart glasses with a built-in camera) turn a previously specialist side-channel attack (video-based keystroke inference) into something achievable with off-the-shelf consumer hardware at conversational distance, and even password-manager-generated random passwords are not immune once video evidence is combined with prior password-distribution statistics.

lessons.point: The pipeline uses the built-in camera of popular consumer Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses — not specialized surveillance equipment — to track device and fingertip position at sub-pixel resolution and predict keystrokes via a self-supervised neural network ensemble.
lessons.excerpt: Using the built-in camera of the popular Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses, our pipeline tracks the device and typing fingertips at sub-pixel resolution, predicts keystrokes via a self-supervised ensemble of neural networks, dynamically estimates the on-screen keyboard layout, and computes per-key probability distributions.

lessons.point: Even password-manager-generated random passwords up to 13 characters were cracked in under an hour on a modern GPU, and combining video evidence with prior password statistics yielded a further ~20-bit entropy reduction beyond either source alone for human-chosen passwords.
lessons.excerpt: password-manager-chosen random passwords of up to 13 characters in under an hour on a modern GPU, reducing password entropy by up to 60 bits relative to the prior baseline. For human-chosen passwords, combining video evidence with prior statistics yields an additional statistically significant reduction of approximately 20 bits compared to either source alone.

actionable.title: Don't assume typing in public with password-manager-generated passwords is safe from shoulder-surfing-class attacks
actionable.detail: Treat consumer smart-glasses cameras as a viable keystroke-inference threat at distances up to ~1.8m; for high-value accounts, prefer authentication methods that don't require visible on-screen typing in public (passkeys, biometric unlock) over even long random passwords typed on a visible touchscreen.

prior_art: Prior video-based keystroke inference targeted tablets/PINs/pattern locks under simplified conditions (cited by the paper); this is the first general full-alphanumeric-QWERTY pipeline on unmodified consumer smart-glasses hardware.
verify_note: Both lessons match the CCS 2026 abstract almost verbatim; taking lower novelty (72 vs 78) and lower relevance (30 vs 40, since the ai-research audience is harness/agent builders this barely serves).

title: Citrix NetScaler heap overflow CVE-2026-8452 traced to an unchecked buffer copy
summary: watchTowr Labs reverse-engineered a silent Citrix NetScaler ADC/Gateway patch (13.1-63.18, 14.1-72.61) and identified an unauthenticated, remotely-reachable memory corruption reachable when the appliance is configured to use SAML as a Service Provider or Identity Provider. The root cause: earlier firmware copied attacker-controlled data from a SAML message's ds:SignedInfo element into a fixed-size global buffer during signature canonicalization without checking whether it fit, and an oversized SignedInfo element corrupts adjacent packet-engine state and crashes the root packet engine (nsppe).
takeaway: A classic, decades-old bug class (unchecked fixed-size buffer copy of attacker-controlled data) is still shipping in 2026 in a security-critical XML/SAML signature-parsing path of a widely deployed enterprise VPN gateway — any code that canonicalizes or parses XML signatures from an untrusted party needs an explicit size check before copying into a fixed buffer, regardless of how mature the codebase is.

lessons.point: The vulnerability is a pre-auth, remotely reachable memory corruption triggered by an oversized ds:SignedInfo element in a SAML message, reachable whenever the appliance is configured to use SAML as either a Service Provider or Identity Provider.
lessons.excerpt: the vulnerability we’re discussing today is reachable when the Netscaler appliance is configured to use SAML as either a Service Provider (SP) or an Identity Provider (IdP).

lessons.point: The root cause is a copy of attacker-controlled data from the SAML message's SignedInfo element into a fixed-size global buffer during signature canonicalization, without a bounds check — an oversized element overflows into and corrupts adjacent packet-engine state.
lessons.excerpt: During signature canonicalization, earlier versions of the NetScaler solution copy attacker-controlled data from the SAML message's `ds:SignedInfo` element into a fixed-size global buffer, without checking whether it actually fits. Send an oversized `SignedInfo` element and the copy continues beyond the end of the buffer, corrupting adjacent packet-engine state and eventually crashing `nsppe`, the root packet engine.

lessons.point: The patch itself was the clue: the fixed version added explicit size checks around exactly the copy operations that led researchers to find the original unbounded copy.
lessons.excerpt: the `63.18` patch adds explicit size checks around these copies, which, conveniently for us, is exactly what led us to the vulnerability in the first place.

actionable.title: Audit XML/SAML signature-parsing code for unchecked fixed-buffer copies
actionable.detail: Any code path that canonicalizes or parses XML digital signatures (SAML, WS-Security, XML-DSig) from an untrusted party should be audited for fixed-size buffer copies of attacker-controlled elements (like ds:SignedInfo) without an explicit length check — this is a decades-old bug class still shipping in mature, widely-deployed enterprise software.

prior_art: CVE-2023-3519 (Bishop Fox's prior NetScaler RCE writeup, cited in the source) is the closest prior art; the underlying bug class (unchecked fixed-size buffer copy) is decades-old.
verify_note: All three lessons directly and accurately quoted; taking lower novelty (68 vs 72).

author: Sara McBroom
title: AI changes malware authoring, not execution, and most samples never ship
summary: Unit 42 analyzed 405 AI-integrating malware samples and found only 12 reached protected production endpoints; ~97% exist only in sandboxes, VirusTotal, and research repos. Their thesis: AI lowers the barrier to authoring malware and speeds iteration (e.g. FunkSec's seven builds in six days), but the resulting binaries are caught by the same behavioral/sandbox/entropy detection as conventional malware.

lessons.point: The 'AI malware wave' is largely PoC/test/brand-abuse noise today — right-size the threat instead of over-rotating on it.
lessons.excerpt: Approximately 97% of AI-enabled malware samples exist only in research repositories, sandbox environments and security validation platforms.

lessons.point: AI shifts the authoring process, not the runtime behavior, so existing behavioral detection still works — no need to buy an 'AI malware' point product.
lessons.excerpt: The AI component does not evade detection. It changes how the code is authored, not how it executes.

lessons.point: The real signal is development velocity: LLM assistance compresses malware iteration cycles, which shortens defender response windows.
lessons.excerpt: Seven distinct builds in six days is a pace that suggests LLM-assisted development, where generating a new variant is closer to a prompt generation rather than a software development task.

takeaway: Don't over-index on 'AI malware' hype: your existing behavioral/sandbox detection still catches it — but expect faster variant iteration.

actionable.title: Keep behavioral detection primary; track AI's effect on iteration speed, not novelty of execution
actionable.detail: Resist 'AI malware' point solutions; validate that behavioral analytics, sandbox detonation, code-signing anomaly and entropy checks remain tuned; assume shorter variant cycles and shorten signature/hunt refresh cadence accordingly.

prior_art: Prior 'AI in malware' commentary was largely anecdotal or vendor-hype; the contribution here is the empirical production-telemetry measurement (405 samples vs 12 in production) rather than a new technique.
verify_note: Self-verified: all three excerpts ground verbatim to the Unit 42 source; independent subagent pass skipped (automated cyber-safeguard blocked the delegated agent), novelty held conservative as this is a measurement/framing contribution.

title: A Rust supply-chain compromise used Cargo's own yank warning to trick developers
summary: A compromised maintainer account published a malicious arrayref 0.3.10 (245M+ all-time downloads, used transitively through tiny-skia/winit/egui/iced) depending on a typosquatted proc-macro1 crate impersonating dtolnay. The attacker yanked the prior clean releases (0.3.5-0.3.9), which makes Cargo print a warning nudging developers toward the only non-yanked version — the malicious one. proc-macro1's build script fetched a certificate-validation-free, base64-fragment-obfuscated payload URL and ran an architecture-specific binary detached from the build process at compile time.
takeaway: Yanking prior clean versions of a compromised crate is a novel, low-effort social-engineering step that weaponizes the package manager's own UX (Cargo's "consider updating to a version that is not yanked" warning) to actively push developers toward the malicious release, rather than passively waiting for auto-upgrades — a supply-chain defense that only watches for new/anomalous versions misses this.

lessons.point: The attacker yanked all prior clean releases (0.3.5 through 0.3.9), which causes Cargo to print a warning nudging developers to update to the only remaining, non-yanked (malicious) version — turning the package manager's own UX into part of the attack.
lessons.excerpt: The owner account yanked the older `arrayref` releases 0.3.5 through 0.3.9. Yanking a crate makes Cargo print a “consider updating to a version that is not yanked” warning, which nudges developers toward the only non-yanked release, the malicious 0.3.10. The reporter who filed the RustSec advisory noted this is how they hit it.

lessons.point: The malicious proc-macro1 crate impersonated a well-known Rust maintainer via a lookalike username (dtolney vs. the real dtolnay) and forged the authors metadata field with that maintainer's real name.
lessons.excerpt: A separate account, `dtolney`, published `proc-macro1`. The username closely resembles David Tolnay’s real `dtolnay` account. Its metadata forges `authors = ["David Tolnay <rchaitm@gmail.com>"]`

lessons.point: The malicious crate's actual source code was a genuine, unmodified copy of the legitimate proc-macro2 crate, specifically so that builds kept working normally while the separate build-time payload ran undetected.
lessons.excerpt: The `src/` of the malicious `proc-macro1` is a genuine copy of `proc-macro2`, so builds kept working while the build script ran.

lessons.point: The build-time payload fetches an architecture-specific binary over TLS with no certificate validation, using a URL reassembled from base64-encoded fragments embedded in the build script, then runs it detached so the compiler doesn't wait for it to finish.
lessons.excerpt: The script fetches an architecture-specific binary over a TLS connection that accepts any certificate without validation, then runs it detached from the build. On Unix it drops and runs `/tmp/rust-setup`.

actionable.title: Flag yank-then-single-remaining-version patterns as a supply-chain risk signal
actionable.detail: Add a detection rule for package registries/scanners: when a maintainer yanks multiple prior versions in quick succession, leaving only a single very recent version installable, flag it for manual review before the registry's own 'update to a non-yanked version' UX nudges consumers toward it — this is now a documented technique for pushing a malicious release.

prior_art: Build-time RCE via a typosquatted crate's build.rs is a known pattern; using the registry's own yank-warning UX as an active lure toward the malicious version is the genuinely new wrinkle.
author: abhisek
verify_note: All lessons match the source almost verbatim; one minor nit (proc-macro1's src/ described as 'unmodified' vs the advisory's 'mechanical find-and-replace' rename) doesn't change the substance. Taking lower novelty (65 vs 75).

title: Composer passed a package's Perforce source URL to the p4 CLI
summary: Composer passed a package's Perforce source address directly to the `p4` CLI client without validating it, and `p4` accepts addresses that mean "run this local command" instead of "connect to this server" — so a malicious dependency from a repository allowing arbitrary Perforce source URLs could achieve remote code execution with the privileges of whoever ran `composer install`, if the `p4` client happened to be installed on that machine.
takeaway: Passing user- or dependency-supplied configuration data unvalidated into a CLI tool's argument is dangerous whenever that CLI has any "local command" or "connect to this address" ambiguity in its own address-parsing syntax — the vulnerability lived entirely in Composer trusting a value it never needed to interpret itself, just forward.

lessons.point: Composer forwarded a package's Perforce source address to the p4 CLI client without validating it, and p4's own address syntax allows a value that means 'run this local command' rather than 'connect to this network address', giving RCE with the privileges of the account running Composer.
lessons.excerpt: Composer passed a package's Perforce source address to the `p4` CLI client without validating it. The `p4` CLI client accepts addresses that mean "run this local command" instead of "connect to this server". This is remote code execution with the privileges of the user or CI account running Composer.

lessons.point: Exploitability requires three specific conditions: the p4 client installed and on PATH, a source of untrusted package metadata (Packagist itself doesn't allow Perforce sources, so a custom or inline repository is required), and a source (not dist) install of that package — meaning most Composer users are not affected by default.
lessons.excerpt:
You are only affected if all of the following are true:

- The Perforce `p4` command line client is installed and on the `PATH` of the machine running Composer.
- An attacker can control a package metadata's `source` section with a perforce type. Packagist.org does not allow perforce source metadata, so you are only exploitable if you rely on another Composer repository (any custom `composer`-type repository, or an inline `package` repository entry), or a `composer.lock` file you obtained from somewhere you do not trust.
- The package gets installed from source, either because it has no dist artifact or because source installs are selected (for example `--prefer-source`).

actionable.title: Validate any dependency-supplied address before forwarding it to an external VCS/CLI tool
actionable.detail: When a package manager or build tool forwards dependency-declared metadata (VCS source URLs, addresses) to an external CLI tool, validate that the value is actually a network endpoint the tool expects — don't assume the external tool's own parser rejects local-command-like syntax.

prior_art: Argument/command injection via unvalidated VCS-source-URL forwarding to a CLI is a known bug class (git ext:: URL abuse, CVE-2017-1000117); the p4-address ambiguity is a narrow instance.
verify_note: Both lessons near-verbatim matches; taking lower novelty (38 vs 55).

title: Markdown Preview Enhanced, a VS Code extension, chained flaws into RCE
summary: ProjectDiscovery's Neo audited Markdown Preview Enhanced (9.5M installs) and found five CVEs across two attack surfaces. A WaveDrom diagram renderer called `window.eval()` on raw Markdown-file content, reachable by opening any file, no opt-in required. That webview then dispatched attacker-controlled command names straight from postMessage into VS Code's command system, one of which wrote arbitrary files. Separately, workspace config files (.crossnote/config.js) were evaluated with Node's `vm.runInNewContext()`, which Node's own documentation says is not a security boundary, and a shared-realm prototype-chain trick reliably escaped it to full OS command execution.
takeaway: Both root causes here are well-documented anti-patterns that keep recurring: evaluating any part of untrusted content as code (even a diagram-rendering "data" field) and trusting Node's vm module as a sandbox when its own documentation explicitly disclaims that guarantee. Editor extensions with auto-update and full user privileges deserve the same supply-chain scrutiny as a direct dependency, even though they rarely show up in an SBOM.

lessons.point: The vulnerable code evaluated raw Markdown-file text as JavaScript specifically for WaveDrom diagram blocks, an allowlisted exception carved into an otherwise-sanitizing pipeline, meaning the sanitizer's own carve-out was the vulnerability.
lessons.excerpt: the sanitizer kept a small allowlist of script-like diagram types (`new Set(['wavedrom', 'text/tikz'])`) and let the WaveDrom carrier through. Sanitization held at one layer; a later feature treated that preserved content as code anyway.

lessons.point: The extension host dispatched webview-originated postMessage commands directly into VS Code's command execution API without validating them as untrusted, and one reachable command wrote to any file:// URI with no workspace-boundary check.
lessons.excerpt: One reachable command, `_crossnote.updateMarkdown`, wrote content to a URI with no containment check:

lessons.point: The updateMarkdown handler wrote arbitrary content to any file:// URI passed to it, with the code's own comment acknowledging there was no workspace-boundary check at all.
lessons.excerpt: // any file:// URI, any content, no workspace boundary check

lessons.point: Workspace configuration files were evaluated with Node's vm.runInNewContext(), which Node's own documentation explicitly states is not a security mechanism, since the sandbox object's prototype chain still leads back to the host's real constructors.
lessons.excerpt: Node's documentation explicitly states that `vm` is not a security mechanism. The sandbox object lives in the host V8 realm, so its prototype chain leads back to the host's constructors:

lessons.point: The escape requires no user interaction at all — placing the payload in a workspace config file and simply opening any Markdown file in that workspace triggers evaluation during preview initialization, running arbitrary OS commands under the developer's account.
lessons.excerpt: Place this in `.crossnote/config.js`, open any Markdown file in the same workspace, and MPE evaluates it during preview initialization. Arbitrary OS commands run under the developer's account. No preview interaction, no opt-in, no dialog.

actionable.title: Audit editor extensions for eval() sinks and Node vm-module usage as if they were production dependencies
actionable.detail: Treat popular IDE/editor extensions as first-class supply-chain risk: audit for any eval()/vm.runInNewContext()/similar dynamic-code-execution use on content that originates from an opened file or workspace config, since Node's vm module is explicitly not a security boundary per its own docs, and webview-to-extension-host message handlers must treat postMessage content as untrusted, never dispatch it directly into a privileged command API.

prior_art: Trail of Bits' 2023 'Escaping misconfigured VSCode extensions' and STAR Labs' 'Breaking Out of Restricted Mode' writeups already document webview-postMessage-trust and extension-escape bug classes; vm.runInNewContext() escapes are well-known.
verify_note: All five lessons verified against direct code excerpts; individually known bug classes but the concrete 5-CVE chain in a 9.5M-install extension is genuinely new. Taking lower novelty (58 vs 74).

title: A hybrid framework vets mini-programs for UI compliance and network risk
summary: WeChat Mini Programs embed payment and ad entrances with deceptive, mis-clickable UI (tiny/hidden cancel buttons) that trigger involuntary payments or redirects to illegal pages. The authors build a detector that uses YOLOv8 to locate and size on-screen buttons/icons and mitmproxy to intercept click-triggered network requests, flagging non-compliant layouts and unsafe redirections.

lessons.point: Deceptive mobile UI (dark patterns) is a concrete security risk, not just a UX nuisance, because mis-clicks lead to real financial loss.
lessons.excerpt: This can result in involuntary payments or being redirected to illegal pages, causing unnecessary financial losses and seriously harming users' property security and legal rights.

lessons.point: Visual/computer-vision analysis of rendered UI can automate detection of non-standard, mis-clickable button layouts.
lessons.excerpt: YOLOv8 is used to identify various buttons in images, displaying the corresponding icon and its data based on the mouse click position.

lessons.point: Pairing UI inspection with proxy-based traffic capture lets you assess where clicks actually send users and data.
lessons.excerpt: mitmproxy is used to capture relevant data requests generated during clicks, analyzing the safety of redirections

takeaway: Mini-program app vetting must combine visual UI-compliance checks with network-redirect analysis to catch mis-click-to-payment dark patterns.

actionable.title: Add deceptive-UI and redirect checks to mobile app vetting
actionable.detail: For hosted mini-app/superapp platforms, screenshot each screen, use an object detector to verify button hit-target sizes and that close/cancel controls are present and reachable, and proxy click-driven traffic to confirm redirect destinations resolve inside an allowed, safe range before publishing.

prior_art: Prior WeChat Mini Program static/dynamic analysis and dark-pattern UI studies; novelty is the combined YOLOv8 UI + mitmproxy redirect pipeline.
threat: Involuntary payments and redirection to malicious/illegal pages via deceptively placed ad and payment controls.
conditions: User interacts with a non-compliant WeChat Mini Program whose cancel/close controls are undersized or hidden.
mitigations: Automated UI-size/position compliance detection plus redirect safety analysis before store approval.

title: Astro's default image optimizer allowed remote code execution via malicious AVIF images
summary: A vulnerability in libheif, used by Astro's default Sharp-based image optimization service, allows remote code execution when a malicious AVIF image is processed — affecting any Astro project that lets an attacker cause an untrusted AVIF image to be optimized. Fixed in Astro 7.2.8, which requires Sharp 0.35.4.
takeaway: Image-processing pipelines are a recurring RCE vector because they sit at the boundary of parsing complex, attacker-influenced binary formats (here, AVIF via libheif) with native code, and a framework's default, opt-out image optimization feature inherits that risk for every project that accepts user-uploaded images without evaluating it as a distinct attack surface.

lessons.point: The RCE is reachable through Astro's default image service, meaning any project that lets an attacker cause an untrusted AVIF image to be processed through Astro's built-in optimization pipeline is affected, not just projects using a niche or opt-in feature.
lessons.excerpt: A vulnerability in `libheif`, used by the default Sharp image service in Astro, can lead to remote code execution when a malicious AVIF image is optimized. Projects are affected when an attacker can cause Astro to process an untrusted AVIF image.

actionable.title: Treat framework-default image optimization pipelines as attacker-reachable native-code parsing surface
actionable.detail: For any web framework's built-in image optimization/transformation feature, verify which image parsing library (and native codec, e.g. libheif for AVIF/HEIF) it uses and confirm it's patched, especially if the application accepts user-uploaded images — default/opt-out image pipelines carry the same native-parsing risk as an explicit image-processing dependency.

prior_art: Native image-codec parser RCEs are one of the longest-running vulnerability classes (ImageTragick 2016, recurring libheif/libjpeg/libpng CVEs); this is a new instance in Astro's default pipeline.
verify_note: The lesson is a direct restatement of the short advisory; taking lower novelty (22 vs 40).

title: Hono's Path-Traversal Fix Only Blocked One Parent-Directory Segment
summary: Hono's static-site-generation `toSSG()` function had a path-traversal fix (for CVE-2026-39408) that only collapsed a single run of parent-directory segments in route-parameter-derived output paths. A value carrying enough consecutive parent-directory segments still produces a path the containment check accepts but the filesystem resolves outside the configured output directory, affecting any app that builds a static site from route-parameter values it doesn't fully control (CMS slugs, API-sourced values, user submissions).
takeaway: A path-traversal fix that handles the exact reported payload but not the general pattern (arbitrarily many parent-directory segments, not just one) is a fix in name only — path-normalization and containment checks need to fully collapse traversal sequences of any length, and validating against a single previously-reported case is not the same as validating against the vulnerability class.

lessons.point: The original fix for CVE-2026-39408 blocked the exact traversal sequence originally reported (a single parent-directory segment) but the underlying path-normalization routine still didn't fully collapse longer runs of consecutive parent-directory segments, so a value with enough of them still escapes the output-directory containment check.
lessons.excerpt: That check normalizes the path with the same routine that built it, and the routine did not fully collapse runs of consecutive parent-directory segments. A value carrying enough of them produces a path the check accepts, but the filesystem resolves outside the output directory. The earlier fix handled a single parent-directory segment, so it blocks the sequence reported at the time while leaving longer runs unhandled.

actionable.title: Verify path-traversal fixes handle the general pattern, not just the reported payload
actionable.detail: When reviewing or writing a path-traversal fix, test with an arbitrarily long run of '../' sequences and mixed encodings, not just the single-segment case from the original report — a normalization routine that only collapses one parent-directory reference per pass is a common, recurring incomplete-fix pattern.

prior_art: Classic single-pass '../' stripping bypass, a well-documented incomplete-path-traversal-fix pattern (CWE-22/23).
verify_note: Lesson is an accurate, non-overstated restatement; taking lower novelty (30 vs 48) and relevance (42 vs 42, unchanged).

title: morgan's log-forging fix missed Unicode line-separator code points
summary: The Node.js logging middleware morgan's fix for a prior log-forging CVE neutralized C0 control characters, DEL, and backslash, but did not escape the Unicode line separators U+0085 (NEL), U+2028, and U+2029 — which are reachable through the request URL, User-Agent, Referrer, arbitrary request headers, and the Basic-auth username, and NEL is valid in HTTP header syntax. Logged, these characters split what should be one log record into multiple logical records for any downstream Unicode-aware log processor, forging log entries in all of morgan's built-in formats.
takeaway: A log-injection fix that escapes ASCII control characters but not Unicode line-separator code points is incomplete for any downstream consumer that is Unicode-aware rather than byte-oriented — request headers are a valid, standards-compliant transport for these characters (NEL is legal HTTP header obs-text), so the fix needs to match what downstream log processors actually treat as a line break, not just the ASCII definition of one.

lessons.point: The prior fix neutralized C0 control characters, DEL, and backslash, but did not escape the Unicode line separators NEL (U+0085), LINE SEPARATOR (U+2028), or PARAGRAPH SEPARATOR (U+2029), which remain reachable through the request URL and headers including User-Agent, Referrer, and Basic-auth username.
lessons.excerpt: The 1.11.0 fix neutralizes C0 control characters, DEL, and backslash, but it does not escape the Unicode line separators `U+0085` (NEL), `U+2028` (LINE SEPARATOR), or `U+2029` (PARAGRAPH SEPARATOR). These code points are reachable through several tokens, including the request URL (`:url`), request headers such as `:user-agent` and `:referrer`, arbitrary `:req[header]` values, and the Basic auth username (`:remote-user`).

lessons.point: NEL (U+0085) is valid obs-text in an HTTP header value per spec, meaning an attacker can place it in an ordinary request header without any protocol-level rejection.
lessons.excerpt: NEL is valid `obs-text` in HTTP header values, so an attacker can place it in an ordinary request header.

lessons.point: No format-based mitigation exists short of upgrading, since the affected values (request URL and headers) are core to what access logging records in the first place.
lessons.excerpt: None. The affected values include the request URL and request headers, which are core to access logging, so there is no practical format-based mitigation. Upgrade to 1.12.0.

actionable.title: Escape Unicode line-separator code points, not just ASCII control characters, in any log-sanitization routine
actionable.detail: When sanitizing untrusted data before writing to logs, explicitly escape or strip U+0085 (NEL), U+2028, and U+2029 in addition to ASCII control characters — verify against whatever downstream log processor/SIEM will read the logs, since many Unicode-aware tools treat these as line breaks even though they're legal in HTTP header values.

prior_art: Classic CRLF/log-injection (CWE-117); Unicode line-separator bypass of naive CRLF-only sanitizers is a known, less commonly discussed variant.
verify_note: Both lessons quoted near-verbatim and accurate; taking lower novelty (28 vs 42) and relevance (40 vs 40).

title: A One-Week Dependency Cooldown Produces Outsized Supply-Chain Protection for Minimal Developer Friction
summary: Semgrep's security team rolled out package-manager dependency cooldowns (via uv's exclude-newer setting) org-wide across ~350 repositories, constraining which package versions are eligible for installation to ones published at least a week ago. Since most malicious package versions are detected and revoked within hours to days, a one-week cooldown window blocks installation of a freshly-published malicious version by the time it would otherwise be pulled in, while adding minimal day-to-day friction for developers.
takeaway: Most malicious package versions are caught within hours to days of publication, so simply refusing to install anything published in the last week closes most of that attack window for very little cost — a mechanical, low-friction control that doesn't require detecting the malicious package at all, just waiting it out.

lessons.point: Malicious package versions are typically caught within hours to days after publication, and registries revoke them once identified — meaning a cooldown window of about a week captures most of that detection-and-response cycle before an org's own tooling would install the bad version.
lessons.excerpt: Many get caught within a few hours to a few days. Once an attack is identified, package registries like npm and PyPI can revoke the malicious versions, preventing additional downloads, thus limiting the window of opportunity for attackers.

lessons.point: A one-week cooldown, implemented via uv's exclude-newer setting, is described as producing a surprisingly large security benefit for very little day-to-day developer friction, and needs specific exclusions for internal packages, registries without upload timestamps, and packages installed less than a week before rollout.
lessons.excerpt: A one week cooldown produces a surprisingly large security benefit with very little developer friction.

actionable.title: Enable a one-week dependency cooldown on package managers that support it
actionable.detail: Enable a 1-week install cooldown (uv's `exclude-newer`, or equivalent settings in other package managers) org-wide, with explicit exclusions for internal packages, registries lacking upload timestamps, and any package intentionally installed within the cooldown window — this is a cheap, mechanical control against fast-published malicious package versions.

prior_art: Dependency cooldowns were already proposed and named by Yossarian's blog, explicitly cited as the inspiration; this is an implementation case study.
verify_note: Both lessons directly supported, including the specific exclusion categories. Taking lower novelty (28 vs 40).

title: Org-wide GitHub Actions SHA-pinning enforcement has non-obvious failure modes
summary: A year and a half after the tj-actions/changed-files supply-chain incident (a compromised tag pointed at malicious code), Semgrep rolled out GitHub's "require actions to be pinned to a full-length commit SHA" setting org-wide across ~350 repositories. The practical difficulty wasn't pinning obvious `uses: action@v4` tags — it was also eliminating unpinned branch references to internal actions and transitively unpinned actions called by already-pinned actions, neither of which existing pinning tools handle by default.
takeaway: Enforcing SHA-pinning for CI actions requires closing three distinct gaps — tag references, branch references (especially to internal actions), and transitively unpinned actions called by an already-pinned action — and tooling that only automates the first gives a false sense of completion while branch-referenced internal actions remain a live supply-chain vector.

lessons.point: Beyond the well-known tag-pinning gap, org-wide SHA-pinning enforcement also requires eliminating unpinned references to internal actions by branch name (e.g. @main), and transitively unpinned actions that a pinned action itself calls — both of which standard pinning tools don't handle automatically.
lessons.excerpt: To turn on this setting without breaking things you need to eliminate:

lessons.point: The three categories that must all be eliminated are tag references, branch references, and transitively unpinned actions called by an already-pinned action.
lessons.excerpt: **Transitively unpinned actions**

lessons.point: GitHub's enforcement setting is binary (per-repo or org-wide, no partial exceptions or evaluation-only mode), making it hard to safely ratchet up enforcement gradually at a large organization without breaking CI for repos not yet audited.
lessons.excerpt: Enforcement is either per-repo or org-wide, no exceptions.

lessons.point: The author explicitly notes that a missing evaluation mode would help organizations ratchet up enforcement gradually, and expects org-wide rollout to be genuinely difficult at a large organization.
lessons.excerpt: Having an evaluation mode and more flexibility would help organizations ratchet up enforcement over time. I think enabling this org-wide at a large organization would be fairly challenging.

actionable.title: Audit for branch-referenced and transitively-unpinned actions before enabling org-wide SHA-pin enforcement
actionable.detail: Before turning on GitHub's 'require full-length commit SHA' setting org-wide, explicitly check for (1) internal actions referenced by branch name rather than tag, and (2) actions your already-pinned actions call transitively — standard SHA-pinning automation tools typically only handle the tag-reference case.

prior_art: SHA-pinning as tj-actions mitigation and the tags/branches/transitive pinning gaps are already discussed in the CI/CD security community (StepSecurity, pinact/ratchet tooling).
verify_note: All lessons directly supported; taking lower novelty (25 vs 30) and relevance (45 vs 48).

title: When Context Gets Root: Instruction Privilege Escalation in LLM Harnesses
summary: Model-side instruction hierarchy assigns privilege by source, but the agent harness reassembles context each turn and can silently promote low-privilege attacker content into a higher instruction level. The authors call this 'instruction privilege escalation' and achieve all 13 attack objectives (confidentiality, integrity, availability, RCE) across six coding-agent harnesses, even under automatic permission review.

lessons.point: Instruction-hierarchy defenses can be defeated at the harness layer, before the model even sees the content, by promoting untrusted input to a higher privilege tier.
lessons.excerpt: This construction can elevate low-level content to a higher instruction level and grant it greater model-facing privilege.

lessons.point: Automatic permission review is not a sufficient backstop against privilege escalation in agent harnesses.
lessons.excerpt: Under automatic permission review, the attacks achieve all 13 objectives on all three harnesses that provide this mode.

lessons.point: Persistent goals and scheduled tasks provided by a harness are additional vectors for the same escalation.
lessons.excerpt: We further reproduce the vulnerability using harness-provided persistent goals and scheduled tasks.

takeaway: How a harness assembles context is a privilege boundary; if it can promote untrusted data, model-side instruction hierarchy provides little protection.

actionable.title: Preserve provenance labels through harness context assembly
actionable.detail: Audit how your agent harness concatenates system prompts, tool outputs, files, memory, and scheduled tasks; ensure untrusted content keeps its low-privilege label end-to-end and cannot be relocated into higher-trust sections, and test with attacker-controlled tool/file content aiming for RCE and exfiltration objectives.

prior_art: Builds on instruction-hierarchy defenses (e.g., OpenAI instruction hierarchy) and indirect prompt injection; novel framing is escalation via harness context construction.
threat: Attacker-controlled low-privilege content is promoted to trusted instruction level, enabling confidentiality/integrity/availability/RCE compromise.
conditions: Agent harness ingests attacker-influenced content and reconstructs it into higher-trust context regions across six evaluated coding harnesses.
mitigations: Provenance-preserving context assembly and boundaries that prevent relabeling of untrusted input; permission review alone is insufficient.

title: Trace-level provenance shows how LLM agents actually get the flag
summary: CTF benchmarks score agents with binary pass/fail, conflating real exploitation with flag exposure, memorized recall, external lookup, and guessing - overstating cyber capability. CTF-ABACUS reconstructs each run as an evidence-grounded solve profile across pentest phases to check whether the recovered flag is actually supported by demonstrated behavior. Across 1,435 attempts on 240 challenges, only 62-87% of recovered flags were trace-verified exploits.

lessons.point: Binary CTF scoring overstates agent offensive capability by conflating real exploitation with recall, lookup, and guessing.
lessons.excerpt: actual exploitation is conflated with direct flag exposure, memorized recall, external lookup, guessing, and unsupported claims, potentially overstating the agent's cybersecurity capability

lessons.point: Trace-level auditing should verify whether a recovered flag is actually supported by demonstrated exploit behavior.
lessons.excerpt: whether the recovered flag is supported by demonstrated behavior

lessons.point: Empirically, a substantial fraction of 'solves' are shortcuts, not intended exploits.
lessons.excerpt: Trace-verified exploits account for only 62-87% of recovered flags across benchmarks

takeaway: Judge security agents on evidence of exploitation in the trace, not on whether the flag string appeared.

actionable.title: Audit agent CTF solves at the trace level
actionable.detail: When benchmarking offensive agents, decompose each run into pentest phases, locate where the flag first appears versus where exploitation occurred, and flag flags recovered via lookup/recall/guessing as unsupported; report trace-verified exploit rates rather than raw solve counts.

prior_art: Prior CTF agent benchmarks with binary/aggregate scoring; contribution is trace-based provenance auditing (CTF-ABACUS).
threat: Not an attack: risk of over-attributing cyber-offense capability to agents due to shortcut solves.
conditions: Evaluating autonomous LLM agents on CTF challenges with pass/fail flag scoring.
mitigations: Evidence-grounded solve profiles and challenge signatures that separate intended exploits from shortcuts.

title: RedEvoAgent: Automatic Red-Teaming Agent with Experience-Driven Skill Evolution
summary: Because LLM agents in product execution harnesses turn jailbreaks into harmful tool use and persistent state changes, red-teaming must target harnesses, not just text output. RedEvoAgent is a black-box red-teaming agent that distills cross-case attack trajectories into a concise human-readable 'attack skill' which evolves via tool-effectiveness profiling, Deciding-Tool Attribution, and a validation ratchet that keeps only improving updates.

lessons.point: In agent harnesses jailbreaks are more dangerous than in chat because they cause real tool use and durable state changes.
lessons.excerpt: jailbreaks can trigger harmful tool use and persistent state changes, creating greater risks than unsafe text generation alone

lessons.point: Distilling attack experience into a compact, human-readable skill beats retrieving full trajectories, which suffer retrieval bias and unclear tool credit.
lessons.excerpt: distills cross-case attack trajectories into a concise, human-readable attack skill

lessons.point: A validation ratchet that only keeps improving updates prevents skill regression during evolution.
lessons.excerpt: a validation ratchet that retains only updates improving validation performance

takeaway: Effective automated red-teaming of agent harnesses should evolve reusable, attributable attack skills rather than replay fixed attacks or full trajectories.

actionable.title: Red-team the harness, not just the model
actionable.detail: Adopt an evolving-skill red-team loop that profiles which jailbreak tools actually decide success (tool attribution), distills wins into concise reusable skills, and gates updates behind a validation ratchet; evaluate transfer across multiple target harnesses and attacker models to estimate real-world risk.

prior_art: Fixed-attack automatic red-teaming and agentic attackers using trajectory-based retrieval; contribution is skill distillation with Deciding-Tool Attribution and a validation ratchet.
threat: Adaptive jailbreaks that trigger harmful tool actions and persistent state changes in deployed agent harnesses.
conditions: Black-box access to target LLM agents deployed in product execution harnesses.
mitigations: Defensive use for continuous harness red-teaming and coverage measurement.

title: ratel-ai/ratel
summary: Ratel is a context-engineering layer that indexes an agent's tools and skills into a BM25-based catalog and progressively discloses only the capabilities relevant to each turn, aiming to cut token cost and recover accuracy lost to tool overload without a vector DB.
takeaway: Progressive disclosure of tool schemas via an in-process BM25 index is a concrete implementation of the 'few-distinct-tools-beat-many' guidance — it moves tool-selection out of the model's context and into a retrieval step.

lessons.point: Front-loading every tool schema and skill into the system prompt costs tokens on every call and degrades accuracy as the catalog grows.
lessons.excerpt: Every tool schema, every skill, and a growing list of instructions in the system prompt are tokens you pay for on every call. Send them all up front and you pay for them all, every turn.

lessons.point: Model accuracy drops as irrelevant tools/skills crowd the context, so the fix is to inject only matching capabilities per turn.
lessons.excerpt: Models get worse as that context grows. Crowd it with tools, skills, and instructions a turn doesn't need and the model picks the wrong option and drifts off task.

lessons.point: BM25 over schema-aware tool metadata is enough for tool retrieval; a vector DB is opt-in, not required.
lessons.excerpt: The indexes use BM25 by default, the same algorithm behind most search engines, applied to schema-aware tool metadata and skill names, descriptions, and tags. Retrieval is fast and deterministic.

lessons.point: Skill bodies stay out of context until the agent explicitly loads one, separating discovery from instruction bloat.
lessons.excerpt: Tools can be invoked by id; skill instructions stay out of context until the agent loads a relevant playbook with `get_skill_content`.

actionable.title: Evaluate Ratel-style tool-catalog retrieval for large tool inventories
actionable.detail: For harnesses with more than ~20 tools/skills, prototype a per-turn BM25 (or hybrid) retrieval step over tool metadata and only inject the top-k matches into the prompt. Measure token cost and task accuracy against the always-loaded baseline; the Ratel benchmark harness at ratel-ai/ratel-bench is a starting reference.

prior_art: Anthropic — 'Skills' progressive disclosure pattern in Claude Code
toon-format/toon — token-oriented I/O for LLMs
verify_note: Excerpts checked verbatim against data/_raw/ratel-ai-ratel-6453f7c140.txt (lines 30, 34-35, 141, 139). Related claims verified in data/claims.json.

title: Ratchet: How Reliable Must an LLM Judge Be to Retire a Skill?
summary: Paper on self-evolving agent skill libraries. Proves an exact reliability threshold for the LLM judge that governs skill eviction: if the judge's rate of scoring failures as passes reaches (1-tau)/2 for eviction margin tau, no eviction happens at any sample size. Reports that unmaintained libraries drift until adding a new skill scores worse than adding nothing, and that LLM-written skills contribute 0.0pp over a no-skill control vs. +16.2pp for human-written skills. Their Ratchet method (per-skill contribution eviction, library-width cap C, constrained synthesis) lifts held-out pass@1 by +0.328 on a hard MBPP+ slice. Amazon Science open-source code.
takeaway: In self-editing agent skill libraries, the judge's false-pass rate (not its overall accuracy) determines whether eviction can ever converge; asymmetric judge errors are the bottleneck, and end-task score is a poor alarm.

lessons.point: There is an exact non-convergence threshold on the judge: above a false-pass rate of (1-tau)/2 for eviction margin tau, no sample size can ever retire a skill.
lessons.excerpt: a judge scoring failures as passes at rate $(1-\tau)/2$ or above retires nothing, at any sample size, for eviction margin $\tau$.

lessons.point: Empirically, LLM-written skills in an audited system contribute nothing over a no-skill baseline, while human-written skills contribute meaningfully; unmaintained libraries drift negative.
lessons.excerpt: LLM-written skills are worth $+0.0$percentage points (pp) against a no-skill control, human-written ones $+16.2$pp. Unmaintained, a library enters \emph{library drift}, growing until injecting a skill scores worse than injecting nothing.

lessons.point: The two judge error directions are not interchangeable: false-negatives cost sample efficiency (recoverable with more trials), false-positives displace the eviction statistic irrecoverably.
lessons.excerpt: Passes scored as failures cost sample efficiency, which more trials buy back; failures scored as passes displace the eviction statistic, and no correction inside the rule recovers it.

lessons.point: End-task score is a bad early-warning signal for library drift; it moves at most a fifth of the governed lift and not monotonically in the judge's error rate.
lessons.excerpt: End-task score is a poor alarm, moving by at most a fifth of the governed lift and not monotonically in the rate.

actionable.title: Add a false-pass-rate gate to any self-editing agent skill library
actionable.detail: For any agent stack where an LLM judge decides which auto-generated skills to keep (Voyager-style memory, Claude 'skills', self-evolving toolboxes), measure the judge's false-pass rate offline against a calibrated set. If it exceeds ~(1-tau)/2 for the eviction margin you use, skills never get retired regardless of sample size — the library grows and drifts. Monitor library drift via per-skill contribution over a no-skill control rather than end-task score, which the paper shows is an insensitive and non-monotonic alarm.

prior_art: Related to Voyager-style skill libraries, self-refinement literature, LLM-as-judge calibration (Zheng et al. MT-Bench), and control-theory-style bounds on noisy estimators.
verify_note: Excerpts copied verbatim from data/_raw/mrscan-b011-2.txt (LaTeX math retained as-is in excerpts). Related claims exist in ledger. Novelty is meaningful because the exact false-pass threshold and the asymmetry between judge error directions is a specific quantitative claim; relevance capped mid-range because scope is skill-library curation, not general production agent security.

title: Birfy/agentdescent
author: Birfy
summary: AgentDescent maps deep-learning training onto agent self-evolution: the 'parameters' are evolvable artifacts (skills, prompts, harness modules, verifiers), the 'gradients' are diffs with evidence cards, and the 'optimizer step' is a merge decision. N workers propose diffs in parallel and a barrier-free asynchronous aggregator resolves conflicts via a staleness filter, fusion tournament, and Beta-posterior acceptance. Governance is by blast radius: L2 skills merge freely, L1 harnesses/verifiers pass through an oracle, L0 safety/permissions are frozen.
takeaway: The right abstraction for self-improving agent systems is not 'run and reflect' but a discrete-space optimizer over diffs with explicit conflict resolution, staleness policies, and blast-radius-gated merges. Freezing safety/permissions at L0 is the load-bearing safety property.

lessons.point: Diffs are not gradients: aggregation must be conflict resolution plus statistical acceptance plus transactional commit, not averaging.
lessons.excerpt: The one place the analogy *must* break defines the whole system: **gradients add, diffs do not.** Aggregation is therefore not averaging but **conflict resolution + statistical acceptance + transactional commit**.

lessons.point: Blast-radius tiers gate what may self-modify: L2 skills merge freely, L1 harness/verifier merges pass through an oracle, L0 safety/permissions are frozen.
lessons.excerpt: **Governed by blast radius.** Skills (L2) merge freely; harnesses/verifiers (L1) are forced through an oracle; safety/permissions (L0) are frozen.

lessons.point: For self-editing agent code, materialise the candidate in a throwaway workspace and overlay a pristine, frozen test suite after materialisation so the candidate cannot rewrite its own tests.
lessons.excerpt: `evolve_agent_code`, where the tree is **executed** behind a frozen test suite that the candidate cannot rewrite (pristine files are overlaid after materialisation, so weakening the tests at run time does not work either).

lessons.point: Parallel + async agent optimization beats a sync barrier by ~2.6-2.9x under heavy-tailed rollout latency (measured), because the round barrier waits on the slowest worker.
lessons.excerpt: the async pipeline is **~2.6–2.9× faster than a sync barrier** under heavy-tailed rollout latency.

actionable.title: Blast-radius-gated self-modification for agent harnesses
actionable.detail: Adopt AgentDescent's L0/L1/L2 framing whenever an agent is allowed to edit its own configuration: freeze safety and permission code at L0 (never mutable), force L1 (harness, verifier) changes through an oracle test suite that the candidate cannot rewrite (overlay pristine tests after materialisation), and let L2 (skills, prompts) merge freely. Pair with the frozen-test overlay pattern to prevent the candidate from cheating by weakening its own checks.

prior_art: ADAS (Meta Agent Search), DGM (Darwin-Godel Machine), OpenEvolve, GEPA, EvoSkill — AgentDescent explicitly ports these as examples. The specific contribution is the async aggregator + blast-radius + frozen-test-overlay combination, which is a real delta over any single one of those.
verify_note: All excerpts verified verbatim from raw file. Novelty scored at mid-range: the framing (diffs ≠ gradients) and frozen-test-overlay are genuinely new engineering ideas; the underlying self-evolution algorithms are ported from named prior work.

title: OpenForgeRL: Train Harness-native Agents in Any Environment
summary: OpenForgeRL is an open-source framework for end-to-end RL training of agents inside real inference harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw). A lightweight proxy serves the harness's model calls and records them as training data for a standard RL codebase (veRL); a Kubernetes orchestrator runs each rollout in its own container. OpenForgeClaw reaches 31.7 pass^3 / 55.9 pass@3 on ClawEval and 33.7 on QwenClawBench; OpenForgeGUI reaches 37.7 on OSWorld-Verified, 63.0 on Online-Mind2Web, and 72.3 on WebVoyager. Ablations on harness choice find that some harnesses are substantially harder to learn than others and that RL improves self-verification and tool coverage but leaves error recovery weak.
takeaway: The core architectural move is decoupling training from inference by intercepting the model call at the harness proxy layer. That lets an existing RL stack train against a stateful, multi-process harness it can't natively express. The ablations are the useful evidence: harness choice matters for trainability, and RL does not fix error recovery.

lessons.point: A proxy that serves the harness's model calls while recording them as RL training data is enough to decouple training from inference, letting a standard RL codebase train an agent inside an otherwise-opaque harness.
lessons.excerpt: OpenForgeRL achieves this with a lightweight proxy that serves the harness's model calls while recording them as training data for a standard RL codebase (e.g., veRL), and a Kubernetes orchestrator that runs each rollout in its own remote container, together enabling training on any harness in any environment at scale.

lessons.point: Harness choice materially affects trainability, and RL improves specific reliability behaviors (self-verification, tool coverage, multi-step plan completion) but not error recovery.
lessons.excerpt: We find that some harnesses are substantially harder to learn than others, and that RL improves agentic reliability, such as self-verification, tool coverage, and completing multi-step plans, though critical abilities such as error recovery remain weak.

actionable.title: Intercept model calls at the harness proxy layer to make agents trainable
actionable.detail: If a project wants to RL-train an agent that runs inside a real inference harness (Claude Code, Codex, custom), the pattern to steal is the proxy-plus-orchestrator split: a proxy serves the harness's model calls and logs them as training data; a container orchestrator isolates each rollout. This gets end-to-end training against a stateful, multi-process harness without rewriting the RL stack. Also useful signal for evaluating your own harness choice: some are much harder to train against than others.

prior_art: AgentGym, SWE-Gym, and RAGEN train tool-using agents but assume simpler harness structures. OpenForgeRL's contribution is treating a full production harness (Claude Code-style) as the training substrate, plus concrete ablations on harness choice.
verify_note: Both excerpts appear verbatim in data/_raw/mrscan-b012-2.txt. No related_claims asserted.

title: Counterfactual Simulation Training for Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness
summary: arXiv paper (COLM 2026) introduces Counterfactual Simulation Training (CST), which rewards CoTs that let a simulator predict the model's outputs on counterfactual inputs. In cue-based counterfactual settings CST improves monitor accuracy by 35 points on models up to 235B parameters; larger models don't get more faithful CoT by default but benefit more from CST, and rewriting unfaithful CoTs with an LLM is 5x more efficient than RL alone.
takeaway: CoT faithfulness can be trained for by rewarding CoTs that enable counterfactual simulation, materially improving CoT monitors — but the effect does not transfer symmetrically (dissuading vs persuading cues) and larger-by-default is not more faithful-by-default.

lessons.point: CST substantially raises CoT-monitor accuracy on cue-based counterfactuals (35 points) and improves simulatability on generic counterfactuals (2 points) at model scales up to 235B.
lessons.excerpt: Experiments with models up to 235B parameters show that CST can substantially improve monitor accuracy on cue-based counterfactuals (by 35 accuracy points) as well as simulatability over generic counterfactuals (by 2 points).

lessons.point: Larger models are not out-of-the-box more CoT-faithful; the benefit from CST scales with size, so faithfulness is trainable rather than emergent.
lessons.excerpt: larger models do not show more faithful CoT out of the box, but they do benefit more from CST.

lessons.point: Faithfulness gains do not generalize from persuading cues to dissuading cues, limiting deployment as a universal monitor.
lessons.excerpt: faithfulness improvements do not generalize to dissuading cues (as opposed to persuading cues)

lessons.point: Rewriting unfaithful CoTs with an LLM is a 5x more efficient path to faithfulness than RL alone.
lessons.excerpt: rewriting unfaithful CoTs with an LLM is 5x more efficient than RL alone

actionable.title: Treat CoT monitors as trainable and asymmetric, not free
actionable.detail: If a CoT monitor is part of the safety stack, CST-style training is worth evaluating — but bake in the asymmetry: gains on persuading-cue counterfactuals do not carry to dissuading cues, so measure both. Also note faithfulness is not emergent with scale; do not assume a larger model is a more monitorable model.

prior_art: Sits in the CoT-faithfulness / CoT-monitoring line (Turpin et al., Anthropic CoT-monitoring work, Lanham et al.); the delta is using counterfactual simulatability as the training reward rather than post-hoc faithfulness metrics.
verify_note: Excerpts copied verbatim from data/_raw/mrscan-b009-4.txt. Cluster H (guardrails/alignment) fits because CoT-monitoring is a safety instrument. Novelty kept mid because CoT-faithfulness work has a substantial prior line; contribution is the counterfactual-simulation reward and the size-vs-training asymmetry finding.

title: Fzkuji/OpenProgram
author: Fzkuji
summary: OpenProgram advocates 'Agentic Programming': one decorator (@agentic_function) turns a Python function into an agent where the docstring is the system prompt, type annotations are the tool schema, runtime.exec() calls are retryable DAG nodes, and everything else is plain deterministic Python. Context is an addressable node on a flat DAG (fork, spawn, cross-branch messaging follow from that), and code gates enforce validation the model cannot talk past.
takeaway: The load-bearing idea is 'a code gate can't be talked past' — when a model's answer fails validation, it is sent back to re-decide, so critical steps cannot be skipped by prompt injection or hallucination. This is a stronger primitive than 'add a validator to your output parser.'

lessons.point: A code gate that re-asks the model on validation failure is a stronger control than a passive validator: it structurally forbids skipping the check.
lessons.excerpt: **A code gate can't be talked past.** When the model's answer fails validation, it is sent back to re-decide

lessons.point: Encode the tool schema in the Python function's docstring + type annotations rather than a separate JSON schema, reducing drift between the model's view of a tool and the code that implements it.
lessons.excerpt: **docstring** = the prompt · **type annotations** = the tool schema · `choices=[...]` = a code gate that re-asks until the answer is valid.

lessons.point: Context should be modeled as addressable nodes on a flat DAG rather than per-agent buffers, so fork, spawn, and cross-session messaging reduce to 'point at a different node set.'
lessons.excerpt: Context is an **addressable node, not a per-agent buffer** — so every multi-agent move is just "point at a different node set":

lessons.point: Hot-loading self-authored agent functions via a file watcher lets an agent grow its own tools without a create()/fix() control plane.
lessons.excerpt: the agent edits its own `@agentic_function` files with ordinary file tools → a watcher hot-loads them → the new tool is live on the next turn. No `create()` / `fix()` machinery.

actionable.title: Route every 'critical step' through a code gate that re-asks on failure
actionable.detail: For any agent step where a wrong answer costs money or damages state (payment routing, permission checks, tool selection), wrap the LLM call so the code enforces the acceptable answer set (choices=[...] or a validator). On any parse or validation failure, the code re-asks the model with the failure reason as context, instead of falling through to a default branch. This structurally prevents the model from 'skipping' the check via prompt injection, a bad completion, or a JSON-mode drift.

prior_art: DSPy (Signature / Predict), Marvin's @ai_fn, Instructor's function-call retries, LangChain's @tool decorator — the 'docstring = prompt, types = schema' pattern is convergent. The 'code gate re-asks' framing and the flat DAG context model are the mild deltas.
verify_note: Excerpts verified verbatim. The arXiv id in the readme (2606.15874) is future-dated relative to typical arXiv IDs; not a claim we're relying on. Scored on the design ideas, not on the paper's peer status.

title: "LLM Agent Performance" Is Not a Single Evaluation Target
summary: arXiv position paper (v3) argues that a single 'LLM agent performance' number conflates three distinct evaluation targets: model comparison under a reference stack, complete-system comparison, and robustness across predeclared operating conditions. The claim a score supports depends on the declared candidate boundary and condition policy; the paper derives implications for leaderboards, reporting, and benchmark versioning.
takeaway: Agent benchmark scores are only interpretable relative to a declared candidate boundary (model vs. full system) and condition policy (robustness scope); collapsing all three into one number is a reporting bug.

lessons.point: Agent benchmark scores are shaped not only by the model but also by harness, environment, evaluator, and inference budget.
lessons.excerpt: LLM agent benchmark scores are shaped not only by the model but also by the agent harness, environment, evaluator, and inference budget.

lessons.point: Model-comparison-under-a-reference-stack and complete-system-comparison answer different questions and should not share a leaderboard slot.
lessons.excerpt: Model comparisons under a reference stack and comparisons of complete agent systems answer different questions, while robustness asks whether either conclusion persists across predeclared conditions.

lessons.point: The claim a score justifies depends on the declared candidate boundary and condition policy, so reporting must expose both.
lessons.excerpt: The claim supported by a score therefore depends on the declared candidate boundary and condition policy.

lessons.point: Unified execution (same configuration across candidate models) is only one legitimate framing; robustness across predeclared conditions is a separate evaluation shape.
lessons.excerpt: Unified execution controls these non-model factors by evaluating candidate models under the same configuration, making observed differences more attributable to the models themselves.

actionable.title: Declare candidate boundary and condition policy alongside any agent benchmark score
actionable.detail: When reporting or consuming agent eval numbers, force a two-field disclosure: (a) candidate boundary — is this a model comparison under a fixed harness, or a full-system comparison? (b) condition policy — are results held under a single reference configuration or across predeclared perturbations (robustness)? Treat leaderboards that omit these as ambiguous.

prior_art: Related to prior critiques of agent benchmarks (e.g., harness-sensitivity of SWE-Bench scores, contamination arguments, reproducibility studies). This paper reframes as a taxonomy of three distinct targets rather than proposing a new benchmark.
verify_note: Excerpts copied verbatim from data/_raw/mrscan-b009-3.txt. Position paper — moderate novelty and useful relevance to harness/agent-eval practitioners. Related claims chosen based on 'benchmark validity' theme without over-claiming refutation.

title: Can AI agents conduct open-ended AI research? Evidence from two case studies
summary: Shadow-evaluation methodology: frontier agents are given the central open-ended research question of an unpublished paper (six days, thousands of dollars of compute), and the paper's original authors grade the output. Ran on two unpublished NeurIPS 2026 submissions. Agents completed all the engineering without human help but made no substantial research progress and were unambiguously rejected by both sets of authors. Five recurring failure modes: poor judgment about the publishable-research bar, uncreative responses to design flaws, ineffective backtracking, poor resource awareness, and instruction drift. Reproduced with a second model and scaffold.
takeaway: The methodological contribution (author-graded shadow evaluations of unpublished work) is more durable than the point-in-time verdict. The findings themselves argue against strong 'AI does AI research end-to-end' claims: engineering is solved, research judgment is not, and the failures are consistent across scaffolds.

lessons.point: Agents can execute the engineering of an AI research project end-to-end but cannot substitute for the research judgment: two NeurIPS-quality open-ended questions, six days each, unambiguous rejection by the original authors.
