lessons.excerpt: The agents completed all of the engineering without human help, yet could not make substantial progress towards answering the research questions. As a result, both papers were unambiguously rejected by the authors.

lessons.point: The failure modes are reproducible across scaffolds and cluster in taste/judgment territory, not compute: poor bar-setting, uncreative response to design flaws, weak backtracking, poor resource awareness, instruction drift.
lessons.excerpt: We identify five recurring failure modes: poor judgment about the bar for publishable research, uncreative responses to shortcomings in the research design, ineffective backtracking from dead ends, poor resource awareness, and instruction drift. A robustness check with a second model and scaffold reproduced these failures.

lessons.point: Shadow evaluation (author-graded, on unpublished work) is a cleaner probe than either narrow benchmarks or blind peer review of AI papers.
lessons.excerpt: Current evaluations either test agents on narrow, verifiable tasks, which excludes open-ended research, or submit AI-generated papers to blind peer review, which is overstretched, stochastic, and suffers from poor review quality.

actionable.title: Agent-driven R&D: engineering-complete, judgment-incomplete
actionable.detail: When evaluating agents for open-ended technical work (not just coding), separate 'can it execute' from 'can it decide what to execute'. This paper's five failure modes (bar-setting, creative recovery, backtracking, resource awareness, instruction drift) transfer cleanly to security-research agents doing exploit discovery or vulnerability hypothesis generation: the engineering runs will pass, the judgment will not. Design harnesses that route judgment calls to humans and let the agent execute the rest.

prior_art: MLE-Bench, RE-Bench, and Sakana AI Scientist attempted narrow or peer-review-graded versions of the same question. Shadow evaluations on unpublished papers with author grading is the methodological novelty here.
verify_note: All three excerpts appear verbatim in data/_raw/mrscan-b012-3.txt. No related_claims asserted.

title: In-Context Examples Suppress Scientific Knowledge Recall in LLMs
summary: COLM 2026 paper showing that adding in-context examples to LLM prompts on latent-structure-recovery tasks (chemistry reaction constants, econ demand elasticities, etc.) systematically shifts the model away from applying pretrained scientific formulas toward empirical pattern fitting, even when those examples were generated by the very formula the model would have applied. Documented across 60 tasks in 5 domains, 6,000 trials, 4 models. Accuracy can go up, down, or stay flat, but the strategy shift is consistent.
takeaway: Few-shot examples don't just 'reinforce' knowledge; they can displace it. On tasks where the pretrained closed-form answer is better than curve-fitting to the demos, few-shot prompting silently makes the model dumber while looking like a helpful nudge.

lessons.point: Adding in-context examples systematically shifts LLMs away from using pretrained domain knowledge toward empirical pattern-fitting, even when the examples were generated by the very formula the model would have applied.
lessons.excerpt: We show that adding in-context examples makes models rely less on pretrained domain knowledge, even when those examples are generated by the very same formula. Rather than reinforcing knowledge-driven derivation, examples shift computation toward empirical pattern fitting.

lessons.point: The strategy shift is consistent across domains but its accuracy consequence is not: the same shift can lower, preserve, or raise accuracy depending on which strategy it displaces.
lessons.excerpt: This displacement is consistent across domains, but its accuracy consequences depend on how the displaced strategy compares to the one that replaces it: the same shift can lower accuracy, leave it unchanged, or appear to improve it.

lessons.point: For practitioners, few-shot examples should be treated as a strategy switch, not a knowledge booster.
lessons.excerpt: For practitioners deploying LLMs on scientific tasks, the message is cautionary: in-context examples may displace, rather than reinforce, the knowledge they are intended to support.

actionable.title: Audit few-shot demos for strategy displacement, not just accuracy
actionable.detail: When adding few-shot examples to a prompt for a task the model can also solve by recalling a formula/rule, the demos may silently shift the model from rule-application to pattern-matching over the demos. Accuracy alone won't reveal this; probe by comparing zero-shot vs. few-shot on cases where the closed-form rule and pattern-fit diverge.

prior_art: Extensive prior work on few-shot brittleness (order sensitivity, format sensitivity, majority-label bias). This paper's specific finding — that same-formula demos still displace knowledge-driven derivation — is a sharper mechanistic claim than the usual 'few-shot is fragile' result.
verify_note: All three excerpts appear verbatim in the abstract text at data/_raw/mrscan-b010-4.txt. No related_claims asserted; note this could feed a future claim on few-shot demos as strategy switches.

title: Zero gap does not mean a contaminated model is restored
summary: The paper argues that the dominant contamination-mitigation metric G-AP (Gap of Aggregate Performance) is misleading: discrete correct/incorrect readouts miss per-question effects, averaging before differencing lets over- and under-suppression cancel, and uniform per-question weighting can be gamed toward the clean model's high-frequency values. The authors propose SA-PPG (Stratified Aggregate of Per-question Probability Gaps), which samples per-question solve probabilities, differences against a clean model, and aggregates within clean-solve-probability strata. They also propose RailCap, a step-wise mitigation that caps trajectory tokens to the runner-up whenever a sample falls onto the greedy path, accumulating suppression until the distribution disperses. Under SA-PPG, prior mitigations' restoration is substantially overestimated and RailCap achieves the lowest gap.
takeaway: Zero G-AP is not proof a contaminated model has been restored. Evaluate mitigation with per-question probability gaps stratified by clean-model solve probability; averaged aggregate metrics conceal over- and under-suppression that cancel. This is directly relevant to cluster-L integrity of eval sets against contamination, even though the paper does not frame itself as red-team methodology.

lessons.point: G-AP hides errors: discrete readouts and pre-difference averaging let over- and under-suppression cancel; uniform per-question weighting can be gamed.
lessons.excerpt: Discrete correct/incorrect readouts cannot characterize per-question performance, averaging before differencing lets over- and under-suppression cancel out, and uniform per-question weighting invites strategies to push solve probabilities onto the clean model's high-frequency values.

lessons.point: SA-PPG replaces discrete readouts with per-question sampled solve probabilities, differences per question, then stratifies aggregation by the clean model's solve probability.
lessons.excerpt: We propose \textbf{SA-PPG} (\textbf{S}tratified \textbf{A}ggregate of \textbf{P}er-question \textbf{P}robability \textbf{G}aps): estimate each question's solve probability by sampling, difference it against the clean model per question, and aggregate within groups defined by the clean model's solve probability.

lessons.point: RailCap sidesteps the estimate-then-suppress pipeline by judging contamination during generation: when a sample falls onto the greedy trajectory, cap the next token to the runner-up until the distribution is sufficiently dispersed.
lessons.excerpt: \textbf{RailCap} instead judges contamination during generation: whenever a sample falls back onto the greedy trajectory, the next trajectory token is capped to the runner-up, accumulating suppression until the response distribution becomes sufficiently dispersed.

lessons.point: Under the stronger metric, prior mitigations' claimed restoration is substantially overestimated.
lessons.excerpt: Across multiple contaminated models and benchmarks, SA-PPG reveals that prior strategies' restoration is substantially overestimated, while RailCap attains the lowest SA-PPG.

actionable.title: Don't trust averaged-gap metrics for contamination mitigation on your evals
actionable.detail: When claiming a leaked benchmark has been 'restored' by decoding-time mitigations, check per-question probability gaps stratified by a clean model's solve probability, not just the average performance gap. This applies to security-eval sets that may have leaked into pretraining — a zero average gap can hide cancelling over- and under-suppression.

prior_art: G-AP metric and prior contamination-mitigation decoding strategies (estimate-then-suppress) are the direct baselines this paper contests.

title: aeonfun/aeon
author: aeonfun
summary: Aeon is a self-hosted framework that runs agent 'skills' (markdown SKILL.md files with frontmatter + a prompt) on cron via GitHub Actions, across six harnesses (Claude Code, Grok, Codex, Pi, Vibe, Kimi). It leans hard on the 'no approval loop' pitch: read-only skills are quarantined from the repo, irreversible actions fail closed, and a Haiku scorer rates every run so a heartbeat/skill-health/skill-repair/self-improve loop can fix broken skills unattended.
takeaway: The interesting bit isn't the marketing ('most autonomous') but the health loop: rate every run 1-5 with a small model, then auto-route low-scorers to a repair skill. Independent scorer plus capability tiers is a cheap self-healing pattern worth stealing.

lessons.point: A skill can be a single markdown file with frontmatter plus a prompt, portable across multiple agent CLIs behind one contract.
lessons.excerpt: A skill is a Markdown file: some frontmatter, then a prompt.

lessons.point: Autonomy needs capability tiers as brakes: read-only skills that can't write, irreversible actions that fail closed, and an optional per-run gate.
lessons.excerpt: Read-only skills can't touch the repo, irreversible actions fail closed, an optional [Fleet Watcher](../docs/CONFIGURATION.md#fleet-watcher-authorization-layer) gates every run, and secrets stay off the command line.

lessons.point: Self-healing agent loops can be built from a small-model per-run scorer plus dedicated health/repair skills.
lessons.excerpt: A model scores every run 1–5; `heartbeat` → `skill-health` → `skill-repair` → `self-improve` detect and fix broken skills without you

actionable.title: Add a per-run Haiku scorer + self-repair loop to any long-running agent
actionable.detail: For any unattended agent workflow, log every run's outputs and score them 1-5 with a cheap model on a fixed rubric. When the rolling score for a skill drops below a threshold, dispatch a repair pass that reads recent transcripts + the skill definition and proposes a fix PR. Combine with capability tiers (read-only / write / irreversible) so failed repairs can't do damage.

prior_art: Voyager (Minecraft, Wang et al. 2023) demonstrated self-authored skills + a critic; AutoGPT's task queue; the specific 'markdown SKILL.md + cron + capability tiers' combination is a modest engineering delta over those.
verify_note: Excerpts verified verbatim. Marketing framing ('most autonomous') is unfalsifiable — scored on the concrete design bits, not the claims about 2M stars secured.

title: universal-tool-calling-protocol/utcp-specification
summary: UTCP is a specification for a protocol-agnostic tool-calling standard (HTTP, WebSocket, CLI, SSE, Text, and MCP) with a plugin architecture, expanded auth options, and comprehensive error typing. Positions itself as an alternative/complement to MCP.
takeaway: UTCP treats MCP as one transport among many; for defenders, this means threat models built around 'MCP tools' need to generalize to any tool-calling transport, and tool-description injection remains a surface regardless of protocol.

lessons.point: UTCP aims to be transport-agnostic for tool discovery and invocation, spanning HTTP/WebSocket/CLI/Text/MCP.
lessons.excerpt: UTCP provides a standardized way for AI systems and other clients to discover and call tools from different providers, regardless of the underlying protocol used (HTTP, WebSocket, CLI, etc.).

lessons.point: v1.0 splits functionality into plugins per protocol, including an MCP plugin.
lessons.excerpt: Multiple Protocol Support: HTTP, CLI, WebSocket, Text, and MCP protocols via plugins

lessons.point: Enhanced auth (API key, OAuth, custom) is a core v1.0 addition, acknowledging auth as a first-class concern for tool-calling protocols.
lessons.excerpt: Advanced Authentication: Expanded authentication options including API key, OAuth, and custom auth

actionable.title: Generalize MCP threat models to protocol-agnostic tool calling
actionable.detail: When enumerating tool-poisoning and tool-description-injection risks, do not scope the analysis to MCP; UTCP-style abstractions push the same attack surface across HTTP/WS/CLI. Audit tool metadata handling in the caller regardless of transport.

prior_art: Model Context Protocol (Anthropic)
OpenAI function-calling / tool-use schemas
threat: A UTCP-style abstraction over multiple transports widens the surface for tool-description injection and metadata drift: a poisoned tool description travels through the caller regardless of whether the underlying transport is MCP, HTTP, or CLI.
conditions: Applies when an agent host adopts UTCP (or any transport-agnostic tool router) and trusts tool metadata pulled from third-party providers. Requires that the caller does not re-validate or sandbox tool descriptions on each fetch.
mitigations: Treat tool descriptions from all transports as untrusted input, pin/checksum tool manifests, apply the same tool-description-injection checks used for MCP (see claim `mcp-tool-descriptions-are-a-prompt-injection-surface`), and use per-tool auth scoping rather than transport-level trust.
verify_note: Excerpts checked verbatim against data/_raw/universal-tool-calling-protocol-utcp-specificati-cc93cec492.txt (lines 10, 25, 26). Cluster F fit is real but content is a spec-repo README, so novelty scored modestly.

title: INTRYGUE: Induction-Aware Entropy Gating for Reliable RAG Uncertainty Estimation
summary: The paper argues standard entropy-based uncertainty quantification (UQ) fails in RAG settings because induction heads that copy the correct grounded answer also trigger 'entropy neurons', inflating predictive entropy and producing false-uncertainty signals on accurate outputs. INTRYGUE gates predictive entropy on induction-head activation patterns and, across four RAG benchmarks and six open-source LLMs (4B-13B), matches or beats a wide range of UQ baselines.
takeaway: For RAG systems, naive token-entropy hallucination detectors are miscalibrated in a predictable way: the same circuit that grounds the answer inflates entropy. Gating on induction-head activation partially separates the two signals.

lessons.point: Standard entropy-based UQ methods misfire in RAG because grounded copying and entropy-neuron activation are mechanistically coupled, so correct grounded answers can present as uncertain.
lessons.excerpt: while induction heads promote grounded responses by copying the correct answer, they collaterally trigger the previously established "entropy neurons". This interaction inflates predictive entropy, causing the model to signal false uncertainty on accurate outputs.

lessons.point: Combining a predictive-uncertainty signal with an interpretability signal (induction-head activation) yields a more reliable hallucination detector than either alone across 4 benchmarks and 6 open-source LLMs.
lessons.excerpt: Our findings demonstrate that hallucination detection in RAG benefits from combining predictive uncertainty with interpretable, internal signals of context utilization.

actionable.title: Don't trust entropy as a lone hallucination signal in RAG
actionable.detail: If a system uses token entropy as an abstain/route-to-human gate for RAG outputs, be aware it will false-positive on correctly grounded answers because of the induction/entropy-neuron interaction. Combining entropy with an internal 'was context actually used' signal is the direction of travel.

prior_art: Semantic entropy (Farquhar 2024) and other UQ-for-LLMs work established entropy-family baselines. This paper's contribution is the mechanistic diagnosis of why they fail in RAG plus a gating fix; the mechanistic framing is the novel piece.
verify_note: Both excerpts appear verbatim in the abstract text at data/_raw/mrscan-b010-1.txt. No related_claims asserted.

title: wanmol/goal-flow
author: wanmol
summary: goalflow is a LangGraph-based framework that transpiles Dify visual DSL exports into runnable, version-controllable Python and pairs them with a code-first agent SDK (agent_kit) — the sales pitch is combining visual workflow graphs with agent loops so a graph node can host an agent and an agent can call a sub-workflow as a tool. Its own README carries a public-warning: the .env* files were previously tracked and credentials still live in git history requiring git filter-repo and rotation before publishing.
takeaway: The interesting artifact here is not the framework — it's the openly documented incident: even production teams shipping agent frameworks leak credentials into git history. Any 'we open-sourced our internal system' PR needs mandatory history scrubbing plus rotation as a gate, not an afterthought.

lessons.point: Extracting an internal agent framework into a public repo routinely leaks credentials via git history; scrubbing tracked .env files after the fact does not clean history.
lessons.excerpt: The `.env*` files are no longer tracked (a `.env.example` template ships in their place), but real credentials still live in **git history** — they must be scrubbed (`git filter-repo`) and rotated before the first public push.

lessons.point: Transpiling a visual-builder DSL (Dify) into runnable, version-controllable Python is a way to escape lock-in without losing the visual authoring surface.
lessons.excerpt: **Visual-first workflows** — design a flow in [Dify](https://dify.ai)'s drag-and-drop editor, then transpile the exported DSL into a runnable, version-controllable LangGraph Python file with one command. No lock-in to Dify's runtime.

lessons.point: For an I/O-bound async streaming pipeline, throughput scales with replicas rather than box size — measured 100 concurrent conversations on 2 vCPU / 4 GB per replica with no TTFT regression.
lessons.excerpt: a two-replica deployment on just **2 vCPU / 4 GB RAM per replica** sustained **100 concurrent conversations with no measurable regression in time-to-first-token**.

actionable.title: Gate every 'open-sourced internal agent framework' on a git-history secret scan and rotation
actionable.detail: Before an internal agent codebase goes public, mandate a two-step gate: (1) run git-history secret scan (gitleaks or trufflehog with --since-commit) across the full history, not just HEAD; (2) rotate every credential the scan finds, then use git filter-repo to remove the blobs. Simply untracking .env files leaves the secrets discoverable in older commits.

prior_art: The Dify-to-code transpilation is convergent with efforts around n8n/Flowise exports; the git-history-secret hazard is well-known (see: signature-based-detection-fails-on-llm-authored-malware and related supply-chain claims). Notable here as an in-the-wild admission in the readme itself.
verify_note: Excerpts verified verbatim. Cluster is B (agent harness). The credential-leak lesson is the one item with independent value beyond the framework itself.

title: Coupling Planning with Episodic Memory in LLM Agents for Software Issue Resolution
summary: PMCoder is a repo-level LLM agent that pairs a hierarchical phase planner with an episodic memory, wired bidirectionally: the current plan phase conditions memory retrieval, and memory-derived trajectory statistics drive stuck detection and replanning. When issue-reproduction verdicts are available, they gate 'done' on execution evidence rather than the agent's own claims. On SWE-bench Verified the coupling adds ~5.0pp over a harness-matched baseline, with consistent direction across Claude Haiku 4.5, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and an OpenHands port.
takeaway: For long-horizon coding agents, treating planning and memory as coupled substrate (with an external execution-verified done-signal) reduces repeated failed edits, empty-patch exits, and context-window exhaustion more than strengthening either alone.

lessons.point: Long agent runs fail because 'done' is inferred from the agent's own claims rather than from execution evidence.
lessons.excerpt: leaving long trajectories vulnerable to stale evidence, repeated failed edits, and verification inferred from the agent's own claims instead of execution evidence.

lessons.point: Coupling planning with episodic memory (plan conditions retrieval; memory stats trigger replanning) beats strengthening either alone.
lessons.excerpt: coupling planning and memory outperforms either component alone and reduces repeated failed actions, empty-patch exits, and context-window exhaustion.

lessons.point: When available, reproduction verdicts should ground verification progress in execution evidence.
lessons.excerpt: When available, issue-reproduction verdicts ground verification progress in execution evidence rather than self-reported completion.

actionable.title: Require execution-evidence gates on coding-agent 'done' signals
actionable.detail: In any long-horizon coding-agent harness, do not let the agent's self-reported completion terminate the run. Wire a reproduction/test gate as the authoritative done-signal, and expose memory statistics (repeat-action count, empty-patch count) to a stuck-detector that triggers replanning.

prior_art: Prior repo-level agents (Agentless, SWE-agent, OpenHands) strengthen planning or memory in isolation; PMCoder's contribution is the bidirectional coupling plus a reproduction-verdict done-signal.
verify_note: All excerpts verbatim from data/_raw/mrscan-b002-0.txt abstract. Cluster B (agent harness design) is defensible; relevance to security engineer briefing is modest — this is agent-quality research, not agent-security research.

title: Dropping the Anchor: Statistical Context Summarization for Distributed Systems via Pulsar Attention
summary: Pulsar Attention replaces Star Attention's static prepended anchor block with a small attention-sink prefix plus Max-IDF-selected cross-block summaries, reducing Phase 1 per-GPU FLOPs by up to 3.3x on RULER with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct at up to 128K tokens.
takeaway: Content-aware summaries chosen by rare-token statistics beat content-blind anchors for distributed long-context attention, at identical KV-cache footprint.

lessons.point: Distributed blockwise attention methods have relied on a static content-blind anchor block, which this work identifies as wasteful.
lessons.excerpt: Distributed blockwise methods such as Star Attention reduce this cost by sharding context across hosts, but rely on prepending a static, content-blind copy of the first block to every host.

lessons.point: Rare-token (Max-IDF) chunk selection plus a small attention-sink prefix can substitute for the static anchor while cutting compute.
lessons.excerpt: We propose Pulsar Attention, which replaces the static anchor with two lightweight, content-aware components: a small attention-sink prefix that stabilizes softmax, and compact cross-block summaries built via a Max-IDF heuristic that selects chunks containing globally rare tokens.

lessons.point: The method claims up to 3.3x FLOP reduction over Star Attention while remaining competitive with dense attention up to 128K tokens.
lessons.excerpt: This reduces the Phase 1 per-GPU FLOPs by up to 3.3x over Star Attention while retaining an identical KV cache footprint.

actionable.title: Watch content-aware anchor replacements for distributed long-context
actionable.detail: If you run distributed long-context inference (Star Attention-style sharding), evaluate whether IDF-driven summary blocks give the same accuracy at meaningfully lower Phase 1 FLOPs before locking in a static anchor.

prior_art: Star Attention (distributed blockwise attention) is explicitly the baseline; attention-sink tokens are a known softmax stabilization trick.
verify_note: Excerpts verbatim from raw fetched abstract. Cluster A (Retrieval and context) fits long-context/attention scope; but paper is purely performance-oriented, no security angle, hence low relevance.

title: Global allocation of resolution and coverage improves KV cache compression
summary: GraceKV frames KV-cache compression as global budget allocation over a prototype tree of layer-KV head-slot atomic units, adaptively trading coverage (adding tree roots) against resolution (splitting nodes) and holding up under 128x compression across long-context tasks without additional training.
takeaway: Framing KV-cache compression as a global resource-allocation problem across layers, heads, and slots outperforms fixed-rule eviction or merging, especially at aggressive compression ratios.

lessons.point: Existing KV-cache compression methods use fixed rules that cannot flow resources across layers, heads, and slots.
lessons.excerpt: Existing KV cache compression methods rely on predefined, fixed compression rules and are typically developed around either token eviction or merging. As a result, cache resources can neither flow freely across layers, heads, and context slots, nor be jointly allocated to balance local resolution and information coverage.

lessons.point: A prototype-tree structure lets adding a new tree root expand coverage while splitting a node adds local resolution, both under one shared budget.
lessons.excerpt: Adding the root of a new tree expands information coverage, whereas splitting a selected node improves local resolution. All candidate actions compete globally for a shared cache budget.

lessons.point: GraceKV holds up under 128-fold compression and ranks first in 24 of 32 experimental settings.
lessons.excerpt: Systematic experiments across diverse long-context tasks and compression ratios show that GraceKV ranks first in 24 of 32 settings and remains robust up to 128-fold compression.

lessons.point: No additional training is required and inference stays on-GPU.
lessons.excerpt: GraceKV requires no additional training, and the entire compression and inference process is performed on the GPU.

actionable.title: Prefer global budget allocation for KV-cache compression
actionable.detail: If you deploy long-context inference and rely on fixed per-layer eviction or merging, benchmark against a global resource-allocation baseline before locking in the strategy; the reported robustness at 128x compression suggests headroom over fixed rules.

prior_art: Token-eviction and token-merging KV-cache compression are the explicit baselines critiqued as fixed-rule.
verify_note: Excerpts verbatim. Cluster A (Retrieval and context) covers long-context behavior and context compression, which fits KV-cache compression for LLMs. No security angle, so relevance stays modest.

title: SSTQ: Privacy-Preserving Vector Quantization via Subsampled Stochastic TurboQuant
summary: SSTQ combines overcomplete equal-norm tight frames, coordinate subsampling, and privacy-aware 1D quantization for local-DP federated optimization; achieves optimal MSE scaling using only log2(N)+b bits per client with a codebook objective that cuts MSE from O(4^b) to O(2^b).
takeaway: For local-DP distributed optimization, tight-frame quantization plus subsampling beats vqSGD-style geometric constructions on communication-utility trade-off.

lessons.point: Existing local-DP vector quantization (e.g., vqSGD) suffers unfavorable dimension-dependent variance.
lessons.excerpt: Existing vector quantization methods, such as vqSGD, use high-dimensional geometric constructions but incur unfavorable dimension-dependent variance.

lessons.point: SSTQ achieves optimal MSE scaling with only log2(N)+b bits per client.
lessons.excerpt: We show that SSTQ achieves optimal mean squared error scaling while using only ⌈log 2 N⌉+bbits per client, where N=Θ(d)is the frame size.

lessons.point: A surrogate codebook objective reduces codebook-dependent MSE scaling exponentially.
lessons.excerpt: We also derive a surrogate privacy-aware codebook objective that reduces the codebook-dependent MSE scaling from O(4 b)to O(2 b).

lessons.point: Analytical derivations were initially produced by an internal Gemini-based agentic system and human-verified.
lessons.excerpt: Some of the analytical derivations were first obtained using a fully automated Gemini-based agentic system developed internally at Google. The authors have verified those derivations and edited them for clarity of presentation.

actionable.title: Note LDP quantization advances for federated systems
actionable.detail: If you build federated learning with local differential privacy, benchmark SSTQ against vqSGD on the same task before assuming vqSGD-family quantizers are state of the art.

prior_art: vqSGD is the named baseline. Local-DP mechanisms (randomized response, Laplace) are classical.

title: openai/openai-agents-python
author: openai
summary: OpenAI Agents SDK is a provider-agnostic multi-agent framework built around a small set of primitives: Agents (LLM + instructions + tools + guardrails + handoffs), Handoffs (agents delegating to other agents), Guardrails (configurable input/output validation), Sessions (auto history), and Tracing. A SandboxAgent primitive runs agents inside a container for long-horizon file/patch/command work; UnixLocalSandboxClient runs it locally on macOS/Linux, DockerSandboxClient on Windows.
takeaway: Modern agent SDKs converge on a small handful of primitives (agent, handoff, guardrail, session, tracing) plus a first-class sandbox client — sandbox-by-default is now table-stakes for long-horizon agent work.

lessons.point: Long-horizon agent frameworks expose sandboxing as a first-class primitive, not an afterthought.
lessons.excerpt: Use a `SandboxAgent` when the agent needs to inspect files, run commands, apply patches, or preserve workspace state across longer tasks.

lessons.point: Guardrails are surfaced as configurable input and output checks at the framework level.
lessons.excerpt: **Guardrails**: Configurable safety checks for input and output validation

lessons.point: Handoffs (agents-as-tools) are the SDK's recommended multi-agent primitive — one agent delegates to another via a tool interface rather than an ad-hoc router.
lessons.excerpt: **[Agents as tools](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/tools/#agents-as-tools) / [Handoffs](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/handoffs/)**: Delegating to other agents for specific tasks

actionable.title: Treat sandbox-by-default as table stakes for any long-horizon agent
actionable.detail: When designing or auditing an agent harness, require that any agent doing file/command/patch work runs through a sandbox client (container, VM, or gVisor). The OpenAI SDK's split of SandboxAgent vs Agent is a useful contract to steal: separate the type so the runtime can enforce the isolation instead of trusting per-call flags.

prior_art: LangChain/LangGraph agent primitives, CrewAI, AutoGen — the primitives here (agents, handoffs, guardrails, sessions, tracing) are convergent industry patterns, not new; the SandboxAgent formalization is the only mild delta and even that mirrors OpenDevin/Devin-style workspace agents.

title: Ask-E: An Environment for Calibrated Question Generation
summary: Ask-E flips the eval loop: instead of training models to answer hard problems, it benchmarks and trains them to generate problems calibrated to a target skill level (exactly one of two reference models can solve it). Training on the generator objective transfers to downstream math benchmarks without new math data or stronger-model supervision. Marginal relevance to security evals — the calibration idea is transferable but no security-specific application here.
takeaway: Generating calibrated questions is itself an eval signal; hard-to-generate problems require capability beyond the target — useful framing for keeping red-team/eval sets ahead of the model.

lessons.point: A generator that produces problems only one of two reference models can solve is a lower-bound witness that the generator has capability beyond the weaker model — inverts the usual answer-based eval.
lessons.excerpt: A generated question is successfully calibrated if exactly one of the two models can solve it, placing it precisely within the target range and differentiating the capabilities of these models.

lessons.point: Training on question generation transfers to answering — improved downstream math benchmarks without additional math training data, stronger-teacher interaction, or correctness reward.
lessons.excerpt: We also show that training on this environment leads to improvements across a number of downstream math benchmarks even with no new math data, no interaction with stronger models, and no correctness-based reward.

lessons.point: Frontier models remain far from saturating calibrated generation, so it works as a live benchmark.
lessons.excerpt: We find that even frontier models achieve below 50% calibration on the benchmark, leaving significant headroom to measure future progress.

actionable.title: Consider inverted-eval framing for red-team set generation
actionable.detail: For red-team/jailbreak eval sets that need to stay ahead of the model, consider a generator target that produces prompts exactly one of two candidate models trip on — treats calibration itself as the eval signal. Note: paper is math-only; no security transfer demonstrated.

prior_art: Adversarial/synthetic problem generation for eval (WildBench-style pairwise difficulty, self-play question generation, evolving jailbreak suites like PAIR/TAP). Calibration-via-two-model-bracket framing is a modest refinement, not a new category.

title: Beyond Scaffold Splits: Structural-Frontier Evaluation Reveals Hidden Failures in ADMET Models
summary: Argues that Bemis-Murcko scaffold holdouts underestimate ADMET-model error on truly novel chemistry. Introduces a label-free structural-frontier split that reserves the sparsest, most physicochemically remote scaffolds and shows large error inflation (taskwise median 87.0%, mean 130.3%) versus a matched scaffold control. Tested robust-training penalties (MV-FREX and three others) do not close the gap.
takeaway: OOD splits chosen by convention can hide model failure at the true generalization frontier; the same critique likely applies to LLM benchmarks, though the paper is chemistry-specific.

lessons.point: The choice of holdout split, not just model capacity, determines whether OOD failure is visible; a frontier-based split inflates error dramatically over the standard scaffold split.
lessons.excerpt: Against a 70/10/20 scaffold control with identical acyclic grouping, the frontier inflates equally weighted primary error with a taskwise median of 87.0% and a skew-sensitive mean of 130.3%

lessons.point: A graph-network head still shows a large frontier gap, so the effect is not explained by low model capacity.
lessons.excerpt: A message-passing graph-network control still shows a large gap (mean 82.8% over four tasks) and does not invert, so a low-capacity head does not explain the effect.

lessons.point: Tested tail-risk and robust-loss penalties fail to reduce frontier error, so split construction and label provenance are load-bearing evaluation constraints in their own right.
lessons.excerpt: Split construction and label provenance are important evaluation constraints in their own right, and the tested training penalties do not resolve the frontier failures we observe.

actionable.title: Analog for LLM eval design: pick holdouts that stress the true frontier
actionable.detail: When building or reviewing eval sets, avoid identifiers-of-convenience (scaffolds, source-domain tags, dataset splits inherited from prior work). Construct a label-free 'frontier' split that reserves the most dissimilar inputs and report both. The finding that a training-time robust penalty does not close the gap generalizes: eval-set curation dominates model-side patches.

prior_art: Standard Bemis-Murcko scaffold splits and the more recent Lo-Hi and DataSAIL splitters, against which this frontier split is compared and shown to be harder on average.

title: Equivariant Sparse Autoencoders: Mechanistic Interpretability of Neural Networks on Symmetric Data
summary: Extends the Linear Representation Hypothesis behind sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to account for data symmetries. Shows on synthetic and scientific datasets that equivariant SAEs avoid failure modes of ordinary SAEs on symmetric data and can produce more useful downstream features despite worse reconstruction, arguing reconstruction is a poor proxy for interpretability.
takeaway: Reconstruction quality can be inversely correlated with feature usefulness for SAEs under symmetries, which weakens reconstruction-based interpretability benchmarks even though the paper focuses on scientific rather than safety-relevant models.

lessons.point: SAE unidentifiability worsens on symmetric data, and priors like equivariance are needed for stable interpretations.
lessons.excerpt: We show that this problem is exacerbated by data symmetries such as rotations that are prevalent in scientific domains.

lessons.point: Reconstruction quality is not a reliable proxy for how useful SAE features are downstream.
lessons.excerpt: reconstruction quality can be inversely correlated with feature usefulness under symmetries, cautioning against its use as a key measure of interpretability

lessons.point: Equivariant SAEs can find features that improve downstream tasks even when their reconstruction gets worse.
lessons.excerpt: the resulting Equivariant SAEs can (1) avoid the pitfalls of existing SAEs on symmetric data and (2) discover features more useful for downstream tasks despite worse reconstructions

actionable.title: Flag caveat: reconstruction is a weak SAE metric
actionable.detail: If any downstream security-adjacent work leans on SAE reconstruction to justify interpretability claims (e.g., steering / refusal-direction work), note this paper as a specific reason to require task-side utility metrics alongside reconstruction.

prior_art: Linear Representation Hypothesis, Anthropic/DeepMind SAE and dictionary-learning interpretability, group-equivariant CNNs (Cohen & Welling).
verify_note: Excerpts verbatim from the arxiv abstract; scientific-data framing keeps this well outside AI-security scope, so cluster=null and low relevance.

title: Hybrid analytical and machine-learning predictors model LLM inference latency and energy
summary: HYMELL is a three-level predictor for LLM inference latency and energy that combines analytical modeling of primitive operations, ML prediction of higher-level components, and an end-to-end model for system overheads across prefill and decode. It covers dense and MoE FFNs and MHA/GQA attention, and reports under 5% error on LLaMA 3 8B on an NVIDIA H100. The pitch is fast, hardware-free design-space exploration for latency/energy-aware LLM deployment.
takeaway: Cost/latency estimation for LLM inference is being reframed as a hardware-free predictor problem, decoupled from actually running the model. For deployment decisions this is useful, but the reported accuracy is a single-GPU, single-model figure — treat it as evidence the approach works on one H100 + LLaMA 3 8B rather than a general-purpose estimator.

lessons.point: Splitting the estimator into analytical primitives + ML for higher-level components + an end-to-end system model captures both prefill and decode phase overheads that pure-analytical or pure-ML predictors miss.
lessons.excerpt: HYMELL models LLM execution through a three-level hierarchy: analytical estimation of primitive operations, ML prediction of higher-level components, and an end-to-end model that captures system-level overheads across both prefill and decode phases.

lessons.point: On a single hardware target the predictor reports high accuracy, which supports using it for design-space exploration without booting the model.
lessons.excerpt: Evaluated on an NVIDIA H100 graphics processing unit (GPU), HYMELL achieves high predictive accuracy; notably, for LLaMA 3 8B, it attains less than 5% error for both prefill and decode phases.

actionable.title: Use hardware-free LLM cost predictors for capacity/routing decisions, not for SLA guarantees
actionable.detail: When choosing between MoE vs dense, GQA vs MHA, or provisioning for a new context length, a predictor like HYMELL can rank options without booting hardware. Do not stake latency SLAs on <5% error extrapolated off one H100 + LLaMA 3 8B calibration — the paper's accuracy claim is bounded to that setup.

prior_art: Analytical roofline models and ML-based predictors for GPU workloads exist; HYMELL is the hybrid variant specialized for LLM prefill+decode.

title: Rethinking Evaluation Paradigms in IBP-based Certified Training
summary: ICML 2026 paper arguing that certified-training methods for adversarial robustness should be evaluated on the Pareto front of natural vs certified accuracy rather than a single hyperparameter configuration. The authors run multi-objective HPO and find prior configurations were substantially undertuned, so reported gains between methods are smaller than assumed.
takeaway: Single-config accuracy numbers over-state progress in certified-training research; Pareto-front comparisons after multi-objective tuning are the more honest bar. Relevant to red-teamers and evaluators building adversarial-robustness benchmarks that need to stay honest across method generations.

lessons.point: Reporting a single natural-vs-certified accuracy point misleads comparisons between certified-training methods, because the metrics are inherently conflicting.
lessons.excerpt: Because these metrics are inherently conflicting, the common practice of reporting a single configuration is problematic: it can mislead conclusions about overall performance and prevents unbiased assessments of the state of the art.

lessons.point: Automated multi-objective HPO reveals prior published configurations were substantially undertuned, so headline gains are smaller than assumed.
lessons.excerpt: This approach often uncovers substantial undertuning in previously reported configurations, yielding superior performance and establishing a new state of the art.

lessons.point: Multi-objective comparison exposes performance complementarities between certified-training methods that single-config reporting hides.
lessons.excerpt: Leveraging these fronts, we present the first comprehensive multi-objective comparison of certified training approaches, showing that prior advancements are less pronounced than assumed and revealing previously unreported performance complementarities.

actionable.title: Score robustness methods on Pareto fronts, not single configs
actionable.detail: When comparing certified-training methods (or any defense with a natural-vs-defended trade-off), publish Pareto-optimal configurations from multi-objective HPO rather than one point per method. Otherwise apparent progress is confounded with tuning budget.

prior_art: Prior IBP/CROWN-IBP certified-training papers reported single natural/certified accuracy pairs; multi-objective evaluation of adversarial-training methods has been discussed but is not the norm.
threat: Overstated adversarial robustness claims propagate into downstream defender product decisions when the defense literature reports cherry-picked hyperparameter configurations.
conditions: Comparing two certified-training or adversarial-training methods using their originally-published hyperparameters, on the same architecture and threat model.
mitigations: Run multi-objective hyperparameter optimisation for each method, publish the Pareto front over natural vs certified accuracy, and pick operating points by application-level risk tolerance rather than a single headline number.

title: SAGEO Arena: A Realistic Environment for Evaluating Search-Augmented Generative Engine Optimization
summary: KDD 2026 paper introducing SAGEO Arena, an end-to-end evaluation environment for Search-Augmented Generative Engine Optimization: the practice of optimizing web documents to raise their visibility in AI-generated answers. Existing benchmarks skip retrieval/reranking and strip structural markup; SAGEO Arena keeps both. Finds current SEO/GEO strategies often degrade performance under a realistic pipeline and that structural (schema) markup helps.
takeaway: SAGEO is the SEO of the LLM era. Realistic end-to-end evaluation shows most optimization tricks that look good on toy benchmarks hurt real retrieval/reranking. Adjacent to prompt-injection-via-web-content but this paper is about visibility, not defense.

lessons.point: Benchmarks that pre-select candidate documents and strip schema markup systematically overestimate SAGEO strategy effectiveness.
lessons.excerpt: existing benchmarks lack end-to-end visibility evaluation of optimization strategies, operating on pre-determined candidate documents that abstract away retrieval and reranking preceding generation. Moreover, existing benchmarks discard structural information (e.g., schema markup) present in real web documents, overlooking the rich signals that search systems actively leverage in practice.

lessons.point: Under realistic conditions, current SAGEO tactics frequently degrade retrieval and reranking rather than improve them, and successful optimization must be tailored per pipeline stage.
lessons.excerpt: Our findings reveal that existing approaches remain largely impractical under realistic conditions and often degrade performance in retrieval and reranking. We also find that structural information helps mitigate these limitations, and that effective SAGEO requires tailoring optimization to each pipeline stage.

actionable.title: SAGEO Arena is a candidate testbed for indirect-prompt-injection experiments on real search pipelines
actionable.detail: The environment reproduces a full generative search pipeline over real web docs including schema markup, which is the exact surface exploited by indirect prompt injection. If Track B ever grows an experimental arm, this is a plausible harness to test injection payloads end-to-end without standing up a bespoke pipeline.

prior_art: Prior GEO/SEO-for-LLMs work (Aggarwal et al. 'GEO: Generative Engine Optimization', 2024); RAG evaluation harnesses like RAGGED, RGB; adversarial-web-document work on injecting instructions into scraped pages.

mitigations: Sanitize schema markup before feeding into ranker/reader; treat retrieved document text as untrusted and enforce instruction/data separation; measure visibility manipulation as part of red-team eval.

title: Topology-Aware Data Movement for Disaggregated GPU Inference
summary: A KV-cache transfer orchestrator for disaggregated prefill/decode inference that discovers interconnect hierarchy and picks NVLink/PCIe/IB/TCP per transfer, with pipelined layer-by-layer transfers and CXL 3.0 overflow tier; projected 3-18x latency reduction over uniform RDMA.
takeaway: Uniform RDMA for KV-cache transfer wastes up to 72x bandwidth headroom; topology-aware transport selection and pipelining reclaim most of it.

lessons.point: Disaggregated inference forces per-request KV-cache transfers on the order of 1.3 GB (Llama-70B) reaching 100 GB/s at production scale.
lessons.excerpt: When prefill and decode run on separate GPU pools, the KV cache must be transferred between them. For a 70B model this is 1.3 GB per request, exceeding 100 GB/s aggregate at production scale.

lessons.point: Existing production systems ignore that GPU-to-GPU bandwidth varies by up to 72x with physical topology.
lessons.excerpt: Yet DistServe, Splitwise, and Mooncake all use uniform RDMA, ignoring that bandwidth between two GPUs varies by 72x depending on their physical relationship: 900 GB/s via NVLink 4.0 within a domain (1.8 TB/s on NVLink 5, widening the gap to 144x), 50 GB/s via InfiniBand across nodes, 12.5 GB/s via TCP across data centers.

lessons.point: Pipelined layer-by-layer transfer overlapped with ongoing prefill hides 76-100% of transfer latency behind computation.
lessons.excerpt: pipelined layer-by-layer transfer that overlaps transmission with ongoing prefill, hiding 76 to 100 percent of transfer latency behind computation depending on transport, with NVLink and PCIe transfers hidden entirely

lessons.point: The authors explicitly cannot run a full evaluation because the hardware is beyond academic reach; results are projected.
lessons.excerpt: Full evaluation requires multi-node clusters with heterogeneous interconnects and CXL 3.0 hardware that is beyond academic resources and not yet available in GPU clouds.

actionable.title: Design KV-cache transport by topology, not uniformly
actionable.detail: If you run disaggregated prefill/decode on heterogeneous interconnects, pick transport per pair (NVLink domain, PCIe, IB, TCP) and pipeline layer-by-layer with prefill; uniform RDMA leaves substantial latency on the table.

prior_art: DistServe, Splitwise, Mooncake are the named baselines. Attention-sink and CXL memory-tiering research exists separately.
verify_note: Excerpts verbatim. Serving-infra paper with no security angle; cluster=null. Note the projected-not-measured caveat: authors admit they lack hardware to fully evaluate.

title: Autonomy-of-Heads: Data-Free Sparse Attention from Frozen Query-Key Geometry
summary: Autonomy-of-Heads (AoH) is a data-free method that classifies attention heads as retrieval or streaming by the spectral geometry of their weight-space query-key projections, avoiding runtime attention scores or calibration prompts. Concentrated spectra flag retrieval heads; diffuse spectra flag streaming heads. At 50% sparsity the abstract reports retention of 96.5% of Full Attention performance on average, with up to 41.4% prefill and 66.0% decode latency reduction and 50.0% KV-cache memory reduction at 256K tokens.
takeaway: Head function (retrieval vs streaming) can be diagnosed from static QK weight geometry rather than from runtime traffic, which removes the calibration-data dependency of prior sparse-attention schemes.

lessons.point: Prior sparse-attention head diagnosis is input-dependent and costly to deploy.
lessons.excerpt: Existing sparse attention and KV-compression methods typically decide which tokens or heads to preserve from runtime attention scores, observation windows, calibration prompts, or learned gates, making head diagnosis input-dependent and costly to deploy.

lessons.point: Retrieval vs streaming heads separate along the effective-rank of the query-key kernel.
lessons.excerpt: concentrated spectra indicate a small number of dominant query-key matching directions and are associated with retrieval heads, whereas diffuse spectra indicate the absence of a dominant global matching direction and are associated with streaming heads.

lessons.point: At 50% sparsity, AoH retains ~96.5% of Full Attention with substantial latency and KV-cache savings.
lessons.excerpt: at 50\% sparsity, AoH retains 96.5\% of Full Attention performance on average while reducing prefill and decode latency by up to 41.4\% and 66.0\%, respectively, and KV-cache memory by 50.0\% at 256K tokens.

actionable.title: None for security engineer
actionable.detail: Inference-cost optimization; no security implication. Note only for long-context serving stacks looking at KV-cache reduction techniques.

prior_art: Prior sparse-attention work (StreamingLLM, H2O, SnapKV, Quest) uses runtime attention scores or calibration prompts; AoH's contribution is data-free spectral diagnosis from frozen QK weights.

title: CoinRAG: Contextualized Information Nugget KV Cache Reuse for Long-Context RAG
summary: arXiv preprint proposes CoinRAG, which replaces chunk-level KV cache reuse with fine-grained 'nugget' KV cache reuse for long-context RAG. On LongBench multi-hop QA, it reports a new Pareto frontier and an average 5.3% relative F1 improvement under a fast prefill latency budget by identifying query-relevant semantic units within chunks and assembling sliced KV representations.
takeaway: Sub-chunk KV cache reuse targeted at query-relevant nuggets outperforms coarse chunk-level cache reuse for long-context RAG on multi-hop QA under fixed prefill latency budgets.

lessons.point: Chunk-level KV cache reuse leaves significant information redundancy and noise on the table; sub-chunk 'nugget' granularity is a lever for lower prefill latency at higher accuracy.
lessons.excerpt: Recent optimization studies on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) have exploited chunk-level KV cache reuse to avoid processing long retrieved contexts for higher efficiency, while significant information redundancy and noise still remain in the coarse-grained chunks.

lessons.point: CoinRAG reports a Pareto-frontier gain over baselines on LongBench multi-hop QA (average 5.3% relative F1 improvement at a standard fast prefill budget).
lessons.excerpt: Extensive evaluations on LongBench multi-hop question answering tasks demonstrate that CoinRAG significantly reduces operational costs and outperforms the other baselines with a new Pareto frontier and an average 5.3% relative improvement in answer quality (F1) under a standard fast prefill latency budget.

lessons.point: The mechanism is two-stage retrieval that first pulls chunks then slices in-chunk semantic units, with offline-computed nugget caches assembled at query time.
lessons.excerpt: instead of full-chunk encoding, CoinRAG identifies query-relevant semantic units within retrieved chunks through two-stage retrieval and seamlessly assembles their sliced KV representations with a chunk-level context.

actionable.title: Consider sub-chunk KV cache granularity when tuning long-context RAG
actionable.detail: If a RAG stack already reuses chunk-level KV caches, revisit whether the reused span is actually the query-relevant slice. CoinRAG-style two-stage retrieval (chunk then nugget) plus offline-precomputed nugget caches is one direction; measure against a chunk-cache baseline on multi-hop QA and prefill latency, since gains outside that regime are unproven.

prior_art: Chunk-level KV cache reuse for RAG (e.g., CacheBlend, PromptCache) and fine-grained context distillation lines; CoinRAG differentiates on nugget-level granularity plus assembly with chunk context.

title: Multi-Agent Forensic Reasoning for Generalizable Deepfake Video Detection
summary: Introduces FaceVid-Forensics-100K (100K videos across 33 synthesis methods including Seedance 2.0) with fine-grained textual annotations and forensic explanations produced via a multi-model aggregation and conflict-resolution pipeline. A multi-agent framework uses four domain-expert agents (texture, lighting, motion, physics) plus a judge agent to reconcile their reports. On out-of-domain sets the framework — built entirely from small open-source MLLMs — beats GPT and Gemini baselines and ranks first across reported metrics.
takeaway: For generalizable deepfake video detection, specialist-agent decomposition across independent forensic perspectives with a judge-agent reconciliation can let small open-source MLLMs beat frontier single-model classifiers.

lessons.point: Single-perspective detectors and single MLLMs miss subtle forgery artifacts and generalize poorly to new generators.
lessons.excerpt: conventional detectors and multimodal large language models (MLLMs), whether operating as a single model or relying on a single analytical perspective, often fail to capture subtle forgery artifacts, limiting their generalization to emerging AI-generated methods.

lessons.point: Splitting forensic reasoning into independent domain-expert agents (texture / lighting / motion / physics) plus a judge reconciler generalizes better OOD.
lessons.excerpt: a multi-agent forensic reasoning framework that employs four specialized domain-expert agents to independently analyze forgery cues from four perspectives: texture, lighting, motion, and physics. A judge agent then reconciles their reports to produce a final prediction together with an explanation.

lessons.point: Small open-source MLLMs in this ensemble outperform closed-source GPT and Gemini on the benchmark.
lessons.excerpt: despite being composed entirely of small open-source MLLMs, our framework outperforms all methods including closed-source GPT and Gemini models and ranks first across all reported metrics on this benchmark.

actionable.title: Multi-perspective agent decomposition as a general detector pattern
actionable.detail: The judge-plus-specialists topology (independent perspective agents whose reports a judge reconciles) is worth borrowing for other 'is this content adversarial?' detection problems — e.g., prompt-injection detection over retrieved documents — where a single classifier tends to overfit to one signal family.

prior_art: Prior deepfake detectors are typically single CNN/transformer classifiers or single-MLLM prompted detectors; the specialist-plus-judge multi-agent decomposition is the novelty.

title: Pre-Inference Routing for Cost-Efficient Document Field Extraction
summary: For document field extraction, routes documents between a cheap and a strong model based on pre-inference difficulty signals (image quality, layout). Cost savings of 31-77% within 0.02 F1 of always-large are reported on receipts and degraded ad-buy forms; routing only helps when the cheap model fails often enough and those failures are predictable. Routers do not transfer across datasets even within a genre; a small labeled pilot is proposed as a go/no-go test.
takeaway: Pre-inference routing pays off only under two joint conditions: the cheap model fails often enough to matter and its failures are predictable from cheap signals; without both, cost-optimization routing is a wash or worse.

lessons.point: Two joint conditions must hold for routing to reduce cost without hurting quality.
lessons.excerpt: We find that routing only helps if two conditions hold: the cheaper model fails often enough to make routing worthwhile, and those failures can be predicted from visible features such as image quality and layout.

lessons.point: When both conditions are met, calibrated routing gets 31-77% cost savings within 0.02 F1 of always-large.
lessons.excerpt: When both conditions are met, the calibrated router reduces cost by 31-33% on receipts and 77% on degraded ad-buy forms while keeping quality within 0.02 F1 of always choosing the large model.

lessons.point: Router must be retrained per dataset and does not transfer across datasets, even within a genre.
lessons.excerpt: The router must be retrained for each dataset and does not transfer across datasets, even within the same genre.

lessons.point: A small labeled pilot correctly predicted whether routing would work in the two cases it was applied.
lessons.excerpt: A small labeled pilot can predict whether routing will work, and in the two cases where we ran it first, the prediction was correct.

actionable.title: Gate model-routing rollouts on a two-condition pilot
actionable.detail: Before deploying cheap-vs-strong model routing, run a small pilot to check both: cheap-model failure rate is high enough to matter, and failures are predictable from cheap pre-inference signals. If either fails, keep a single model. Assume routers do not transfer across datasets.

prior_art: Standard single-model document-extraction pipelines are the baseline; the paper positions itself against always-strong and always-cheap defaults.
threat: N/A (cost-optimization paper; no direct adversarial threat model).
conditions: Multi-genre document extraction with paired cheap/strong models where cheap-model failures correlate with visible pre-inference features (image quality, layout).
mitigations: N/A (this is an efficiency method, not a security control).

title: Same Answer, Different Confidence: Protocol Sensitivity in LLM Confidence Calibration
summary: Paper auditing how the choice of measurement protocol (which answer is scored, under which prompt, which readout) determines whether verbalized confidence or token-likelihood confidence appears better calibrated. Across four QA datasets and three 7-8B instruct models, the ranking flips in 4 of 12 settings under ECE and 9 of 12 under AUROC purely from protocol choice. In a twelve-study audit, five prior comparisons never state the protocol.
takeaway: Whether verbalized confidence beats token-likelihood confidence is not a property of the model; it is a property of the (answer, context, readout) protocol, and published comparisons routinely leave that protocol unspecified.

lessons.point: Twelve operational-protocol variants swing the sign of the ECE comparison between verbalized and likelihood confidence in a majority of settings under AUROC.
lessons.excerpt: Across four QA datasets and three 7-8B Instruct models this changes which signal performs better, by point estimate, in 4 of 12 settings under ECE and 9 of 12 under AUROC.

lessons.point: The reordering is not a rescaling artifact — AUROC is invariant to order-preserving transforms, so the change reflects actual item reordering.
lessons.excerpt: The AUROC result cannot come from rescaling the likelihoods, since AUROC is invariant to any common order-preserving transformation; the items are ordered differently.

lessons.point: Verbalized confidence is sensitive to surface answer formulation: swapping a correct alias for the canonical reference raises confidence by 0.072 even though both are correct.
lessons.excerpt: replacing an accepted TriviaQA alias with the canonical reference raises confidence by $0.072$ although both answers are correct.

lessons.point: The audit finds many published comparisons omit the protocol choice entirely.
lessons.excerpt: Published comparisons diverge on this, and in a twelve-study audit five never state the choice.

actionable.title: Report answer, context, and readout when comparing LLM confidence signals
actionable.detail: If you rely on model confidence — for abstention, deferral to human, or LLM-judge scoring — the ranking of verbalized-confidence vs. token-likelihood is protocol-dependent. When picking between them, fix and document (a) which answer slot is scored, (b) under which prompt context, and (c) which readout (span vs. first token) is used, and re-benchmark on your task; do not rely on published ordering.

prior_art: Extends the LLM-confidence-calibration line (Tian et al., Kadavath et al., Xiong et al.) by showing published results diverge because of unstated protocol choices rather than model differences.

title: Logit-lens over visual attention detects and mitigates LVLM object hallucination
summary: A CVPR 2026 highlight paper on object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models. The authors find that real and hallucinated objects receive equally strong visual attention in mid-to-late layers, so attention magnitude is not the diagnostic. Applying Logit Lens to high-attention visual regions distinguishes them: real-object regions decode to the correct token, hallucinated ones do not. The paper decomposes hallucination into two mechanisms (visual uncertainty from confusable regions, contextual prior from co-occurrence) and proposes a training-free Detect-Mitigate framework: Logit-Lens Consistency Check for detection plus High-Attention Regions Masking (HARM) and Visual Evidence Enhanced Decoding (VEED) for mitigation.
takeaway: For LVLM reliability work, attention magnitude is a weak signal because real and hallucinated targets attract comparable attention; what the attended-to features decode to under a Logit Lens is a stronger detector. This is a vision-model finding, not an agent-harness or security finding.

lessons.point: Attention magnitude does not separate real from hallucinated objects in LVLMs; both get strong attention in mid-to-late layers.
lessons.excerpt: we find that both real and hallucinated objects receive equally strong visual attention in the model's mid-to-late layers, suggesting that the key issue may not be how much the model attends, but what it attends to and why.

lessons.point: Logit Lens over high-attention visual regions provides a detection signal: real regions decode to the target token, hallucinated ones do not.
lessons.excerpt: we decode the visual features of high-attention regions using Logit Lens, and observe that regions corresponding to real objects can be correctly decoded to the target object tokens, whereas those for hallucinated objects cannot.

lessons.point: Two distinct hallucination mechanisms need different remedies: visual uncertainty is fixed by masking confusable regions; contextual prior persists after masking and requires evidence-enhanced decoding.
lessons.excerpt: (i) visual uncertainty, triggered by semantically similar or confusable regions; masking these regions eliminates the hallucination. (ii) contextual prior, triggered by strong co-occurrence priors; even when the initially attended region is masked, the hallucination persists and attention drifts to other regions.

actionable.title: News-lane only — LVLM hallucination detection, not agent security
actionable.detail: Track for interpretability-adjacent techniques (Logit Lens as a detector) that might transfer to text-only LLM hallucination or refusal analysis. No claim work — LVLM visual grounding is outside the 13-cluster scope in interests.yaml.

prior_art: Logit Lens interpretability technique; prior work attributing LVLM hallucination to insufficient visual attention (this paper contests that framing).

title: Semantic Adapter Routing with Fine-Tuning Task Embeddings
summary: ARIADNE reframes PEFT adapter routing as classification over task embeddings and, without touching adapter weights, recovers 97.4% of Oracle task performance on 23 tasks and scales to 44 adapters at 89.7% accuracy. Its companion GRACE handles the case where training data isn't available by reconstructing an adapter's fine-tuning data from output logits alone via a modified contrastive-decoding-diffing (CDD) procedure, then using the synthesized data to build task embeddings; across three backbones (Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen2.5-32B) GRACE recovers 72-100% of Oracle accuracy.
takeaway: Routing at inference time can be done training-free by task-embedding-nearest-neighbor over adapters. The under-the-radar bit is GRACE: an adapter's fine-tuning data is recoverable from its output logits alone. That is a mild but real data-leakage surface for anyone who ships PEFT adapters on public hubs.

lessons.point: Adapter routing that never touches adapter weights or requires supervised training is viable at scale: 97.4% of Oracle on 23 tasks, 89.7% selection accuracy across 44 adapters.
lessons.excerpt: Evaluated on 23 tasks, ARIADNE recovers 97.4% of Oracle task performance and scales to 44 adapters at 89.7% selection accuracy, without touching a single adapter parameter.

lessons.point: Fine-tuning data can be reconstructed from an adapter's output logits alone via contrastive decoding diffing. The synthesized data is good enough to build usable task embeddings.
lessons.excerpt: GRACE, which recovers an adapter's fine-tuning data from its output logits alone via a modified contrastive decoding diffing (CDD) procedure. Synthetic data generated from CDD-UM is then used to construct task embeddings.

actionable.title: PEFT adapters on public hubs leak their training data through logits
actionable.detail: If teams publish PEFT adapters on Hugging Face or third-party hubs, note that logit-level access to the adapted model is sufficient for a plausible reconstruction of the fine-tuning data (GRACE's contrastive-decoding-diffing procedure). Treat 'adapter released, base weights private' as a partial rather than clean privacy boundary.

prior_art: Adapter-routing work (Arrow, LoraHub) established the problem framing; task-embedding classification is a standard technique. The mildly novel piece is GRACE reconstructing training data from logits alone, which extends contrastive-decoding-diffing (Zhu et al.) into a training-data-recovery tool.

title: Intelligence per Watt: Measuring Intelligence Efficiency of Local AI
summary: Proposes Intelligence per Watt (IPW) as a metric for local LLM inference, evaluating 20+ local models and 8 accelerators on 1M real queries, and finding that local LMs already answer 88.7% correctly with IPW improving 5.3x from 2023-2025.
takeaway: A large fraction of real-world queries can be redistributed to local inference on power-constrained hardware, and IPW is a compact way to track that shift over time.

lessons.point: Small local LMs already handle the bulk of real single-turn queries.
lessons.excerpt: local LMs successfully answer 88.7% of these queries, with accuracy varying by domain

title: Self-Distillation Enables Continual Learning
summary: Introduces Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT), an on-policy method that uses a demonstration-conditioned model as its own teacher, turning expert demonstrations into on-policy training signals. lessons.excerpt: Learning from expert demonstrations, the primary alternative, is dominated by supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which is inherently off-policy.

lessons.excerpt: SDFT leverages in-context learning by using a demonstration-conditioned model as its own teacher, generating on-policy training signals that preserve prior capabilities while acquiring new skills.

title: ZCA whitening calibrates WEAT against anisotropy in embedding bias tests
summary: Proposes ZCA whitening as a pre-processing step for the Word Embedding Association Test (WEAT), which assumes an isotropic embedding space that most modern LMs do not satisfy. Across 70 model-task combinations (10 WEAT suites, 7 models), whitening reduces anisotropy, improves semantic-similarity benchmark scores for anisotropic models, and flips significance status on over 30% of WEAT results — effect sizes shift in both directions.
takeaway: Bias measurements produced by WEAT on modern anisotropic embedding spaces are unreliable in both directions; prior fairness-audit numbers should be re-examined with a geometric calibration step.

lessons.point: WEAT presumes isotropy but most widely used LM embedding spaces are not isotropic.
lessons.excerpt: It relies on cosine similarity as a measure of semantic association, which assumes that the embedding space is approximately isotropic. However, prior work has reported that many widely used language models do not satisfy this assumption, raising concerns about the reliability of bias measurements.

lessons.point: After ZCA whitening, over 30% of WEAT results change significance status, with effect sizes shifting in both directions.
lessons.excerpt: After calibration, over 30\% of WEAT results change significance status, and effect sizes shift in both directions depending on bias category.

lessons.point: Uncalibrated WEAT can both overestimate and underestimate encoded associations, so past bias reports should be re-evaluated.
lessons.excerpt: These shifts suggest that uncalibrated measurements may both overestimate and underestimate the associations encoded in the embedding space.

actionable.title: Discount pre-2026 WEAT-based bias numbers
actionable.detail: If an internal fairness or bias-audit report cites WEAT effect sizes on modern LM embeddings without a whitening or isotropy correction, treat the numbers as unreliable in either direction. Ask for re-runs with a calibrated space before acting on them.

prior_art: Prior anisotropy work (Ethayarajh 2019, BERT-flow, whitening for STS) motivates the geometric problem; the contribution is applying ZCA specifically as a WEAT pre-processing step and quantifying how much significance flips.

title: LiveMem: Maintaining Memory State Continuity in Long-Running LLM Inference
summary: arXiv preprint proposing LiveMem, an intrinsic memory mechanism that augments a pretrained full-attention LLM with a persistent memory state (independent of the KV window) so long-running assistants keep useful information after originating tokens are evicted. Evaluated on LongMemEval; framed as a machine-learning mechanism paper, not a security paper.
takeaway: Long-lived agent memory research keeps moving from retrieval-plus-summarization toward intrinsic persistent state — an architectural shift worth tracking for the agent-memory attack surface but with no direct security finding here.

lessons.point: The problem being solved is 'state continuity under context turnover': keeping useful computation alive after the tokens that produced it are evicted from the context.
lessons.excerpt: We formulate this missing inference capability as \emph{state continuity under context turnover}: carrying computation forward through a fixed-capacity memory state whose lifetime is independent of the active context.

lessons.point: LiveMem is described as an intrinsic (weights/attention-level) memory, not an external retrieval or summarization layer — which matters for defenders because it means poisoning would target the model's own state, not a swappable RAG store.
lessons.excerpt: We introduce an intrinsic memory method, \textbf{LiveMem}, which augments a pretrained full-attention LLM with a memory state that preserves the historical information over the whole lifecycle while the main attention path retains a bounded KV window.

lessons.point: The paper claims useful information survives beyond the active window, evidenced by answering questions whose supporting text has been removed from context.
lessons.excerpt: Experiments on LongMemEval show that LiveMem is able to answer the question based on the memory state, even when the supporting evidence has been removed from the current context, and evidence-distance analysis shows that useful information persists beyond the active window.

actionable.title: Track intrinsic-memory LLMs as a new agent-memory attack surface
actionable.detail: Intrinsic persistent memory shifts the poisoning target from an external vector store to model-internal state. Note the direction for future threat-model work but do not derive a security claim from this preprint on its own.

prior_art: Extends the long-line of long-context / memory-augmented LLM work (Memorizing Transformers, Longformer, memory-tokens); complementary to RAG.
threat: None claimed in this paper. Adjacent security concern: intrinsic memory that survives context turnover expands the window in which cross-session memory poisoning would persist inside model state rather than in a swappable retrieval store.
conditions: Applies only to deployments that adopt intrinsic memory architectures like LiveMem for long-running assistants; ordinary bounded-KV models are unaffected.
mitigations: None in scope for this paper. General agent-memory hygiene (input provenance labels, memory-write gating, periodic memory audits) would apply if such architectures ship.

title: Provable Training Data Identification for Large Language Models
summary: Reframes membership-style training-data identification as a set-level inference problem with a distribution-free method (PTDI) that uses conformal p-values plus a Jackknife-corrected Beta boundary estimator to control the false identification rate via Benjamini-Hochberg.
takeaway: Treating training-data identification as set-level inference with FIR control gives statistically defensible answers rather than instance-wise scores whose error rate is opaque.

lessons.point: Instance-wise membership inference scores do not by themselves control the set-level error rate; auditors need FDR-style guarantees.
lessons.excerpt: existing works typically treat this task as an instance-wise identification without controlling the error rate of the identified set, which cannot provide statistically reliable evidence

lessons.point: Conformal p-values plus BH give a distribution-free path to provable false identification control for training-data audits.
lessons.excerpt: By applying the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure to the scaled p-values, we select a subset of data points with provable and strict false identification control

actionable.title: Report set-level FIR when auditing training data claims
actionable.detail: When investigating whether a corpus was used to train a model, prefer PTDI-style set-level inference with a stated false identification rate over raw per-example membership scores.

prior_art: Builds on membership inference attack literature (Shokri et al. 2017 and follow-ups) and conformal prediction; the contribution is combining them with a Beta-boundary estimator for BH.
threat: Loose relevance: MIA-style training-data identification is used both offensively (privacy attacks) and defensively (copyright/consent auditing); this paper is the audit side, not an attack.
conditions: Requires a set of known unseen data to calibrate conformal p-values; strong assumptions about the audit distribution.
mitigations: For model providers wanting robust rebuttals to data-provenance claims, standardize on FIR-controlled set-level audits rather than trading anecdotes about per-example memorization.

title: SABRE: Scalable and Automated Benchmarking of VLMs under Stress
summary: SABRE is a pipeline that turns a 'Test Primer' (a Markdown task design with a data schema) into structured specs, generated or edited images, and QA pairs, then filters out samples an existing VLM already solves and hands the rest to human reviewers. Its SABRE-Prior instance targets four stress axes (unexpected entities, counterfactual textures, noncanonical attribute counts, language-elicited answers) and reports 17.8 percent to 31.3 percent macro-average accuracy across six VLMs, with counting and spatial pilots showing the pipeline generalizes.
takeaway: A red-team methodology for VLM stress tests: filter out anything a reference VLM solves, keep only samples that force reliance on visual evidence over language priors.

lessons.point: Automated filtering by a reference VLM plus human validation is used to keep stress-test samples that current models actually fail on.
lessons.excerpt: Automated filtering removes candidates solved by a Filtering VLM, while human review verifies candidate validity and supports annotation correction and localized image repair.

lessons.point: On SABRE-Prior, current VLMs score far below chance-adjusted expectation across six models, with a mean of 22.6 percent.
lessons.excerpt: Across six VLMs, macro-average accuracy ranges from 17.8% to 31.3% (22.6% mean).

actionable.title: Adopt filter-by-reference-model pattern in AI-security eval sets
actionable.detail: For red-team benchmarks (jailbreak sets, agent trap corpora, prompt-injection suites), reuse SABRE's discipline: auto-drop anything that a reference model already solves or refuses correctly, then human-verify the survivors. Keeps eval sets from silting up with resolved cases and preserves signal on live failure modes.

prior_art: AutoBencher, DynaBench, and other adversarial-example curation pipelines; SABRE's contribution is the Test Primer specification and integrated image generation and human repair loop.
