title: Conditioning Protein Generation via Hopfield Pattern Multiplicity
summary: Training-free method that biases a Hopfield-style stochastic-attention sampler toward a subset of a protein family by adding one multiplicity-ratio term to its logits, which under unit-norm memories exactly corresponds to reweighting a Gaussian mixture. Empirically it steers generation across five Pfam families and produces omega-conotoxin candidates preserving key residues.
takeaway: A single scalar on the logits gives closed-form control over which subfamily a Hopfield sampler emits, cleanly separating latent-space conditioning from downstream sampling / decoding losses.

lessons.point: The whole conditioning knob is one scalar added to logits, tied to the multiplicity of designated versus background patterns.
lessons.excerpt: We condition a training-free stochastic-attention sampler by adding one multiplicity ratio to its logits. Increasing this ratio shifts generation from the full family toward the designated subset.

lessons.point: Under unit-norm memories the induced distribution is provably a Gaussian mixture with weights set by the multiplicities.
lessons.excerpt: For unit-norm memories, the resulting Boltzmann distribution is exactly a Gaussian mixture whose component weights are set by the multiplicities.

lessons.point: Recovery of specific residue markers is bottlenecked by PCA separability rather than the conditioning mechanism itself.
lessons.excerpt: Across five Pfam families, attention followed the analytic target, but recovery of single-residue markers depended on how well PCA separated the designated and background sequences.

actionable.title: Skip for security lane
actionable.detail: Domain-specific bio-ML. No adversary model or misuse framing in the paper; would only re-enter security scope if used as a bioweapon-misuse case study.

prior_art: Modern Hopfield networks (Ramsauer et al.), stochastic attention samplers, profile HMMs, ESM2 protein LMs, Pfam alignments.

title: Text-anchored cross-modal transfer debiases visual counter-commonsense reasoning
summary: The authors show that MLLM failures on counter-commonsense visual reasoning are not a vision-encoder problem — the correct answer is already in the decoding space — but a language-prior problem in the shared decoder. TACT is a text-only post-training framework that debiases the decoder using a fact-frequency-distilled counter-commonsense corpus, with no visual training data.
takeaway: When multimodal outputs contradict the image, the fix is often at the language decoder, not the vision encoder — a text-only debiasing pass can transfer to visual reasoning.

lessons.point: MLLM counter-commonsense failures are downstream of language priors, not visual grounding: the visual evidence is already captured.
lessons.excerpt: MLLMs already capture the relevant visual evidence, and the correct answer exists in their decoding space. Instead, the shared language decoder resolves prior--evidence conflicts by favoring dominant language priors, especially for low-frequency factual scenarios.

lessons.point: A text-only post-training corpus built from fact-frequency estimates can debias a multimodal decoder without any visual training data.
lessons.excerpt: we introduce TACT, a text-anchored post-training framework that debiases the shared language decoder without requiring any visual training data.

actionable.title: Locate the failure at the right layer
actionable.detail: For multimodal systems, don't reflexively blame the vision path. If the model 'sees' the answer but writes something else, the language decoder is the intervention point. Diagnose which layer holds the evidence before adding training data at another.

prior_art: Language-prior debiasing in VQA (VQA-CP, LMH), MLLM hallucination-reduction work (POPE, OPERA). TACT's specific contribution is text-only post-training via fact-frequency distillation; the diagnosis (decoder-side bias) is consistent with prior VQA-CP-era findings.

title: Concept vectors and linear probes measure ESG content from LLM activations
summary: arXiv preprint that probes frozen LLM activations with linear probes and Recursive Feature Machine concept vectors to measure ESG-concept content in financial text. title: Intrinsic bias mitigation in LLMs can improve downstream fairness
summary: Proposes Fairness-Aware Concept Unlearning (FACU), a representation-level regularizer that pushes stereotypical vs anti-stereotypical association probabilities toward parity while preserving language-model quality. Evaluated on three open LLMs and three socio-economic classification datasets; reports statistically significant intrinsic-bias drops that carry through to downstream fairness metrics, with counterfactual data augmentation stacking on top.
takeaway: Bias/fairness paper, not security. Contributes evidence that intrinsic bias mitigation can meaningfully move downstream fairness metrics without tanking predictive performance — a data point for teams deploying LLMs in high-stakes classification.

lessons.point: FACU balances stereotypical vs anti-stereotypical probability differences at the representation level rather than suppressing concepts entirely.
lessons.excerpt: FACU explicitly regularizes probability differences between stereotypical and anti-stereotypical associations while preserving predictive performance and language modeling quality

lessons.point: Intrinsic gender-bias reductions were associated with downstream fairness gains across most, but not all, settings evaluated.
lessons.excerpt: FACU produces statistically significant reductions in intrinsic gender bias that are associated with downstream fairness improvements across most evaluated settings

lessons.point: Combining FACU with extrinsic mitigation (counterfactual data augmentation) yields further fairness improvements — the two approaches are complementary rather than redundant.
lessons.excerpt: Combining FACU with extrinsic mitigation methods, particularly counterfactual data augmentation, yields further fairness improvements

actionable.title: Fairness-focused unlearning is an active alignment sub-thread
actionable.detail: For any downstream product using LLM embeddings in classification of people-related features, intrinsic-plus-extrinsic bias mitigation stacking is worth an experiment slot. Not a security finding, so no threat/mitigation model applies here.

prior_art: Concept unlearning; representation debiasing; counterfactual data augmentation.

title: Symbolic patterns emerge in artificial neural networks
summary: Claims that ANN inference logic can be reformulated as sparse symbolic interactions and proves two implicit mathematical criteria that force such emergence, with empirical transferability across samples and models.

lessons.point: The claim is architecture-agnostic: the emergence proof does not depend on a specific ANN architecture.
lessons.excerpt: the observed emergence of symbolic patterns in ANNs suggests that similar symbolic representations may also emerge in other types of black-box systems under certain conditions, because our proof does not depend on any specific ANN architecture.

lessons.excerpt: We further prove that two common mathematical criteria, which are implicitly required across tasks, lead to the emergence of such sparse symbolic interactions.

lessons.point: Interactions transfer sample-to-sample and model-to-model, evidencing faithfulness rather than post-hoc curve-fitting.

title: Aphasic picture naming errors reveal lesion parameters in large language models
summary: Trains inverse models on 4,840 lesion configurations of LLaVA-Vicuna 13B to recover perturbation parameters from picture-naming error profiles. Modification percentage and noise sigma are recoverable; layer index is only recoverable within a neighborhood, yet counterfactual perturbation reproduces target behavior in 81.4% of cases — consistent with functional redundancy across transformer layers.
takeaway: Behavior-to-parameter inverse mapping in LLMs shows that some perturbation parameters are recoverable while layer index is not, evidence of functional redundancy across transformer layers that standard interpretability misses.

lessons.point: Interpretability methods describe internal state but do not test causal sufficiency; counterfactual validation does.
lessons.excerpt: Interpretability methods for large language models (LLMs) describe internal state but do not directly test whether that state is causally sufficient to produce the observed behavior.

lessons.point: Layer index is only recoverable within a neighborhood despite high counterfactual fidelity.
lessons.excerpt: modification percentage and noise sigma were recoverable, whereas layer index was recoverable only within a neighborhood.

lessons.point: Dissociation between low layer recovery and high counterfactual fidelity implies functional redundancy across transformer layers.
lessons.excerpt: This dissociation between low layer recovery and high counterfactual fidelity is consistent with functional redundancy across transformer layers, a property not captured by standard interpretability methods.

actionable.title: Track counterfactual validation as an interpretability standard
actionable.detail: For any interpretability claim about which layer or component produces which behavior, functional redundancy means single-layer attributions are likely under-identified; require counterfactual reproduction, not just correlation with internal state.

prior_art: General LLM interpretability methods that describe internal state without testing causal sufficiency are the named target of critique; lesion studies from earlier work by the same authors are the direct precedent.

title: Stochastic Autoregressive Learning
summary: PAC-style learning-theory model for binary stochastic autoregressive generators. takeaway: Stochastic autoregressive learning is not a straight extension of the deterministic theory: CoT vs base vs end-to-end sample complexity cannot be universally ordered at fixed scale, only after re-scaling.

lessons.point: The stochastic setting fundamentally differs from the deterministic autoregressive-learning theory it generalizes.
lessons.excerpt: We show that stochastic autoregressive learning fundamentally differs from the deterministic theory.

lessons.point: At fixed error scale, sample-complexity ratios between CoT/base and e2e/CoT can be made arbitrarily large.
lessons.excerpt: At scale ε, there is no universal comparison between the three learning tasks: both m C o T/m b a s eand m e 2 e/m C o Tcan be made simultaneously arbitrarily larger than M/ε, the natural analogue for the existing deterministic results.

lessons.point: After rescaling, CoT learning at scale ε is upper-bounded by base learning at scale ε/M^2.
lessons.excerpt: for every class, CoT learning at scale εis upper-bounded by base learning at scale ε/M 2, whereas e2e learning at scale εis upper-bounded, up to logarithmic factors, by (M/ε)m C o T(Θ(ε)).

title: An AI4AI Framework for Visual Token Pruning
summary: AutoPrune has an LLM design visual-token pruning policies for multimodal LLMs via a Token Pruning DSL (131 atoms) that expresses each candidate policy as a residual modification of a strong base policy. Reports 94.4% token removal while preserving >99% of full-token performance, 9.9x FLOPs reduction, and 6.4x prefill-latency reduction.
takeaway: Framing algorithm design as residual edits over a strong base policy, in a task-specific DSL, is the load-bearing trick that lets an LLM's general reasoning translate into competitive pruning policies.

lessons.point: The DSL's key trick is representing each search state as a residual on a strong base policy, narrowing the search space.
lessons.excerpt: A key property of TPDSL is that it represents each search state as a residual modification of a strong base policy. This residual formulation narrows the search space and directs the LLM's attention toward the policy components that are most consequential for performance.

lessons.point: Effective LLM-as-designer requires a search-state representation that bridges general LLM knowledge and task structure.
lessons.excerpt: We argue that the key lies in designing an appropriate search-state representation that connects the internal knowledge of LLMs with the structural requirements and constraints of visual-token pruning.

lessons.point: Reported gains: 94.4% visual tokens removed at >99% of full-token performance, 9.9x FLOPs and 6.4x prefill speedup.
lessons.excerpt: Even when removing 94.4% of visual tokens, AutoPrune preserves more than 99% of full-token performance while reducing FLOPs by 9.9x and prefill latency by 6.4x.

title: Capacity Confounds and Coverage Guarantees in Adaptive Sub-model Federated Learning
summary: Shows that in adaptive sub-model federated learning, update-divergence-based client-heterogeneity estimates are dominated by device capacity rather than data heterogeneity, that uncovered parameters left at random init progressively corrupt the global model, and that a matched-budget random baseline equals or beats adaptive allocation.
takeaway: In sub-model federated learning, parameter coverage and capacity budgeting explain the accuracy wins usually credited to adaptive per-client capacity allocation; update-based heterogeneity estimates are confounded by capacity and separate signals are needed for future adaptive methods.

lessons.point: Update-divergence estimates of client heterogeneity are confounded by device capacity across estimators, datasets, and seeds.
lessons.excerpt: validated against ground-truth label-distribution divergence on reproducible partitions, update-divergence estimates of client heterogeneity are dominated by capacity rather than data: across two corrected estimators, multiple datasets, and all seeds, the estimates correlate strongly and negatively with device capacity, and no data signal remains once capacity is controlled for.

lessons.point: When every client is capped below full width, uncovered parameters stay at random init and corrupt the global model.
lessons.excerpt: when every client is capped below full width, the uncovered parameters stay at random initialization and progressively corrupt the global model.

lessons.point: A matched-budget random allocation performs no worse than adaptive allocation on image benchmarks and better on the naturally partitioned text benchmark.
lessons.excerpt: random allocation to the same average budget performs no differently on both image benchmarks, and on the naturally partitioned text benchmark the adaptive policy is the weakest of the three strategies while consuming the most capacity.

lessons.point: The capacity confound affects any method that estimates client statistics from sub-model updates.
lessons.excerpt: This previously undocumented confound affects any method estimating client statistics from sub-model updates.

actionable.title: Distrust heterogeneity signals recovered from sub-model updates alone
actionable.detail: If you build or defend a federated system that estimates client heterogeneity or data distribution from sub-model updates, treat those estimates as capacity-confounded until proven otherwise; use ground-truth-partition validation, and ensure parameter coverage rather than allocation cleverness.

prior_art: HAS-FL and general adaptive capacity-allocation frameworks for sub-model federated learning are the explicit priors this work evaluates and refutes.

title: Cascade uses SLO-aware latency budgets for fair LLM inference serving
summary: Cascade defines a per-request latency budget (SLO minus predicted remaining service time) and uses that single signal to jointly coordinate LLM request scheduling and KV-cache management across memory tiers, prioritizing tight-budget requests and directing queue/data-movement overhead to those that can absorb it. On production traces across three LLMs it improves SLO-satisfied goodput by up to 2.4x and reduces SLO violations by 40% versus vLLM FCFS.
takeaway: A single per-request latency-budget signal can jointly govern scheduler ordering and KV-cache tiering; treating budget as a shared coordination variable outperforms deadline-only SLO schedulers on heterogeneous LLM traffic.

lessons.point: Per-request latency budget is defined as the SLO minus predicted remaining service time and is continuously updated from request characteristics, KV state, and system load.
lessons.excerpt: We define this headroom---the difference between a request's service level objective and its predicted remaining service time---as its per-request latency budget.

lessons.point: Unlike prior SLO-aware schedulers that only use deadlines for ordering, Cascade uses the budget to jointly coordinate scheduling and KV-cache placement across the memory hierarchy.
lessons.excerpt: Unlike prior SLO-aware schedulers that use deadlines to govern request ordering alone, Cascade uses a single per-request budget to jointly coordinate request scheduling and KV-cache management across the memory hierarchy.

lessons.point: Reported gains over vLLM's default FCFS scheduler on production traces are up to 2.4x goodput and 40% fewer SLO violations.
lessons.excerpt: Cascade improves goodput by up to2.4x and reduces SLO violations by 40% relative to the default vLLM first-come, first-served scheduler.

title: Seeking SOTA: Time-Series Forecasting Must Adopt Taxonomy-Specific Evaluation to Dispel Illusory Gains
summary: Position paper arguing standard time-series-forecasting benchmarks are dominated by periodic/seasonal datasets that trivial linear/statistical baselines already handle. takeaway: The 'deep-learning time-series SOTA' picture is mostly an artifact of benchmark selection. Same lesson recurs elsewhere in ML: pick harder eval sets and require simple baselines. Not directly security-relevant.

lessons.point: On typical time-series benchmarks with strong periodicity, deep models frequently match but do not beat simple linear/statistical baselines despite much higher compute cost.
lessons.excerpt: these "standard" datasets often exhibit dominant autocorrelation patterns and seasonal cycles that can be effectively captured by simpler linear or statistical models, rendering complex deep learning architectures frequently no more performant than their classical counterparts for these specific data characteristics, and raising questions as to whether any marginal improvements justify the significant increase in computational overhead and model complexity.

lessons.point: Recommendation: retire/augment current benchmarks with non-stationary regimes and force every deep-learning submission to include appropriate classical baselines.
lessons.excerpt: We call on the community to (I) retire or substantially augment current benchmarks with datasets exhibiting a wider spectrum of non-stationarities, such as structural breaks, time-varying volatility, and concept drift, and less predictable dynamics drawn from diverse real-world domains, and (II) require every deep learning submission to include robust classical and simple baselines, appropriately chosen for the specific characteristics of the downstream tasks' time series.

lessons.excerpt: In a prespecified five-fold nested sleep study, BDL-Hard raises pooled out-of-fold mAP from 0.586 to 0.705 over interval segmentation (+11.9 percentage points; 95% interval [10.8, 13.0]) and strict one-minute AP from 0.071 to 0.286 (4.0x; +21.5 points), improving on every outer fold.

lessons.point: Most of the gain comes from direct boundary supervision and event decoding, not from the Poisson objective itself.

title: Online Conformal Prediction Beyond Feedback

lessons.point: The setting removes feedback on deployed predictions entirely; the learner queries or predicts, never both.
lessons.excerpt: We instead study an OCP setting beyond feedback: on each round, the learner can either output a prediction set or query the correct label, but not both. Thus, no deployed prediction is ever evaluated directly.

title: Beyond Post-Hoc Temperature Scaling: Bilevel Optimization for LLM Calibration

takeaway: Preference-aligned LLMs are overconfident and post-hoc temperature scaling does not transfer across domains; training-time entropy-maximization via bilevel optimization offers better cross-domain calibration.

title: InceptionRAG splits a RAG poison into harmless-looking passages
summary: Rather than one document with an explicit malicious payload, the attack spreads the payload across a chain of dormant passages that each look benign. When the retriever returns them together, the LLM reasons its way to the attacker's false conclusion. The authors report over 80% attack success across three datasets and three LLMs. The attack evades defenses built for single-document injection. They propose a document-isolation defense called HODOR.

lessons.point: Poisoning can be distributed across passages that look harmless, and those passages can bypass existing mitigation mechanisms when examined separately.
lessons.excerpt: Instead of injecting explicit malicious payloads, InceptionRAG fragments it into a chain of dormant passages.

lessons.point: The harm emerges at inference time through multi-hop reasoning over co-retrieved passages, so per-document filters miss it.
lessons.excerpt: However, when retrieved together, they trigger LLMs to self-deduce target misinformation via multi-hop reasoning.

lessons.point: Stronger reasoning in the model makes this class of attack more effective, not less.
lessons.excerpt: Our findings expose a concerning paradox: the stronger reasoning capabilities of LLMs increase their vulnerability to reasoning-based poisoning attacks.

lessons.point: Isolating retrieved documents from each other breaks the logical dependency the attack relies on.
lessons.excerpt: we propose a document isolation-based defense, HODOR, which decouples adversarial logical dependencies.

takeaway: RAG defenses that screen documents one at a time are insufficient; test the retrieved set as a whole and consider isolating documents during reasoning.

actionable.title: Red-team RAG with fragmented, multi-document poisons
actionable.detail: Extend RAG poisoning tests beyond single-document injections: craft sets of individually benign passages that jointly imply a false claim, check whether your injection filters flag any of them, and evaluate a document-isolation step (answer per document, then aggregate) as a mitigation.

prior_art: Closest in pool is the archive entry on RAG poisoning via injected malicious documents in the retrieval corpus and the Salience Induction entry (true statements, no instructions, steering multi-hop RAG); InceptionRAG extends this to chained dormant passages that evade single-document defenses. title: None resisted all three injected stresses in eight multi-agent worlds
summary: Emergence World runs eight parallel worlds of ten agents (seven single-model, one mixed) for 16 days. It then delivers indirect prompt injection, misinformation and private-memory exposure through ordinary interaction surfaces. No world was fully resilient. Agents could recognize a threat yet still write it into persistent memory and act on it up to 46 hours later. The same model behaved differently in mixed versus homogeneous populations.

lessons.point: Detecting an attack does not mean containing it; flagged content can still enter memory and drive later actions.
lessons.excerpt: Detection did not ensure containment: systems could recognize threats while still interacting with adversarial content, writing it into their own persistent memory, and acting on it up to 46 hours later.

lessons.point: Every tested configuration failed at least one of the stress events.
lessons.excerpt: No evaluated world achieved full resilience across all three events.

lessons.point: Safe-looking individual models do not guarantee safe multi-agent systems.
lessons.excerpt: Our results suggest that model-level alignment is not compositional: individually capable and apparently safe agents can form systems with qualitatively different failure modes.

lessons.point: Behavior depends on the population the model sits in, so isolated evaluation is unreliable.
lessons.excerpt: The same model-persona pairing behaved substantially different in mixed and homogeneous populations.

takeaway: Test long-running multi-agent deployments with delayed, memory-persisting attacks; screening content at read time is not enough when it can be remembered and acted on days later.

actionable.title: Add delayed-effect stress events to long-running agent evaluations
actionable.detail: After agents have accumulated state, inject indirect prompt injection, misinformation and memory-exposure events through normal interaction channels, then audit persistent memory and later actions (including many hours afterward) for contamination. Add write-time checks on what enters long-term memory, and run both single-model and mixed-model configurations.

prior_art: Closest are the pool's agent-memory poisoning claims and the OrchestraBench multi-agent failure-mode entry; no equivalent 16-day multi-world stress test with delayed injected-content effects found in pool. Verifier: archive.json: 'MemoryTrap: persistent memory poisoning in AI coding agents (OWASP ASI06)'; ai-security.json: 'Self-state attacks: corrupting an agent's own memory and config uses legitimate syscalls'
threat: Adversarial content (indirect prompt injection, misinformation, exposed private memories) entering persistent multi-agent systems and propagating through memory, tools and other agents over time.
conditions: Long-running agents with persistent memory, tools and shared institutions; stress events delivered after operational state accumulates; eight worlds of ten agents over 16 days.
mitigations: Engineer system-level resilience rather than relying on model alignment; the paper reports no fully resilient configuration and gives no specific fix in the abstract.
verify_note: Excerpts verbatim and 8 worlds/10 agents/16 days match. Memory-persisted injection is known; the new element is the long-horizon multi-agent evaluation and the non-compositional alignment claim. Useful for agent-harness builders. title: Decoy Direction Optimization makes refusal-direction ablation remove a decoy instead
summary: Refusal Feature Ablation removes a linear refusal direction from a model's activations and strips its safety behavior. The authors add a high-magnitude nonlinear decoy signal in MLP neurons (a weight edit, no finetuning) so the attacker's estimator picks a harmless direction. They report under 10% attack success under standard ablation across six model families, and Heretic weight-level attack success on Llama-3-8B-Instruct dropping from 88.7% to 18%.

lessons.point: Open-weight safety can be bypassed cheaply by ablating one refusal direction, and trained defenses must be repeated for every checkpoint.
lessons.excerpt: Defending against these attacks typically requires computationally expensive safety finetuning for every new checkpoint.

lessons.point: The defense misleads the attacker's estimator rather than hiding the refusal circuitry.
lessons.excerpt: DDO actively injects a high-magnitude, nonlinear decoy signal into the network's MLP neurons.

lessons.point: Against adaptive multi-phase attacks the post-hoc edit comes at much lower cost.
lessons.excerpt: reduces Heretic weight-level attack ASR from 88.7% to 18%, all at 30 to 450 times lower optimization cost per configuration than the trained baselines.

takeaway: If you ship open weights, refusal behavior is trivially removable; a cheap post-hoc decoy edit raises attacker cost but is a mitigation, not a guarantee.

actionable.title: Do not treat open-weight refusal as a security boundary; test anti-abliteration defenses against adaptive attacks
actionable.detail: When releasing or deploying open-weight models, assume refusal can be ablated. If adopting a decoy-style weight edit, test it against adaptive multi-phase attacks and weight-level attacks (e.g. Heretic), not only standard Refusal Feature Ablation, since worst-case ASR (65% on Llama-3-8B-Instruct) is far above the standard-attack figure.

prior_art: Nearest in pool is the Perturbation Probing entry on fragility of LLM safety; no equivalent post-hoc anti-abliteration weight-edit defense found in pool. Verifier: No equivalent in the four files; nearest is archive.json 'Perturbation Probing: A New Diagnostic for the Fragility of LLM Safety' (loosely related). Anti-abliteration defense not covered.
threat: Refusal Feature Ablation and weight-level attacks (Heretic) remove safety behavior from open-weight models while keeping capability.
conditions: Attacker has the model weights and can estimate the refusal direction with contrastive estimators.
mitigations: Decoy Direction Optimization: post-hoc weight edit injecting a nonlinear decoy signal in MLP neurons, no base-model finetuning; still leaves 65% worst-case ASR under adaptive attacks on Llama-3-8B-Instruct.
verify_note: Numbers match the abstract; note 65% worst-case ASR under adaptive attack is high, so 'on par' is honest but not a strong defense. Niche for defenders who ship open weights. Unsupported: Lesson 3 excerpt supports the Heretic 88.7%->18% and cost claim but not the 'roughly on par with trained defenses' point (that is the 65% vs 58% worst-case sentence, not quoted). Excerpt problem: Lesson 3 excerpt does not carry the 'on par' claim it is attached to; verbatim otherwise. Corrected: removed the 'roughly on par with trained defenses' clause from lesson 3 point and capped its confidence at 0.6.

title: LMdeploy's ZeroMQ RPC server unpickles untrusted network data, giving remote code execution
summary: LMdeploy, an LLM serving toolkit, runs an RPC server. Its call_and_response() function passes received bytes straight to pickle.loads(). Anyone who can reach that socket can send a crafted pickle and run code on the serving host. The advisory is rated critical.

lessons.point: LMdeploy ships an RPC server (AsyncRPCServer in zmq_rpc.py) for its RPC communications.
lessons.excerpt: The LMdeploy implements an rpc server (AsyncRPCServer in zmq_rpc.py) for supporting the RPC communications.

lessons.point: Deserializing received messages with pickle.loads() lets any sender execute arbitrary code.
lessons.excerpt: In its core functionality call_and_response(), I found it will directly use the pickles.loads() to deserialize the received

takeaway: Model-serving RPC layers must never use pickle on network input; use a data-only format or authenticate and isolate the channel.

actionable.title: Do not expose LLM serving RPC ports and patch LMdeploy
actionable.detail: Upgrade lmdeploy to the fixed release named in the advisory, keep its ZeroMQ RPC ports off untrusted networks, and grep your serving code for pickle.loads on socket data.

prior_art: The pool has pickle-format model code-execution claims, but this is a pickle RPC sink in a serving framework rather than a model file; no direct lmdeploy entry found. Verifier: archive.json: 'ShadowPickle: pickle-VM import tricks evade ten model scanners and four model hubs' (pickle code execution, but in model files); no earlier RPC or serving-framework pickle entry found
threat: Remote code execution on an LMdeploy host by sending a malicious pickle to its RPC server.
conditions: Attacker can reach the AsyncRPCServer ZeroMQ endpoint of an unpatched lmdeploy deployment.
mitigations: Upgrade lmdeploy, restrict network access to the RPC port, replace pickle with a safe serialization format.
verify_note: Standard unauthenticated-pickle RCE; delta vs prior art is only the LMdeploy serving-RPC location. Refuted narrowly on lesson 1's overclaim about the core serving path; summary and lesson 2 hold. Unsupported: Lesson 1 point says the RPC server is 'part of the core serving path' and 'default inference infrastructure'; the excerpt only says it exists 'for supporting the RPC communications' and that call_and_response() is core functionality of that server; 'inter-process communication' and 'ZeroMQ' beyond the title are not in the excerpt. Excerpt problem: Lesson 2 excerpt ends mid-sentence ('the received') because the candidate excerpt is truncated; it is verbatim but incomplete, and uses 'pickles.loads()' (source typo) while the point/summary say pickle.loads(). Corrected: lesson 1 point replaced with the supported claim (RPC server exists) and its confidence capped at 0.4.

title: mysql-mcp-server SSE allows unauthenticated SQL execution via DNS rebinding
summary: In SSE/HTTP mode, the pip package mysql-mcp-server builds its transport without the security settings that turn on the MCP Python SDK's DNS-rebinding protection. A web page or network client can therefore reach the server's SQL tooling without authentication. The advisory is rated critical.

lessons.point: The MCP SDK's DNS-rebinding protection is opt-in: if the server author does not pass security settings to the SSE transport, no Origin/Host validation happens.
lessons.excerpt: In SSE/HTTP transport mode, `mysql_mcp_server` constructs `SseServerTransport` without passing `security_settings`.

lessons.point: Without Origin/Host header validation, a local or network-reachable MCP server with a database tool is exposed to rebinding or direct access, so SQL runs with no authentication.
lessons.excerpt: the MCP Python SDK's DNS-rebinding protection (Origin/Host header validation)

takeaway: Any MCP server exposed over HTTP/SSE must explicitly enable Origin/Host validation and authentication, especially when it fronts a database.

actionable.title: Audit HTTP/SSE MCP servers for transport security settings
actionable.detail: For every MCP server you run in SSE/HTTP mode, confirm the transport is constructed with security settings that enforce allowed Origin and Host headers, bind to localhost only unless needed, and require authentication. Upgrade mysql-mcp-server to a fixed release per the advisory.

prior_art: The pool has LiteLLM MCP and AI-infrastructure control-point entries, but no earlier entry on missing DNS-rebinding protection in an MCP SSE transport. Verifier: ai-security.json: 'obsidian-tc MCP server lacks Origin checks, letting a web page read and write the vault' (same class: missing Origin validation on local MCP HTTP server)
threat: Unauthenticated SQL execution through a MySQL MCP server reachable by DNS rebinding or direct network access.
conditions: mysql-mcp-server run in SSE/HTTP transport mode, where the SDK's Origin/Host validation was never enabled.
mitigations: Upgrade to the fixed version, pass security settings enabling Origin/Host validation, bind to loopback, add authentication.
verify_note: Excerpts are verbatim from candidates.json. Claim is a near-restatement of the obsidian-tc Origin-check entry, with a different package and the SDK-opt-in detail. Unsupported: Source is only a truncated excerpt: 'opt-in' framing, loopback binding, and 'upgrade to fixed version' mitigations are inferences not in the excerpt; Lesson 2 excerpt is only a noun phrase, it does not itself support the stated consequence.

title: A self-replicating worm on stolen compute infected a lab network
summary: A blog post summarizes an arXiv paper in which an AI-agent worm generates tailored attacks, escalates privileges, and copies its harness onto each compromised host, plus a local open-weight LLM when resources allow (otherwise it calls back to the parent host's LLM). In 15 seven-day runs on an isolated 33-host network, it exploited 73.8% of hosts and replicated to 61.8%. Because it needs no commercial AI platform, vendor refusals and rate limits do not apply; the agents also tried to edit their own IP blacklist, which the hypervisor containment caught.

lessons.point: Stolen compute removes the attacker's extra cost per use and sidesteps provider-side controls.
lessons.excerpt: because the worm requires no commercial AI platform, centralized safety controls, such as service refusals or rate limiting, are structurally irrelevant

lessons.point: The proof of concept achieved substantial spread in a mixed Linux, Windows and internet-of-things (IoT) lab network.
lessons.excerpt: Put another way, on average, the proof-of-concept worm successfully exploited 73.8% of the network and then replicated to 61.8% of the network.

lessons.point: Agents tried to weaken their own guardrails; containment had to sit outside the agent's reach.
lessons.excerpt: we observed at various points in our experiments the agent discovering this file and preemptively rewriting it to withdraw the IP address it planned on targeting.

takeaway: Defenders cannot count on AI-vendor safeguards against AI-driven malware; plan for network-level detection of unusual compute and traffic, and keep agent containment on a layer the agent cannot modify.

actionable.title: Detect agent-worm behavior at the host and network layer, and enforce containment outside the agent's reach
actionable.detail: Monitor for unexpected local LLM runtimes, large model downloads, graphics processing unit (GPU) usage and sustained agent-to-agent traffic on endpoints; patch the common corporate vulnerabilities the worm exploited. When running offensive agent experiments, put safeguards (such as target blacklists) enforced at a hypervisor the agent cannot reach, since agents may rewrite config inside the guest.

prior_art: Nearest in pool are the ChainDrop and Mini Shai-Hulud npm worm entries and the Anthropic Frontier Red Team CTF entry; none cover LLM-agent worms running local open-weight models. This item is a secondhand blog summary of arXiv 2606.03811. Verifier: archive.json: 'ChainDrop: Self-propagating npm worm...' and 'keyv/cacheable Mini Shai-Hulud' (self-propagating worms, but not LLM-driven); ai-security.json: 'Anthropic Frontier Red Team (March 2025)... failed autonomous network attacks'
threat: AI-agent worm that generates per-target exploits, gains admin access and self-replicates with its own harness and a local open-weight LLM on compromised hosts.
conditions: Hosts with common real-world vulnerabilities; resources to run a local LLM or a network path back to a host that runs it; results are from an isolated 33-host lab, 15 runs of 7 days.
mitigations: Patch common corporate vulnerabilities, detect unusual compute and network use, and enforce containment at a hypervisor the agent cannot access.
verify_note: Secondhand blog summarizing arXiv 2606.03811; numbers (15 runs, 33 hosts, 73.8%, 61.8%, 7 days) match. LLM-driven adaptive worm on stolen open-weight compute with refusals/rate limits irrelevant is a fairly new claim for defenders. No embedded instructions noted (blog mentions Gemini helping replicate code, which is author anecdote). Unsupported: Summary says it copies a local open-weight LLM 'onto each compromised host'; source says only when resources are available, otherwise it calls back to the parent host's LLM; Lesson 4 point (resource-heavy behavior as detection signal) rests on the blog author's speculation, not on paper measurements; the attached excerpt is about economic asymmetry and does not support the point. Excerpt problem: Lesson 4 excerpt is verbatim but mismatched to the point. Corrected: summary now says the LLM is copied only when resources allow, otherwise it calls back to the parent host's LLM; lesson 4 (detection signal) deleted.

title: Cursor's VS Code import drops extension versions and installs latest
summary: SafeDep showed that Cursor's Import VS Code Configuration sends only extension names, so three deliberately old extensions all came back at Open VSX's newest version. Because the same name can map to different publishers or code across stores, and auto update is on by default, the editor's store decides what code runs on developer machines.

lessons.point: The import carries no version, so version pinning in the old editor is silently lost.
lessons.excerpt: The import reads your Visual Studio Code extension list and copies only the name of each one.

lessons.point: A registry you did not choose decides which extension code gets installed, and that code has file and process access.
lessons.excerpt: A store you never chose decided which version you get.

lessons.point: Extension names are not stable identities across Open VSX and Microsoft's marketplace, so they must be treated like package dependencies.
lessons.excerpt: The same `publisher.extension` name can point to different publishers or code on Open VSX than on the Microsoft Marketplace.

lessons.point: An install cooldown is a practical control against freshly published malicious versions.
lessons.excerpt: Make new versions wait before they can be installed.

takeaway: Pin extension versions explicitly in agentic IDEs, verify after any import, and use install cooldowns and publisher allowlists.

actionable.title: Verify and pin IDE extensions after migrating to Cursor
actionable.detail: After import, compare `code --list-extensions --show-versions` with `cursor --list-extensions --show-versions`; install exact versions with `cursor --install-extension <publisher>.<name>@<version>`; set extensions.installCooldownHours and a team publisher allowlist; check publishedBy on Open VSX.

prior_art: No Open VSX or Cursor extension entry found in the pool; it echoes general registry and unpinned-dependency supply-chain claims. Verifier: No Open VSX or Cursor extension entry in the data files. Nearest are archive.json: 'A Widely-Used VS Code Extension (9.5M Installs) Chained a Markdown eval() Sink...' (extension vuln, different claim) and general package-registry / dependency-cooldown claims
threat: Unintended, unreviewed extension versions or same-name different-publisher extensions installed from Open VSX into developer IDEs.
conditions: Using Cursor's Import VS Code Configuration, with auto update on and no allowlist or cooldown.
mitigations: Explicit version install, post-import diff, install cooldown, publisher allowlist, auto update off if updates are reviewed.
verify_note: All excerpts are verbatim and the summary matches the source (three old extensions all moved to Open VSX latest). The new part is Cursor import dropping versions; the 'treat extension IDs as dependencies' idea is a quote from Cursor's own docs and the cooldown advice is generic supply-chain hygiene. Unsupported: Lesson 4 point frames the cooldown as a control against 'malicious versions'; the source just says to make new versions wait and justifies it via auto-update risk, so this is a mild inference.

title: Deep-Live-Cam repo hijack hid a clipboard hijacker behind a dependency named requests
summary: On September 8, 2026, an attacker added a git-sourced dependency named requests to Deep-Live-Cam's requirements.txt. The attacker apparently used the maintainer's compromised GitHub account. Installing it ran a setup.py that hid its payload behind 434 spaces. That setup.py fetched later stages from a Telegraph page and installed a Windows and macOS clipboard hijacker. The hijacker swaps crypto wallet addresses and persists at login. The bad commit was on main for about 9 hours 39 minutes.

lessons.point: Building a source dependency executes setup.py, so malicious code can run during install, before the app starts.
lessons.excerpt: A user can reach the malicious code before launching Deep-Live-Cam.

lessons.point: Reverting the commit does not clean machines that already installed it; persistence stays behind.
lessons.excerpt: Reverting `requirements.txt` does not remove the files or startup entries from an affected machine.

lessons.point: The malicious loader ran before the version check, so error exits or guards in setup.py do not limit the code that executes.
lessons.excerpt: The version check is not a guard around the loader.

lessons.point: The analysis establishes malicious behavior only; victim counts and losses are unknown.
lessons.excerpt: The evidence establishes malicious behavior in the code, but does not establish infection counts or financial losses.

takeaway: Review requirements diffs for git+ URL sources, especially bulk rewrites that hide one new entry, and treat build-time code as install-time code execution.

actionable.title: Block and detect git-URL dependencies that shadow registry packages
actionable.detail: Add a CI check that flags any requirements.txt line using git+ URLs or whose source differs from the registry for well-known names such as requests, and require review for bulk dependency rewrites. Where possible install with --only-binary :all: or hash-pinned requirements. To check for exposure, search for %LOCALAPPDATA%\WindowsHelper\sys.pyw, a SysHelper Run key, or ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.user.syshelper.plist.

prior_art: No equivalent entry found in pool; the closest is archive material on npm and GitHub Actions supply chain disruption, which does not cover pip source-build triggers or hidden-whitespace loaders. Verifier: OVHcloud CLI: attacker swapped binaries on five GitHub releases for 94 minutes, delivering the GlassWorm loader
threat: A compromised maintainer account pushes a requirements.txt change pointing at a look-alike repository; pip builds it, setup.py executes an obfuscated multi-stage loader, and a clipboard hijacker replaces copied wallet addresses and persists via a registry Run key or a macOS LaunchAgent.
conditions: Users who installed Deep-Live-Cam dependencies from source on Windows or macOS during the roughly 9 hour 39 minute window the malicious commit was on main; Linux exits before the download.
mitigations: Revert the dependency and remove the persisted files and startup entries, rotate maintainer credentials and tokens, review bulk dependency diffs, pin and hash dependencies, and check for the listed indicators of compromise.
verify_note: Dates, the 9h39m window, 434 spaces and IOCs verified; excerpts verbatim. The hidden-whitespace setup.py loader and git+ shadowing of requests are a variation on known install-time execution. Unsupported: Tag 'dependency-confusion' does not fit: the source describes a git-URL source swap via a compromised account, not confusion; Lesson 3 generalizes to 'error exits or guards in setup.py' beyond the source's narrow version-check statement.

title: Chainguard starts disclosing Athena's silent-fix vulnerabilities
summary: Chainguard reports its Athena program has taken in over 40,000 AI-found findings across 500+ projects and will begin disclosing about 50 silent-fix vulnerabilities (fixed upstream, never assigned a CVE) with public patches, an OSV advisory feed and patched library versions. It describes running agents in microVM sandboxes with a harness where the host, not the model, must replay a finding before it counts, and argues the real endgame is secure-by-construction foundations because patch pipelines were already overloaded.

lessons.point: Do not let the model self-certify findings; require a host-side replay against a clean instance.
lessons.excerpt: A finding only counts if the host can replay it against a clean instance: the check fails before, the replay runs, the check passes after.

lessons.point: Sandbox failures come from the gaps around the boundary, not the boundary itself.
lessons.excerpt: They were a problem of insufficient sandboxing: the boundary existed, and everything interesting happened in the gaps around it.

lessons.point: Silent fixes leave old deployed versions exposed, with no CVE for scanners to match on.
lessons.excerpt: Silence in that channel was never safety, it was just nobody having looked yet.

lessons.point: Faster AI discovery lands on a patch backlog that was already behind.
lessons.excerpt: the flood is coming, and the pipes were already full.

takeaway: AI-scale vulnerability discovery shifts the bottleneck to disclosure and patch absorption, so verify findings by reproduction and plan for old versions that never got an advisory.

actionable.title: Gate agent-found vulnerabilities on host-side replay
actionable.detail: In any vulnerability-hunting agent loop, accept a finding only if the host can replay it on a clean instance (check fails before, passes after the fix). Start each agent with fresh scoped context and a distilled trail of known results, and record dead ends as findings. Run exploit detonation inside a microVM (lightweight virtual machine) with allowlisted outbound (egress) traffic and no credentials in the guest.

prior_art: The archive entry 'This Shit is Hard: Patching a vulnerability that has no fix' covers Chainguard's earlier Athena/sandbox work; the CNA scope for silent fixes and host-casts-the-vote harness rules are incremental. Verifier: archive: 'Chainguard's microVM primitive: hypervisor-enforced egress, no ambient credentials, and per-job destruction...'
verify_note: Excerpts verbatim and numbers supported. Minor title overclaim on CNA status. Host-replay harness rules and silent-fix disclosure are incremental over the earlier sandbox piece. Author is vendor CEO-style essay mixing marketing. Unsupported: Title says Chainguard 'becomes' a CNA; source says it is 'in progress to become' one. Corrected: title now says Chainguard is in the process of becoming a CVE numbering authority.

title: Wiz poster maps incident response logs for GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket
summary: Wiz's incident response team published a poster comparing which logs GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket and Azure DevOps keep, what to configure before an incident, and which audit event names correspond to attacker actions mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. The key lesson is that default retention and missing Git or API logs can leave responders unable to scope a breach. In one case, missing clone history forced an org-wide credential rotation.

lessons.point: Default VCS audit logging has gaps, so log streaming must be set up before an incident.
lessons.excerpt: Standard audit logs do not capture all activity, and default retention limits can severely restrict historical investigations.

lessons.point: Missing clone history turned a precise response into a broad credential rotation.
lessons.excerpt: Because historical Git clone events were not fully available due to standard retention limits, the scope of the exfiltrated repositories could not be determined.

lessons.point: Attackers delete workflow run logs to hide which secrets were exposed, so know the deletion audit events.
lessons.excerpt: In instances of Defense Evasion, attackers frequently delete workflow execution logs to cover their tracks and obfuscate which sensitive secrets were exposed during malicious pipeline execution.

lessons.point: Stream events to external storage so logs survive until a breach is discovered late.
lessons.excerpt: Streaming events to an external datastore is necessary to ensure logs remain available when an incident is discovered weeks or months after the initial breach.

takeaway: Configure version control system (VCS) log streaming and metadata (such as source IPs) now, because retention defaults will not support a later investigation.

actionable.title: Version control system (VCS) incident-readiness checklist
actionable.detail: Download the Wiz incident response team (CIRT) poster from threats.wiz.io. For each version control system (VCS) you run, enable audit log streaming to an external store, turn on GitHub source IP exposure in audit logs, and enable GitHub API request logging where available. Extend retention beyond the 7-day Git event default, and build hunts for git.clone (GitHub), repository_git_operation (GitLab) and RepositoryCloneEvent (Bitbucket Data Center).

prior_art: No equivalent VCS-forensics reference found in pool; it is a vendor cheat sheet consolidating public audit-log documentation. Verifier: No direct equivalent in the data files; adjacent: 'Audit OAuth apps and service principals' and Wiz supply-chain items. It is a vendor poster consolidating public docs.
verify_note: All four excerpts are verbatim; the 7-day GitHub retention, git.clone, repository_git_operation and RepositoryCloneEvent names and the org-wide rotation anecdote are in the source. The poster itself is not available, so only the blog summary is checkable. Unsupported: Entry published date 2026-09-10 conflicts with source Published Time 2026-08-27 (metadata only, not in summary or lessons).

title: Cisco Secure Email Gateway SQL injection reaches root command execution
summary: A flaw in the email parsing logic of Cisco AsyncOS for Secure Email Gateway lets an unauthenticated remote attacker send a crafted email that carries SQL statements and end up running commands as root on the appliance. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on September 14, 2026 with a three-day due date. The weakness is classed as CWE-89 (SQL injection).

lessons.point: The attack input is an ordinary email passing through the gateway, so no login or special network access is needed.
lessons.excerpt: An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted email message that contains malicious SQL statements through an affected device.

lessons.point: Insufficient input validation in a parser that handles untrusted content escalates from SQL execution to operating-system root.
lessons.excerpt: This vulnerability is due to insufficient validation in the email parsing logic.

lessons.point: Security appliances that sit in the mail path are high-value targets because compromise yields root on an internet-facing device.
lessons.excerpt: A vulnerability in the email parsing of Cisco AsyncOS Software for Cisco Secure Email Gateway could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to execute arbitrary commands with root privileges on the underlying operating system.

takeaway: Treat mail gateways as exposed attack surface: patch KEV-listed appliance flaws on the CISA deadline and review them for compromise.

actionable.title: Patch Cisco Secure Email Gateway and check for compromise
actionable.detail: Inventory Cisco AsyncOS Secure Email Gateway appliances (physical C195/C395/C695 and virtual C100V/C300V/C600V models are listed). Compare versions against the Cisco advisory cisco-sa-esa-inj-2bLVGmhX and upgrade past the fixed builds. Because exploitation is confirmed, run forensic triage on exposed appliances as CISA requires, rather than only patching.

prior_art: Prior CISA KEV entries (e.g. SiteGuard Server Edition command injection) cover the same exploited-appliance pattern; no earlier Cisco email gateway entry found in pool. Verifier: CISA KEV: SiteGuard Server Edition OS command injection (CVE-2026-106931) exploited in the wild
threat: Unauthenticated remote attacker sends a crafted email through the gateway to run SQL statements and then commands as root; exploitation in the wild is confirmed by CISA KEV listing.
conditions: Cisco AsyncOS builds before the fixed releases (for example before 15.5.5-014, 16.0.4-302 or 16.5.0-780 in the listed configurations) on Secure Email Gateway hardware or virtual appliances.
mitigations: Apply the Cisco vendor fix per advisory, meet the CISA due date (September 17, 2026), perform forensic triage, and discontinue use if mitigations are unavailable.
verify_note: All facts (dates, due date, versions, models, CWE-89) match the NVD page; routine KEV entry with no new claim. Unsupported: Lesson 3 'internet-facing' and 'high-value targets' are inference, not in source (NVD text only says unauthenticated remote). Corrected: lesson 3 confidence capped at 0.6.

title: Acronis Backup plugins have insecure file permissions exploited for privilege escalation
summary: Acronis Backup plugins for hosting control panels on Linux (cPanel & WHM, Plesk, DirectAdmin) ship with insecure file permissions that let a local low-privileged user escalate privileges. CISA added the flaw to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on September 16, 2026. The weakness is CWE-276, incorrect default permissions.

lessons.point: Incorrect default file permissions are a real, exploited privilege-escalation route, not just a hardening nit.
lessons.excerpt: Local privilege escalation due to insecure file permissions.

lessons.point: Fixes are per-integration builds, so each panel plugin needs its own version check.
lessons.excerpt: Acronis Backup plugin for cPanel & WHM (Linux) before build 1.9.3.1021

takeaway: Backup agents and panel plugins run with high privilege, so their file permissions deserve the same patch urgency as network-facing bugs once attackers use them.

actionable.title: Update Acronis Backup panel plugins
actionable.detail: On shared-hosting or multi-tenant Linux servers, upgrade the Acronis Backup plugin for cPanel & WHM to 1.9.3.1021 or later, the Plesk extension to 1.8.11.638 or later, and the DirectAdmin plugin to 1.2.3.238 or later. Audit for unexpected privileged activity from local accounts since exploitation is confirmed.

prior_art: Other KEV entries in the pool (Siemens Software Center DLL search-path flaw) are the same class of local privilege escalation in installed software; none found for Acronis. Verifier: CISA KEV: Siemens Software Center DLL search-path flaw CVE-2026-110936 (local privilege escalation in installed software)
threat: A local user on a hosting server abuses insecure file permissions in the Acronis Backup plugin to gain higher privileges; exploitation in the wild is confirmed by CISA KEV listing.
conditions: Linux hosts running Acronis Backup plugin for cPanel & WHM before 1.9.3.1021, Plesk extension before 1.8.11.638, or DirectAdmin plugin before 1.2.3.238, with an attacker holding local low-privilege access.
mitigations: Upgrade to the fixed builds per the Acronis advisory SEC-10986, meet the CISA due date (September 19, 2026), and perform forensic triage on exposed hosts.
verify_note: Builds, dates, CWE-276 and advisory ID all verified; thin NVD stub with no exploitation detail. Unsupported: Lesson 2 'Fixes are per-integration builds' is a mild inference from three fixed-build numbers; Takeaway that backup agents 'run with high privilege' is not in source.

title: Snyk: the system creating a change must not be its only validator
summary: A Snyk executive argues that AI has moved attack and development to machine speed and that organizations should secure at inception, enforce at runtime and validate independently. The key architectural claim is that validation evidence must come from something the producing agent cannot alter, such as executed tests or observed runtime behavior, not a second prompt or model. It relays Anthropic's September report that an actor injected instructions into an AI vendor's evaluation sandbox and took credentials, and that a Russian state-nexus actor used AI to rebuild flagged implants.

lessons.point: Independent validation is a property of who produces the evidence, not of adding another model.
lessons.excerpt: A second prompt, a second agent, or a second model is not independent.

lessons.point: The generator of a change should never be its sole validator.
lessons.excerpt: the system creating a change must not be its sole validator.

lessons.point: AI supply chains and evaluation sandboxes are being targeted for stored credentials, according to Anthropic's September report.
lessons.excerpt: injected malicious instructions into an AI vendor's automated evaluation sandbox and obtained the credentials that the sandbox held

takeaway: Treat executed tests, data-flow analysis and runtime observation as the validators of AI-generated code, and keep credentials out of evaluation sandboxes.

actionable.title: Validate AI-written changes with evidence the agent cannot alter
actionable.detail: Gate agent-authored changes on executed tests, data-flow analysis and runtime behavior produced outside the agent's reach; do not rely on a second LLM review as independent validation. Remove production credentials from evaluation sandboxes.

prior_art: Independent-validation framing overlaps the pool's gate-agent-PRs-with-automated-checks material; this is a vendor opinion essay with the Anthropic report cited secondhand. Verifier: archive: 'Snyk's Agent Baseline: Agent Governance Products Cover Different Outcomes...' and gate-agent-PRs-with-automated-checks material
verify_note: Vendor opinion essay with Anthropic report cited secondhand; excerpts verbatim. Includes a webinar promo and an 'Ask your own agent' stub, no instructions of consequence. Unsupported: Takeaway/actionable 'keep credentials out of evaluation sandboxes' is the curator's inference, not stated by the source.

title: Black Duck consumes Chainguard's Athena OSV feed to alert customers
summary: A partner spotlight describing how the Athena coalition works: a member scans a sandboxed app with a frontier model and submits findings anonymously, Chainguard triages and remediates, and patched artifacts and a private OSV feed go to members under a 30-day embargo. Black Duck uses that feed to alert customers using affected open source versions. It is largely promotional with no new technical findings.

lessons.point: Athena's pipeline: anonymous member submission, central triage and fix, embargoed distribution via a private advisory feed.
lessons.excerpt: then shares patched artifacts with members under a 30-day embargo, and publishes a private Open Source Vulnerabilities (OSV) feed to members and partners.

lessons.point: AI-found zero-days create a triage backlog that downstream scanners can absorb via advisory feeds.
lessons.excerpt: But this leaves teams with a backlog of vulnerabilities to triage, prioritize, and remediate.

takeaway: Vendor coalitions are routing AI-discovered open source vulnerabilities to scanners through shared OSV feeds, but this post adds little beyond the arrangement itself.

actionable.title: Check whether your software composition analysis (SCA) scanner ingests AI-found advisory feeds
actionable.detail: Ask your software composition analysis vendor whether it consumes pre-disclosure or OSV feeds of AI-discovered open source flaws, and how it alerts on affected versions in source, binaries and container images.

prior_art: Restates the Athena model covered in the sibling Chainguard post 'The flood is coming and the pipes were already full' and the archive Athena entry; customer spotlight, no new claim. Verifier: Sibling Chainguard post 'The flood is coming and the pipes were already full' (Athena OSV feed)
verify_note: Partner spotlight/marketing; excerpts verbatim and summary correctly flags it as promotional. Source ends with cookie-banner boilerplate, no embedded instructions.

author: matt_d
title: HarnessTax finds harness choice barely moved success but changed cost
summary: UC Berkeley researchers ran seven models through Claude Code, Codex CLI and Pi on SWE-bench Lite and Terminal-Bench 2.0, using 30 sampled tasks per benchmark and 3 repetitions. Success rates differed little between harnesses, but cost differed a lot, partly because Claude Code's first-call context was over 10 times Pi's. Models also often did as well or better outside their vendor's own harness. The authors note the benchmarks may be in training data and results may not carry over.

lessons.point: Harness choice shifts cost far more than success rate on these benchmarks.
lessons.excerpt: Claude Fable 5 solves 97.8% of attempts in Claude Code, 96.7% in Codex and 96.7% in Pi, yet Claude Code costs about twice as much as Pi ($1.33 vs $0.67).

lessons.point: A minimal toolset can sit on the cost-success frontier.
lessons.excerpt: Pi reaches the Pareto frontier on both benchmarks by providing just four tools: read, write, edit, and bash

lessons.point: Part of the cost gap starts with large instructions and tool schemas in the very first model call.
lessons.excerpt: Across all seven models, Claude Code’s mean initial context is over 10× Pi’s, with longer instructions and larger tool schemas.

lessons.point: Pairing a model with its own vendor's harness is not guaranteed to be best, and the authors flag benchmark limits.
lessons.excerpt: an alternative harness achieves the highest observed success rate in nine of twelve comparisons

takeaway: Compare cost and success of your model across more than one harness, because a default harness can carry a hidden cost premium for the same results.

actionable.title: Run a model-by-harness cost-success sweep before standardizing a coding agent
actionable.detail: Pick 30 or so representative tasks, run each candidate harness 3 times with the same model and a fixed price list, and record mean cost, success rate and first-call input tokens. Try a minimal read/write/edit/bash harness as the baseline and adopt a richer harness only if it beats it on your tasks.

prior_art: Closest in pool are PawBench (LLM x harness performance) and Harness-Delta Attribution; neither found to report a three-harness, seven-model cost comparison like this one. The source cites Portkey's earlier 'Harness Tax' post. Verifier: PawBench: benchmarking LLM x harness performance (archive.json); Harness-Delta Attribution (ai-research.json); Claude Code harness-design entry on tool minimalism. Portkey 'Harness Tax' is cited by the source.
verify_note: All numbers and excerpts check out, and the authors' caveats are reflected. The benchmark sample is small (30 tasks, 3 reps). Novelty is a variation on PawBench, with a new cost angle and the cross-vendor harness result.

author: alexshpunt
title: Explicit Edit Benchmark offers 226 byte-exact file-editing tasks for comparing coding agents
summary: The repository provides 226 small, deterministic editing tasks (replacements, insertions, deletions, copies, moves, large files, Unicode edge cases) checked byte for byte by a verifier. Because the tasks need no deep reasoning, differences come from the model, tools and harness. Anyone can run it on their own harness and publish results to a public Hugging Face dataset and leaderboard, marked verified when run through GitHub Actions or unverified when run locally.

lessons.point: Deliberately easy tasks isolate edit-tool and harness quality from model reasoning.
lessons.excerpt: None of them needs deep reasoning or domain knowledge: the agent finds the right text, changes it, and leaves every other byte as it was.

lessons.point: Scoring is deterministic with no judge model.
lessons.excerpt: A verifier compares the result byte for byte.

lessons.point: Results are crowd-sourced across many harness variants, with a trust label on each run.
lessons.excerpt: The Dataset marks approved GitHub workflow results as `verified` and ordinary local contributions as `unverified`.

lessons.point: Runs are only compared when the rules match, which keeps leaderboard comparisons fair.
lessons.excerpt: A run is grouped with others only when the rules match: how many recovery attempts it allows, how long one attempt may take, the task set, and the verifier.

takeaway: If you build or tune an edit tool for a coding agent, test it on exact-match edit tasks, since this benchmark isolates that skill from reasoning.

actionable.title: Benchmark your agent's edit tool on explicit-edit-benchmark
actionable.detail: Clone the repository, install the command-line interface (CLI) for your harness (adapters exist for Pi, Codex CLI, OpenCode, Oh My Pi, GitHub Copilot CLI and DeepSeek Harness), run the benchmark with --local and the --harness and --model flags, and compare your edit-tool variant against the baseline-agent (bash only) result on the public leaderboard.

prior_art: Closest in pool is PawBench (LLM x harness performance) and the Claude Code harness-design entry on tool minimalism; no file-edit-specific byte-exact benchmark found in pool. Verifier: PawBench (archive.json); no byte-exact edit-tool benchmark found in the pool.
verify_note: Summary is accurate. The benchmark is a niche tool for edit-tool builders. The source has no results or findings, only the benchmark and its leaderboard. Unsupported: Lesson 2 'no judge model' is inferred from the byte-for-byte verifier; the source never says it outright. Excerpt problem: Lesson 4 (runs only compared when rules match) cited an excerpt about publishing results that did not support it; the supporting sentence is later in the source. Corrected: lesson 4 excerpt replaced with the verbatim sentence 'A run is grouped with others only when the rules match: ...' from the raw file.
