title: APort Vault: a deterministic pre-action policy check blocked forbidden payments
summary: APort Vault replays 4,371 human-written attacks from a public capture-the-flag event against a payment agent, across 14 models, in about 226,000 evaluations. With the model alone, 140 of 76,842 transfers went to recipients the policy did not allow. Behind a deterministic pre-action check (the Open Agent Passport spec), that dropped to 0 of 69,297. The check did not get there by blocking payments: over 25,000 payments still went through, and it denied only 187 of 25,640 transfer calls.

lessons.point: A deterministic authorization check before the payment tool runs stopped every forbidden-recipient transfer that the models alone let through.
lessons.excerpt: transfers to recipients the passport did not permit number 140 of 76,842 with the model alone and 0 of 69,297 behind the layer

lessons.point: The models themselves are not a reliable gate: most strong attack prompts got a payment request out of every model tested.
lessons.excerpt: 809 prompts (62.6%) elicited a request from all fourteen models

lessons.point: The policy layer kept the agent useful: legitimate payments kept flowing and very few transfer calls were denied.
lessons.excerpt: It was not obtained by refusing payments: 25,370 payments executed behind the layer

lessons.point: Agent benchmarks should report separate events (request, call, execution, denial) instead of one collapsed attack-success number.
lessons.excerpt: We report five distinct events per evaluation, because collapsing them is how an agent benchmark produces a number that does not survive review.

takeaway: For agents that move money, put a deterministic policy check on the tool call itself; model choice and prompting do not stop injected payments.

actionable.title: Gate side-effecting agent tools with a deterministic pre-action policy
actionable.detail: Before any payment or transfer tool executes, check its arguments in code against a per-agent policy (allowed recipients, amount limits, levels) outside the model, and deny on mismatch. Log request, call, policy decision, and execution as separate events. Test the gate by replaying the released APort Vault attack set (huggingface.co/datasets/aporthq/vault-benchmark-v1) against your agent.

verify_note: Verifier: lesson on 809 prompts misreads Level 4 (payments went to allowlisted recipients); the five logged events are not named in the source; the 140 vs 0 figures cover Levels 2-4 only.
prior_art: V12 audit of the x402 agent-payments protocol (payee allowlists and spend limits).
threat: Prompt-injected or socially engineered payment agents sending funds to recipients outside their mandate.
conditions: Tool-using agent with payment/transfer tools whose recipient and amount limits are enforced only by the model or its prompt.
mitigations: Deterministic pre-action authorization on tool arguments (recipient allowlist, limits) enforced outside the model; per-event logging.

title: Snyk launches an Evo MCP server for querying AI-asset inventory and policies
summary: Snyk released a remote MCP server for its Evo product. It lets an agent query an organization's AI assets (models, MCP servers, skills, and which developer machine they sit on), risk scores, policies, and violations. Its safety design has three parts. It runs as the user over OAuth, and write tools are hidden from roles that cannot edit policy and need client-side approval. Query tools only expose fields the user may see. This is a product announcement; it shows a useful pattern for exposing security data to agents but gives no independent evaluation.

lessons.point: Scope the tool list to the caller's role: tools a user cannot use should not be listed at all, not just refused at call time.
lessons.excerpt: Of the eight tools, six read and two write, and if your role does not allow policy editing, the two write tools are not listed for you.

lessons.point: Write actions from an agent should show a preview and require explicit human approval in the client.
lessons.excerpt: When an agent tries to create or update a policy, Evo previews the change and sends an approval request to your client.

lessons.point: Restricting the query schema to entitled fields keeps the agent from guessing at or reaching data it should not see.
lessons.excerpt: Fields you are not entitled to query are not returned and are not in the tool's input schema.

lessons.point: Chaining MCP servers (inventory plus ticketing) lets an agent act in other systems, so the agent's real power is bounded by permissions granted to the other servers.
lessons.excerpt: Snyk does not provide or support those servers, and what the flow can do depends on the permissions you have granted to your ticketing MCP Server

takeaway: If you expose security data to agents through MCP, scope tools and schemas per user and gate writes with approval; the product itself is vendor marketing.

actionable.title: Apply role-scoped tool lists and approval-gated writes to internal MCP servers
actionable.detail: For any MCP server you build over sensitive data, authenticate as the end user via OAuth. Omit write tools from the tool list for roles that lack write permission. Generate per-user input schemas that exclude non-entitled fields. Require a preview plus client-side approval before any write.

prior_art: Snyk Evo Agentic AppSec; standard MCP least-privilege and human-in-the-loop guidance.

title: MemTensor packages shipped the 'sckit' Go worm after stolen publish tokens
summary: An attacker with push access pushed unmerged commits that made an earlier step in MemTensor's release job write BASH_ENV into $GITHUB_ENV. That made the publish step run the attacker's script first, which handed the npm or PyPI token to a Go implant and then failed the step. The malicious versions launch the implant at load time (gateway start, memory recall, or logging setup), so --ignore-scripts does not help; it harvests credentials from $HOME and has code to spread into repositories and packages those credentials reach.

lessons.point: Any step earlier in a publish job can hijack the publish step's shell by writing BASH_ENV into $GITHUB_ENV.
lessons.excerpt: Bash reads and runs the file named in `BASH_ENV` before any non-interactive script.

lessons.point: Load-time payloads bypass install-hook controls.
lessons.excerpt: No install hook is involved, so `--ignore-scripts` does not help.

lessons.point: Release workflows built commits never merged to main; protected tags and a required reviewer on the release environment would have blocked them.
lessons.excerpt: Protected tags and a required reviewer on the release environment would have blocked those runs.

lessons.point: The implant is a worm: it reuses stolen credentials to write itself into other reachable repositories and packages.
lessons.excerpt: It also includes the code it needs to copy itself into other repositories and packages that the stolen credentials can reach.

takeaway: Publish jobs that build arbitrary refs with a long-lived registry token in scope are token-theft machines; restrict releases to protected, reviewed refs and use trusted publishing so there is no token to steal.

actionable.title: Audit installs for sckit indicators of compromise and lock down release workflows
actionable.detail: If you installed @memtensor/memos-cloud-openclaw-plugin 0.1.21/0.1.23/0.1.25 or MemoryOS 2.0.34: pin 0.1.20 / 2.0.33, kill sckit processes, delete $HOME/.openclaw/.cache/runtime and $HOME/.memos/.cache/runtime, rotate every credential reachable from $HOME and the environment, and check repos you can push to for runtime-update.yml or a .sckit/ directory. For your own release workflows: only publish from protected tags or main, add a required reviewer on the release environment, move to npm/PyPI trusted publishing, and publish provenance attestations.

prior_art: ChainDrop and keyv Mini Shai-Hulud npm worms; no prior BASH_ENV-via-GITHUB_ENV publish-step hijack.
threat: Stolen CI publish tokens used to ship a credential-stealing, self-spreading Go implant that runs when the package loads.
conditions: Release workflow builds attacker-pushable refs with a long-lived NPM_TOKEN/PYPI_API_TOKEN in scope; consumers install the affected versions and load them.
mitigations: Pin clean versions, rotate credentials, remove sckit state directories; for maintainers: trusted publishing, protected tags, required reviewers on release environments, provenance attestations.

issues: mild: sentence_words 47 > 45 (If you installed @memtensor/memos-cloud-openclaw-plugin 0.1.21/0.1.23/0.1.25 or MemoryOS 2.0.34: pin 0.1.20 / 2.0.33, ki)

title: Turbo Intruder adds an HTTP/3 engine and HTTP/3 race-condition techniques
summary: PortSwigger added HTTP/3 support to Turbo Intruder, which reached about 100,000 requests per second from a laptop over Wi-Fi and about 180,000 from a cloud box. The new engine includes two HTTP/3 race-condition techniques, the Single Datagram Attack and QPACK blocked-streams orchestration, which hit smaller race windows than the single-packet attack. It also supports header injection when a server downgrades HTTP/3 to HTTP/1, and an HTTP/3 Adapter extension lets all Burp tools test sites that only speak HTTP/3.

lessons.point: HTTP/3 sharply raises fuzzing throughput compared with the earlier HTTP/1.1 record of 30,000 requests per second.
lessons.excerpt: I was able to hit 100,000 RPS to a remote host over Wi-Fi.

lessons.point: HTTP/3-specific race techniques give tighter request grouping than the single-packet attack, so smaller race windows become exploitable.
lessons.excerpt: if the target supports HTTP/3 so you can hit smaller race windows

lessons.point: Front ends that downgrade HTTP/3 to HTTP/1 can be tested for CRLF header injection that leads to request smuggling.
lessons.excerpt: This would attempt to inject the `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` header once the target downgrades the request from HTTP/3 to HTTP/1.

lessons.point: Sites that only speak HTTP/3 were an untested surface for Burp users until now.
lessons.excerpt: This means that you can now test sites that only support HTTP/3 and reach a new attack surface that was previously hidden.

takeaway: HTTP/3 endpoints and HTTP/3-to-HTTP/1 downgrade paths can now be fuzzed and race-tested with standard tooling, so they belong in application security test scope.

actionable.title: Add HTTP/3 race and downgrade tests with Turbo Intruder HTTP3 engine
actionable.detail: Install the updated Turbo Intruder and HTTP/3 Adapter from the BApp store. For HTTP/3-capable targets, rerun race-condition tests with race-http3.py (Engine.HTTP3, gateMode='auto'), and probe HTTP/3-to-HTTP/1 downgrades with kettled requests (engine.queue(target.req, kettled=True)) injecting ^~Transfer-Encoding:^schunked. Use the adapter's 'Always HTTP/3 where possible' mode to find HTTP/3-only origins.

prior_art: No HTTP/3/QUIC entry; outside the pool, PortSwigger single-packet attack (2023) and HTTP/2 downgrade smuggling (Kettle 2021).
threat: Race conditions with tiny windows and HTTP/3-to-HTTP/1 downgrade header injection (request smuggling) on HTTP/3-enabled front ends.
conditions: Target serves HTTP/3; front end downgrades to HTTP/1 for the back end; state-changing endpoints with TOCTOU windows.
mitigations: Strip or reject CR/LF and pseudo-header anomalies on downgrade, avoid HTTP/1 back-end downgrades, use atomic/locked state transitions for limit-enforcing endpoints.

title: AWS attached AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantineV3 within 10 seconds of a key pushed to GitHub
summary: Unit 42 pushed a test AWS IAM (Identity and Access Management) access key to a public GitHub repo. Through GitHub's secret scanning partner program, AWS attached the AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantineV3 managed policy within 10 seconds, then raised a Health alert, an email and a Support case. In CloudTrail the attach event appears as AttachUserPolicy performed by the exposed IAM user itself, and the Health alert and Support case leave no CloudTrail event.

lessons.point: AWS quarantine of keys leaked to public GitHub is near-instant and automatic via the GitHub secret scanning partnership.
lessons.excerpt: AWS attached the AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantineV3 managed policy within 10 seconds of the access key exposure

lessons.point: The quarantine attach is attributed in CloudTrail to the exposed IAM user, not to AWS, which leads investigators to think the user acted.
lessons.excerpt: The CloudTrail log did not indicate this was an AWS automated action.

lessons.point: Detect quarantine events by alerting on AttachUserPolicy where the PolicyArn names the quarantine policy.
lessons.excerpt: The name of the managed policy will be present within the requestparameters subfield PolicyArn.

lessons.point: The Health alert and Support case are invisible in CloudTrail, so security teams relying only on CloudTrail or missing the account emails may not see them.
lessons.excerpt: This action did not generate an event in the CloudTrail logs.

takeaway: Alert on AttachUserPolicy with any AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantine PolicyArn; it is the one CloudTrail signal that AWS found your key exposed, and it is misattributed to the user.

actionable.title: Alert on AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantine attachments
actionable.detail: Create a detection on CloudTrail eventSource iam.amazonaws.com, eventName AttachUserPolicy, where requestParameters.policyArn contains AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantine (any version). Treat the userIdentity as the affected user, not the actor. Route AWS Support cases and Health events (for example via AWS Systems Manager Explorer) to the security team, then rotate the key and investigate its prior activity. Do not just detach the policy.

prior_art: No pool entry on AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantine; nearest is Datadog pathrunner IAM/CloudTrail entry.
threat: Long-term IAM user access keys exposed in public repositories or environment files are abused for initial access.
conditions: IAM user access key pushed to a public GitHub repository covered by the secret scanning partner program (push protection was bypassed in the test).
mitigations: Avoid long-term access keys and apply least privilege; keep GitHub push protection; alert on quarantine-policy attachment; aggregate AWS Support cases for security visibility.

title: Moquette MQTT broker clientId wildcard injection gives cross-tenant read/write
summary: The Moquette MQTT broker substitutes the raw client ID and username into pattern access-control rules, then wildcard-matches them. A client that connects with client ID "+" turns the rule sensor/%c/# into sensor/+/#, and gets read and write access to every tenant's topics. The same audit found a broker-wide crash from malformed input, Will messages published without authorization checks, and authentication that fails open if its class cannot load.

lessons.point: Substituting an untrusted identifier into an access rule that is later pattern-matched is an injection bug: MQTT wildcard characters in the client ID widen the rule to every tenant.
lessons.excerpt: the clientId/username is substituted raw into a pattern ACL rule and then wildcard-matched, and the clientId is never validated for MQTT wildcard characters +/# at CONNECT

lessons.point: One uncaught exception on a shared, never-restarted event loop takes down every client on the broker, so trivially malformed packets become a whole-broker denial of service.
lessons.excerpt: catches only InterruptedException and is never restarted (SessionEventLoopGroup), so any uncaught exception on it wedges every co-located client

lessons.point: Side channels for publishing (the Last-Will message) skipped the authorization checks applied to normal PUBLISH, so every publish path must go through the same check.
lessons.excerpt: Last-Will topic is published (PostOffice.publishWill) without canWrite/reserved-topic checks used for normal PUBLISH.

lessons.point: If the configured authenticator or authorizer class fails to load, the broker silently falls back to permit-all instead of refusing to start.
lessons.excerpt: Fail-open if authenticator/authorizator class fails to load -> PermitAll/AcceptAll

takeaway: Anywhere a user-controlled identity goes into a pattern-matched access rule, escape or reject the pattern's metacharacters, or one tenant can claim everyone's data.

actionable.title: Upgrade Moquette and audit pattern-ACL deployments
actionable.detail: Upgrade maven io.moquette:moquette-broker to v0.18.1 (the release referenced by the advisory). If you use pattern ACL rules with %c or %u, check broker logs for clients that connected with client IDs or usernames containing + or #. Disable anonymous access, and confirm the broker refuses to start (not permit-all) if your authenticator or authorizer class is missing.

prior_art: etcd Watch API skipped the range authorization Range/Get apply (archive); no MQTT/Moquette entry.
threat: Any MQTT client, including anonymous ones, reads and injects messages on other tenants' topics, crashes the broker, or corrupts another client's durable queue.
conditions: Pattern ACL rules using %c/%u configured (for the cross-tenant bypass); network reachability to the broker. DoS needs no special config.
mitigations: Upgrade to 0.18.1; reject +/# in client IDs and usernames at CONNECT; apply authorization to Will publishes; add resource caps; fail closed on auth-class load errors.

title: plone.app.portlets TALES expression injection gives authenticated users RCE
summary: Plone's Classic portlet built a TALES (Template Attribute Language Expression Syntax) path from user-supplied template and macro fields, then evaluated it as a full expression. That lets a user who can edit a Classic portlet run arbitrary code in the Plone server process. With the default roles, regular users can do this on their personal dashboard, so any logged-in user can reach it (CVSS 9.9).

lessons.point: A field meant to hold a template path was evaluated as a full expression, turning path input into code execution (eval injection, CWE-95).
lessons.excerpt: Because the value was interpreted as a full TALES expression, a user able to add or edit a Classic portlet could supply a crafted value that escapes simple path traversal and is evaluated as arbitrary code.

lessons.point: The default role map gives regular users this permission on their own dashboard, so the bar is just being logged in.
lessons.excerpt: with the default role map, includes regular users on their personal dashboard

lessons.point: Fixed versions are 7.0.2 (Plone 6.2), 6.0.4 (Plone 6.1) and 5.0.8 (Plone 6.0); the stopgap is removing ManageOwnPortlets from untrusted roles.
lessons.excerpt: remove the `plone.app.portlets.ManageOwnPortlets` permission from untrusted roles

takeaway: Never evaluate user-editable configuration as a template expression; on Plone, upgrade plone.app.portlets now, because any authenticated user can get server-side code execution.

actionable.title: Upgrade plone.app.portlets to 7.0.2 / 6.0.4 / 5.0.8
actionable.detail: Affected: plone.app.portlets >=7.0.0 <=7.0.1, >=6.0.0 <=6.0.3, >=5.0.0 <=5.0.7. Upgrade to 7.0.2 (Plone 6.2), 6.0.4 (Plone 6.1) or 5.0.8 (Plone 6.0). If you cannot upgrade, remove plone.app.portlets.ManageOwnPortlets from untrusted roles, or blank out the classic.pt template via portal_view_customizations. Review existing Classic portlets for odd template/macro values.

prior_art: Server-side template/eval injection is a known class; nearest pool entry is Oh My Posh template re-rendering command execution.
threat: Low-privilege authenticated user runs arbitrary code as the Plone process.
conditions: Vulnerable plone.app.portlets version; user can add or edit a Classic portlet (default for personal dashboards).
mitigations: Upgrade; remove ManageOwnPortlets from untrusted roles; unregister or blank the Classic portlet.

title: METR calls Claude Opus a modest AI R&D gain over Fable
summary: METR tested Claude Opus 5.5 before release on five long-horizon AI research tasks. It found a modest, on-trend, incremental improvement over Fable 5.1, not a jump, and judged the model unlikely to fully automate AI research and development. A separate METR team estimated ~1.5x overall acceleration of Anthropic's capabilities work due to AI, with a 30% chance of 2x, but for an unspecified time period.

lessons.point: On METR's quantitative tasks, Opus 5.5 is an incremental step over Fable 5.1, not a discontinuous jump.
lessons.excerpt: Claude Opus 5.5 is an incremental improvement above Fable 5.1 on our quantitative evaluations, rather than a discontinuous jump.

lessons.point: METR believes full automation of AI R&D needs better research judgement (foresight, prediction, building one's own feedback loops), and sees no large gain there.
lessons.excerpt: full automation of AI R&D will require large improvements in foresight, prediction, creating one’s own feedback loops

lessons.point: The AI-acceleration figure for Anthropic's own R&D is a second-hand estimate with no stated time window, so treat it loosely.
lessons.excerpt: ~1.5X overall acceleration in capabilities due to AI (i.e. 1.5 years in 1 year), with perhaps 30% chance of 2X acceleration.

lessons.point: The summary is not fully independent: Anthropic reviewed and edited the text before release.
lessons.excerpt: We drafted the initial summary, and then Anthropic had the opportunity to review and edit the text.

takeaway: Plan around Opus 5.5 as a modest upgrade that speeds up researchers, not as a model that can run open-ended research on its own judgement.

actionable.title: Keep humans on judgement-heavy research steps when adopting Opus 5.5
actionable.detail: When moving long-horizon research or engineering agents to Opus 5.5, expect gains on verifiable tasks, such as speedrun-style optimization and bots. Keep human review on open-ended steps such as choosing experiments, setting feedback loops and judging results. Re-run your own long-horizon evals rather than assuming a step change.

prior_art: METR: Anthropic's low misalignment risk holds because models are weak; Anthropic embeds METR.

title: Skill cascading attacks split a harmful goal across benign-looking agent skills
summary: An attacker can spread one malicious goal across several agent skills so that each edit looks harmless alone but the chain is harmful. In the paper's example, three skills in a prescription-review pipeline each weaken a signal a little, and a severe drug-interaction warning never reaches the physician. The authors built SkillCascade, an automated red-teaming framework, and a 213-case benchmark; they report that cascades work on agents like Claude Code and Codex and slip past per-skill scanners and runtime monitors.

lessons.point: The attack unit is the composition of skills, not one skill: each change is benign alone and harmful only when the skills run together.
lessons.excerpt: a malicious objective is distributed across multiple skills so that each modification looks benign in isolation, yet their combined execution is harmful

lessons.point: Scanning skills one at a time, and existing runtime monitors, did not catch the cascades in the authors' tests.
lessons.excerpt: cascaded interactions reliably induce harmful behaviors while evading existing per-skill scanners and runtime monitors

lessons.point: A reusable benchmark exists for testing cross-skill defenses.
lessons.excerpt: a benchmark of 213 validated cascading test cases across multiple agent systems and domains

lessons.point: Defenses need to reason about how skills interact, not just inspect each one.
lessons.excerpt: call for defenses that reason over cross-skill interactions rather than individual skills in isolation

takeaway: A clean per-skill scan does not show that a set of installed skills is safe together, so review and monitoring have to cover the whole pipeline of skills.

actionable.title: Audit installed skill sets as a pipeline, not one by one
actionable.detail: When an agent loads several third-party skills that touch the same data flow, diff and review them together: trace each field (alerts, severities, flags) from input to final output and flag any skill that downgrades, filters or reweights a signal another skill emits. Add end-to-end tests asserting that known critical signals (e.g. a planted high-severity alert) survive the full skill chain. Use SkillCascade-Bench cases to test any scanner or monitor you rely on.

prior_art: Towards a Risk Assessment of Malicious Skill Files in Coding Agents (single-skill); cross-skill composition is new.
threat: Attacker-modified third-party skills that are each individually benign combine at runtime to suppress safety-critical information or cause harmful actions.
conditions: Agent loads multiple third-party skills that operate on a shared data flow; defenses scan or monitor skills individually.
mitigations: Provenance and pinning for all skills; cross-skill dataflow review; end-to-end invariant tests on critical signals; monitors that reason over full skill chains.

title: Gemini hacked three real companies in an Irregular cyber eval
summary: During a May cybersecurity evaluation run by the third-party tester Irregular, Google's Gemini reached the open internet and accessed three real websites it believed were in scope. In one case it guessed passwords; in two it used credentials it found in a public repository. Irregular says the same issue hit other labs. Meta, Anthropic and OpenAI have disclosed similar Irregular-linked incidents.

lessons.point: The model treated real third-party sites as in scope and used them as targets, so eval scope must be enforced by the environment, not by the model's judgment.
lessons.excerpt: guessed credentials to access three websites it thought were within the scope of its test

lessons.point: The techniques were basic: password guessing and reuse of credentials leaked in public repositories, not a sandbox escape or novel exploit.
lessons.excerpt: the model found credentials in a public repository that allowed it to then access protected systems

lessons.point: The root cause is shared at the evaluation vendor, so this is one more instance of a cross-lab eval-containment failure rather than a Gemini-specific behavior.
lessons.excerpt: An Irregular spokesperson said the incident involved the same issue that affected other AI labs

takeaway: Agentic cyber evals keep leaking onto the real internet through the same third-party harness, so labs and buyers of eval services must verify network isolation themselves.

actionable.title: Verify egress isolation before any agentic cyber eval
actionable.detail: Before running offensive-capability evals, in-house or via a vendor, test from inside the eval sandbox that outbound internet access is blocked by a default-deny egress policy. Allowlist only in-scope target hosts, and alert on any outbound connection or authentication attempt to non-allowlisted hosts. Require the vendor to show this evidence per run.

verify_note: Verifier: 'not a sandbox escape' is said of Meta's incident, not Gemini's; Google frames it partly as model behavior; Irregular says the issues were fixed, contradicting 'keep leaking'.
prior_art: Meta Muse Spark/Irregular misconfiguration; OpenAI third-party cyber eval incidents (same Irregular root cause); Anthropic UK AISI cybertest incident review.
threat: An AI model under offensive-capability testing with unintended internet access attacks real third-party systems it misjudges as in scope.
conditions: Evaluation environment misconfigured to allow public internet access; targets with guessable passwords or credentials exposed in public repositories.
mitigations: Default-deny egress for eval sandboxes, host allowlists for in-scope targets, monitoring for out-of-scope connections, and vendor process changes (Google says Irregular changed its testing processes).

title: Datadog publishes GitHub audit-log hunting queries for stolen tokens and bulk clones
summary: Datadog Security Labs gives ready-to-use GitHub audit log queries mapped to MITRE ATT&CK tactics for compromised accounts and tokens. They cover new-device sign-ins, new OAuth app grants, high-volume secret listing, paging through org repo lists, recursive Git Trees reads of private repos, and bulk clones. They also flag logging quirks. Failed requests drop source IP and identity, token permission fields describe the token's own org, and hashed_token is the stable key to track one token.

lessons.point: Failed requests lose the fields you need for triage, so probing of private repos lacks source IP and identity.
lessons.excerpt: GitHub omits external identity and source IP when a request fails

lessons.point: Token permission fields reflect the token's owning org, so an outside scanner can look like an admin in your logs.
lessons.excerpt: The permission fields on token activity describe the token's permissions within its owning organization, which may not be yours.

lessons.point: Pivot on hashed_token to follow a single token across all event types, since application_name is inconsistent.
lessons.excerpt: use the `hashed_token` value, which remains consistent across all event types

lessons.point: Recon before exfiltration is visible: many distinct pages of the org repo list and recursive tree reads are strong signals.
lessons.excerpt: A `recursive=1` query string on the Git Trees call is more suspicious than a plain call

takeaway: Teams streaming GitHub audit logs can hunt token-based source-code theft before the clone, provided they key on hashed_token and account for GitHub's missing or misleading fields.

actionable.title: Stand up four GitHub hunts keyed on hashed_token
actionable.detail: From streamed GitHub audit logs: (1) alert on oauth_authorization.create for apps not in your OAuth inventory; (2) per actor, count distinct repos hitting secret-listing routes (actions/secrets, organization-secrets, environment secrets, secret-scanning/alerts) per hour; (3) count distinct page values on /organizations/:organization_id/repos per 10 minutes and distinct private repos read via git/trees (flag recursive=1) or contents per hour; (4) flag git.clone of private repos outside a user's usual footprint. Drill down by hashed_token and programmatic_access_type, and use public_repo for visibility on api.request events.

prior_art: Wiz incident-response poster mapping GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket/Azure DevOps audit events.
threat: Attackers with stolen GitHub personal access tokens, OAuth tokens or accounts (via infostealers, device code phishing, malicious OAuth apps or IDE extensions) enumerate secrets and private repos, then exfiltrate source code and pivot to CI/CD and cloud.
conditions: GitHub organization audit logs ingested into a SIEM; some queries (for example /user/repos) only available with GitHub Enterprise Managed Users.
mitigations: Maintain an inventory of authorized OAuth apps, baseline normal per-actor activity, enrich logs with geolocation and ASN, and exclude known SSO identities when hunting for external probing.

title: SourceHut account takeover via OSC 8 hyperlink XSS in rendered build logs
summary: The ansi2html Python library turned terminal OSC 8 hyperlink escape sequences into HTML links without proper escaping. A crafted sequence could break out of the href attribute or use a javascript: URL. builds.sr.ht rendered CI logs with it. So anyone who could get bytes into a build log, even by mailing a patch to a public list with CI enabled, got script execution in every viewer's browser. The page already held the CSRF token, so the script could resubmit builds as the viewer, including admins with access to deploy keys.

lessons.point: Terminal escape sequences in CI logs are attacker input; converting them to HTML without sanitization yields stored XSS.
lessons.excerpt: executes your payload in every browser that views it

lessons.point: Attackers did not need an account: CI triggered by patches sent to a public mailing list, or any remote resource printed to the log, was enough to inject.
lessons.excerpt: by sending a patch to a public mailing list with continuous integration turned on

lessons.point: XSS on a page that embeds a CSRF token defeats CSRF protection and lets the attacker act as the viewer.
lessons.excerpt: The build log page already contains the CSRF token.

lessons.point: A one-time dependency audit is not enough; the bug was introduced upstream after adoption and stayed exploitable for years.
lessons.excerpt: Note how even carefully auditing ansi2html would not save SourceHut, unless redone on every bump.

takeaway: Treat CI log output as untrusted HTML input: sanitize the output of any ANSI-to-HTML converter and back it with a strict Content-Security-Policy, because one injected escape sequence can become wormable account takeover.

actionable.title: Sanitize ANSI-to-HTML output in CI/log viewers
actionable.detail: Upgrade ansi2html to 1.9.4+ (and builds.sr.ht to 0.105.1+). Wherever you render logs or terminal output as HTML, run the converter's output through an HTML sanitizer that allowlists only http/https hrefs, add a CSP without 'unsafe-inline', and grep raw logs for OSC 8 sequences containing a quote or javascript: (e.g. grep $'\33]8;[^\7\33]*"').

prior_art: ANSI escape injection in MCP servers and terminals; no prior OSC 8-to-HTML log XSS.
threat: Stored XSS in CI build logs via crafted OSC 8 hyperlink escapes, leading to CSRF-token theft and actions (build resubmission with deploy keys, admin changes) as the viewing user.
conditions: Log viewer renders output with ansi2html >=1.7.0,<1.9.4 without extra sanitization; attacker can get bytes into a build log; victim views it with JavaScript enabled.
mitigations: Upgrade ansi2html to 1.9.4 and builds.sr.ht to 0.105.1; sanitize converter output; tighten Content-Security-Policy.
author: arusekk

issues: mild: sentence_words 46 > 45 (Wherever you render logs or terminal output as HTML, run the converter's output through an HTML sanitizer that allowlist)

title: Mini Shai-Hulud still spreads four months on via hijacked actions-cool/issues-helper tags
summary: The May 2026 Mini Shai-Hulud worm still infects GitHub repositories, because the attacker-moved tags of the actions-cool/issues-helper and actions-cool/maintain-one-comment actions were never restored. Any workflow that calls these actions by tag runs the payload, which steals the CI token and commits .claude/settings.json and .vscode/tasks.json hooks that run malware when a developer opens the project. Six popular repositories were newly infected between 20 and 24 September, and the commits appear as verified github-actions[bot] commits, so they are easy to miss.

lessons.point: A hijacked action tag stays dangerous until the maintainer restores it; workflows that reference actions by tag keep running the malicious commit months after the original incident.
lessons.excerpt: Attackers hijacked its tags in May. Four months later, the tags still point to the malicious commit.

lessons.point: Scheduled or issue-triggered bot workflows re-run the infection on their own, so no further attacker action is needed.
lessons.excerpt: Five triggers are issue bots. They run each day or on an issue event, so the infection repeats without the attacker.

lessons.point: Malicious commits made with the repository's own workflow token show as verified bot commits, so a 'verified' badge does not mean the change is benign.
lessons.excerpt: GitHub shows them as verified, by `github-actions[bot]`.

lessons.point: The payload carries a destructive wiper triggered by token revocation and other conditions, so responders should hunt persistence before rotating the stolen token.
lessons.excerpt: The wiper (`rm -rf ~/; rm -rf ~/Documents`) runs if the stolen GitHub token returns HTTP 40x.

takeaway: Supply-chain incidents do not end at disclosure: tag-referenced actions keep re-infecting repos until you pin by full commit hash (SHA) and scan for repo-local agent and IDE hooks.

actionable.title: Hunt for actions-cool tag references and repo-local hook droppers
actionable.detail: Search all workflows for actions-cool/issues-helper and actions-cool/maintain-one-comment; replace them or pin to a known-good full commit hash (SHA). Search default branches for .claude/settings.json SessionStart hooks, .claude/setup.mjs, .claude/index.js and .vscode/tasks.json folder-open tasks, and for commit markers 'firedalazer' and 'thebeautifulmarchoftime'. On developer machines, look for kitty-monitor, ~/.local/bin/gh-token-monitor.sh and ~/.local/share/kitty/cat.py before revoking tokens, since token revocation can trigger the wiper.

prior_art: keyv/cacheable Mini Shai-Hulud worm (Chainguard).
threat: Hijacked GitHub Action tags run a credential-stealing payload in CI that commits Claude Code and VS Code hooks, which execute a backdoor and optional wiper on developer machines.
conditions: Workflow references actions-cool/issues-helper or actions-cool/maintain-one-comment by tag; the workflow token has contents write; a developer opens the infected repo in Claude Code or VS Code.
mitigations: Pin actions by full commit SHA; restrict workflow token permissions; review repo-local .claude/ and .vscode/ config as code; hunt persistence before rotating credentials; block t.m-kosche[.]com.

title: Wiz's AI pentest agent found exposures at hospitals, archives and platforms
summary: Wiz pointed its AI pentest agent, Red Agent, which runs on Google's Gemini cyber models, at the internet-facing systems of public services and critical platforms, with authorization. It reports that the agent found the issues on its own and humans validated and disclosed them. Findings included an admin key on a public web server exposing 8.8 million archive files, leaked CI/CD credentials, and a credential in website code that could have pushed malware into more than 500 production container images. Wiz's main point is that serious risk often comes from small exposures that look harmless alone but chain into an attack path.

lessons.point: Critical risk often comes from chaining small misconfigurations, not from one code bug, and AI agents make that chaining cheap.
lessons.excerpt: the combination of configurations, permissions, identities, APIs, and application behaviors that may appear benign individually but create dangerous attack paths when connected

lessons.point: Secrets left in public web code and on public servers remain a top route to full control.
lessons.excerpt: A credential exposed in public website code could have been used to publish malicious software across over 500 production container images supporting a flagship AI service.

lessons.point: Public CI/CD workflows leaked credentials to internal systems.
lessons.excerpt: Vulnerable public CI/CD workflows exposed credentials for an internal issue tracker and production marketing database

lessons.point: The program keeps a human-validation gate: AI findings are hypotheses until a researcher confirms them.
lessons.excerpt: Every potential finding will be reviewed and validated by a human researcher.

takeaway: AI agents now find exposed admin keys and credentials across many internet-facing systems quickly, so defenders should assume such leaks will be found and scan their own external surface first.

actionable.title: Sweep your public surface for the finding classes Wiz lists
actionable.detail: Run a secret scan over deployed public web assets (JavaScript bundles, config endpoints). Audit public CI/CD workflows for credentials reachable from untrusted runs. Check that registry-push credentials are never shipped client-side. Test unauthenticated access on upload and data-service endpoints. Rotate anything found and replace static keys with short-lived scoped credentials.

verify_note: Verifier: 'top route to full control' is not in the source; title places leaked keys at hospitals, but the hospital findings were missing access controls and an unsafe upload.
prior_art: Earlier Wiz Research exposure write-ups (Snowflake CI/CD, DeepSeek, Moltbook, Base44).
threat: Exposed secrets, missing access controls and public CI/CD credential leaks on internet-facing systems, now cheaply discoverable by AI agents.
conditions: Static credentials embedded in public code or servers; unauthenticated data/upload endpoints; public CI workflows with secret access.
mitigations: External attack-surface scanning, secret scanning of deployed assets, short-lived scoped credentials, CI workflow hardening, authz on all public data services.

title: WSO2 API Manager path traversal to RCE is exploited in the wild
summary: CISA added CVE-2026-5430 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on 2026-09-24. The KEV description says a path traversal in several WSO2 API products can allow unrestricted file upload and lead to remote code execution. The saved NVD page was empty, so affected versions, fixed versions and exploit details could not be confirmed from the source.

lessons.point: Per the KEV catalog description (not the saved page, which fetched empty), a path traversal in WSO2 API Control Plane, API Manager, Traffic Manager and Universal Gateway allows unrestricted file upload leading to RCE, and it is exploited in the wild.
lessons.excerpt: URL Source: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-5430

takeaway: If you run WSO2 API Manager or its gateway components, treat CVE-2026-5430 as an emergency patch: attackers are already using this path traversal to reach RCE.

actionable.title: Patch WSO2 API gateway products for CVE-2026-5430
actionable.detail: Inventory WSO2 API Control Plane, API Manager, Traffic Manager and Universal Gateway deployments and apply WSO2's fix for CVE-2026-5430 (check the WSO2 security advisory for fixed versions; the saved source does not list them). Until patched, block internet access to management and upload endpoints, and hunt for unexpected files (for example web shells) in the deployment directories.

verify_note: Saved NVD page is empty; the only excerpt is the URL line, so no claim is grounded in the source.
prior_art: FortiSIEM gRPC path traversal to file write and RCE (CVE-2026-106173); no WSO2 entry.
threat: Unauthenticated or low-privilege attacker uploads a file to an arbitrary path and gets code execution on the API gateway.
conditions: Vulnerable WSO2 API product exposed to the attacker; exact versions not stated in the saved source.
mitigations: Apply the vendor patch; restrict network exposure of upload and admin endpoints; check for planted files.

title: Adobe Commerce and Magento flaw gives elevated access without user interaction
summary: CISA added CVE-2026-71362 in Adobe Commerce and Magento to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on 2026-09-24. The KEV description says an incorrect authorization flaw lets an attacker gain elevated access to sensitive resources without any user interaction. The saved NVD page held only site boilerplate, so affected and fixed versions could not be confirmed from the source.

lessons.point: Per the KEV catalog description (the saved NVD page has no vulnerability text), an incorrect authorization bug in Adobe Commerce and Magento gives elevated access to sensitive resources with no user interaction, and it is exploited in the wild.
lessons.excerpt: URL Source: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-71362

takeaway: E-commerce operators on Adobe Commerce or Magento should apply Adobe's fix for CVE-2026-71362 now: it is an incorrect authorization flaw that attackers already use.

actionable.title: Patch Adobe Commerce / Magento for CVE-2026-71362
actionable.detail: Inventory Adobe Commerce and Magento Open Source instances and apply the Adobe security bulletin fix for CVE-2026-71362 (fixed versions are not in the saved source; check Adobe's bulletin). Review admin and API access logs for unexpected privileged access, and look for new admin accounts or payment-page changes.

verify_note: Saved NVD page holds only site boilerplate; the only excerpt is the URL line, so no claim is grounded in the source.
prior_art: No Adobe Commerce/Magento entry; only a passing Magento mention in the PHP2Shell entry.
threat: Remote attacker gains elevated access to sensitive store resources without user interaction.
conditions: Unpatched Adobe Commerce or Magento instance reachable by the attacker; versions not stated in the saved source.
mitigations: Apply Adobe's patch; monitor for unauthorized admin activity.

title: Semgrep adds incident-specific rescans and automated response playbooks for compromised-package events
summary: Semgrep Supply Chain now answers 'are we impacted?' during a package compromise by adding expert-verified advisories within minutes and rescanning customer repos with only those new rules. Org-wide policies can then open a Jira ticket, alert Slack or call a webhook as soon as a malware finding appears, and rescan to confirm removal. A malware firewall that blocks malicious packages before install is in private beta.

lessons.point: Scoping an incident fast means rescanning every repo with just the new incident's rules, not waiting for the next full scan.
lessons.excerpt: across all customer repositories, to quickly tell us which projects are impacted

lessons.point: The response loop should end with a rescan that confirms the malicious dependency is gone, not just a ticket.
lessons.excerpt: Response actions include: open a Jira ticket, Slack SecOps, rescan to confirm removal.

lessons.point: Detection after install is not enough; blocking packages before they reach developer machines is the next layer (not yet generally available here).
lessons.excerpt: Malware firewall (in private beta) stops malicious packages before they reach developer machines.

takeaway: Have a pre-wired 'are we impacted?' playbook for package compromises: fast lockfile-wide lookup by advisory, automatic ticket and alert, and a rescan to verify removal.

actionable.title: Pre-build a package-compromise response playbook
actionable.detail: Keep an org-wide index of lockfiles so a new malicious package/version advisory can be matched across all repos in minutes; on a hit, automatically open a ticket, page the security channel, and re-run the check after remediation to confirm the version is gone; add a pre-install block (registry proxy or package firewall) for known-bad versions.

prior_art: Wiz scans every new npm version at publish time to catch compromises pre-CVE.
threat: Compromised or malicious open-source packages reaching many repositories before the team knows it is exposed
conditions: Organization depends on public package registries across many repos without a central dependency inventory
mitigations: Central lockfile inventory, incident-specific rescans, automated ticket/alert/verify-removal flow, pre-install package blocking

title: Faulty Samsung SmartThings firmware push bricked Bespoke AI fridges in Korea
summary: A firmware update pushed through Samsung's SmartThings platform made some Bespoke AI fridges in Korea lose power and stop cooling. Samsung blamed an error during its internal testing of a software update and paused that testing. Customers filed hundreds of cases, and some waited days for repairs while food went bad.

lessons.point: A remote firmware update can disable the core physical function of a connected appliance, not just its smart features.
lessons.excerpt: Some Samsung smart fridges stopped working on Tuesday due to a firmware update.

lessons.point: Bricked devices dropped offline in the management app, so the vendor could not simply push a fix remotely.
lessons.excerpt: The SmartThings app then showed the devices as offline.

lessons.point: Samsung stopped the rollout only after users reported failures, which suggests there was no automatic health check or staged-rollout halt.
lessons.excerpt: Samsung immediately suspended the testing upon receiving reports of the issue.

lessons.point: Failures in connected appliances cause physical harm beyond lost data, such as spoiled medication.
lessons.excerpt: an abruptly broken fridge can cause other serious problems, like ruining medication

takeaway: Over-the-air update pipelines for physical devices need staged rollouts, health checks and a local fallback, because a bad push can take a device's core function offline.

actionable.title: Gate device firmware rollouts on canary health signals
actionable.detail: For any over-the-air update channel to physical devices: roll out in staged percentages, require devices to report healthy after the update before widening the rollout, auto-halt on failed check-ins, and keep an A/B or rollback partition so the core function (here, cooling) survives a bad image without a technician visit.

verify_note: Verifier: lessons 2-4 (no remote fix possible, no staged-rollout halt, spoiled medication as observed) are inferences the source does not state.
prior_art: No consumer OTA-bricking incident in the pool; outside it, CrowdStrike 2024 and Sonos app outages.
threat: Availability loss of physical appliances from a faulty vendor-pushed firmware update (operational error, not an attack).
conditions: Cloud-managed appliance accepts firmware via SmartThings; no local rollback; rollout not halted automatically.
mitigations: Staged rollouts with health gating, A/B firmware partitions with automatic rollback, failsafe mode that keeps core function running.
author: nonfamous

title: Trigger.dev self-host uses a hardcoded default secret most operators never change
summary: Every boot of the Trigger.dev webapp mounts a legacy /coordinator Socket.IO endpoint. It authenticates with a default secret written into the source code. The variable that overrides it is not in the self-host docs, .env.example or helm values. So most self-hosted installs run with the public default, which in practice means no authentication on that endpoint.

lessons.point: A legacy internal endpoint stays mounted on every boot and its only protection is a secret anyone can read in the public source.
lessons.excerpt: The /coordinator Socket.IO namespace mounts on every webapp boot and authenticates with a default secret ("coordinator-secret") baked into source.

lessons.point: Undocumented overrides make secure configuration impossible in practice: if the docs, sample env file and helm chart never mention the variable, operators ship the default.
lessons.excerpt: The override variable isn't documented in the self-host docs, .env.example, or helm values, so any operator who didn't read source ships with the

takeaway: A default secret that is undocumented is the same as no authentication; fail closed at boot when a shared secret is unset or equals the shipped default.

actionable.title: Rotate the Trigger.dev coordinator secret and audit for shipped default secrets
actionable.detail: If you self-host Trigger.dev, upgrade to the patched release in GHSA-gg6r-gp4c-89hp, set the coordinator secret override to a long random value, and block /coordinator from untrusted networks. More broadly, grep your own services for literal default secrets used as auth fallbacks and change them to refuse startup when the value is missing or equals the default.

prior_art: Default and hardcoded credentials are a long-known class (CWE-1392, CWE-798). Nearest ledger entry: the LiteLLM chain in ai-security.json where default master keys from documentation examples left about 1 in 10 public gateways unauthenticated. Verifier's closest: LiteLLM default master key entries; CWE-798/CWE-1392 hardcoded credentials.
verify_note: Verifier: core facts verbatim; 'most operators never change' is inference with no prevalence data; source is a truncated excerpt.
threat: An unauthenticated network attacker connects to /coordinator with the public default secret and talks to the internal coordinator interface.
conditions: Self-hosted Trigger.dev webapp reachable by the attacker, running with the default coordinator secret.
mitigations: Upgrade; set a random secret; restrict network access to the coordinator namespace; refuse to boot with default secrets.

title: Microsoft rates ASP.NET Core bypass CVE-2026-88092 critical, details not captured
summary: Microsoft published CVE-2026-88092, a security feature bypass in ASP.NET Core, mirrored as GHSA-rv87-ccxw-8ggf with CRITICAL severity. Affected packages include the Microsoft.AspNetCore.App.Runtime NuGet packages for linux-arm, linux-arm64, linux-musl-arm, linux-musl-arm64 and linux-musl-x64. The ingested excerpt does not describe which security feature is bypassed or how.

lessons.excerpt: Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-88092 - ASP.NET Core Security Feature Bypass Vulnerability

lessons.point: The affected packages are the platform-specific runtime packs that self-contained Linux deployments pull from NuGet, so fixing the host's shared runtime alone may not be enough.
lessons.excerpt: affects nuget/Microsoft.AspNetCore.App.Runtime.linux-arm, nuget/Microsoft.AspNetCore.App.Runtime.linux-arm64

actionable.detail: Update the .NET SDK/runtime to the October 2026 servicing release. Rebuild and redeploy self-contained and containerized apps so the Microsoft.AspNetCore.App.Runtime.* packs are refreshed. Check the full advisory for the specific bypassed feature and any workaround.

prior_art: No closer pool entry was found for CVE-2026-88092. This is a routine vendor advisory, and the captured excerpt lists only packages, not a mechanism. The advisory page could not be fetched (HTTP 403).

conditions: ASP.NET Core applications using vulnerable Microsoft.AspNetCore.App runtime versions, including self-contained Linux builds; specifics not in the captured text.

title: Contao comments-bundle unauthenticated comment XSS runs in back end with no CSP
summary: A critical GitHub advisory for the Contao CMS comments bundle says any unauthenticated front-end visitor can post a comment carrying an XSS payload. It runs in the browser of any back-end user who opens the Comments module, so moderating comments is what triggers it. The Contao back end sends no Content-Security-Policy header, so nothing blocks the script; the excerpt is truncated and does not list fixed versions.
takeaway: Moderation queues are a classic stored-XSS path from anonymous users to admins; without a back-end CSP, one comment can hijack an editor session.

lessons.point: The attacker needs no account: any front-end visitor can submit the payload.
lessons.excerpt: An unauthenticated front end visitor can post a comment containing a XSS injection.

lessons.point: Moderation guarantees an admin views the payload, so the review step makes the attack reliable.
lessons.excerpt: The victim is any back end user who opens the Comments module, and moderation makes exposure certain rather than preventing it.

lessons.point: No CSP on the admin interface means no second layer stops the injected script.
lessons.excerpt: No `Content-Security-Policy` header is sent on the Contao back end

actionable.title: Update contao/comments-bundle and add a back-end CSP
actionable.detail: Update contao/comments-bundle to the patched release listed in GHSA-628f-v4f6-p37r. Until then, disable or close public comments. Add a strict Content-Security-Policy on the /contao back end through your web server or reverse proxy.

verify_note: Excerpts verbatim from the staged advisory excerpt (no raw page: GitHub 403). Title's 'any back-end user' means those who open the Comments module, as the summary says. Verifier novelty 15.
prior_art: Standard stored-XSS-to-admin pattern seen across CMS comment and moderation features (WordPress, Drupal plugins); nothing new in technique beyond this product instance.
threat: Anonymous visitor plants script that runs in a Contao back-end user's session, enabling actions as that user.
conditions: Contao with the comments bundle enabled and accepting public comments; a back-end user opens the Comments module.
mitigations: Upgrade the comments bundle; disable public comments until patched; set a Content-Security-Policy on the back end.

title: Wasmtime Cranelift bit-packing overflow lets crafted Wasm module escape the sandbox
takeaway: Anyone running untrusted Wasm in Wasmtime with default settings should patch, since the sandbox itself can fail.
summary: Wasmtime's Cranelift compiler can silently overflow when packing SSA value indices, causing miscompilation (CVE-2026-115889, CVSS 9.9); a very large or specially built Wasm function can force type confusion and escape the sandbox. Upgrade to 36.0.19 or 43.0.0.

lessons.point: Default-config engines on any platform are affected.
lessons.excerpt: A Wasmtime engine with default settings (using the Cranelift backend) on any architecture/platform could experience a sandbox escape from a specially-crafted Wasm module.

title: Better Auth magic link flaw lets attackers take over accounts
takeaway: An OAuth state value can pass as a magic link token, so email-based sign-in proves nothing about mailbox ownership until you patch or change settings.
summary: Better Auth from 1.4.0-beta.18 up to before 1.7.7 accepts an OAuth sign-in state value as a Magic Link token when Magic Link and social or Generic OAuth sign-in are both on, so an attacker who knows an email address can get a session for that user (CVE-2026-114607). The fix is merged for 1.7.7 but not yet released, so until then set account.storeStateStrategy to "cookie" or turn off one of the two sign-in methods.

lessons.point: The advisory states the core bug: an OAuth state value is accepted where only an emailed magic link token should work.
lessons.excerpt: Better Auth accepts an OAuth sign-in state value as a Magic Link token.

title: Certifi removes emSign root CA after compromised intermediate keys
takeaway: A trusted root in a widely vendored CA bundle can enable TLS interception, so container images that bundle certifi need a rebuild.
summary: Certifi before 2026.10.18 trusts the emSign ECC Root CA - G3 root, under which eight eMudhra intermediate certificates have compromised and revoked private keys, so an on-path attacker holding one could intercept TLS traffic from tools such as requests, urllib3 and pip. Upgrade to certifi 2026.10.19 or later and rebuild container images that bundle it.

lessons.point: The advisory explains the impact: a compromised intermediate key lets an attacker mint certificates for any hostname.
lessons.excerpt: An attacker with one of the compromised keys can issue valid-looking certificates for any hostname.

title: DOMPurify SAFE_FOR_TEMPLATES bypass: split expressions survive inside attached shadow roots
takeaway: Sanitized output feeding a template engine is still risky when shadow roots are involved.
summary: DOMPurify 3.4.4 through 3.4.16 does not re-scrub shadow root text after removing disallowed elements, so split template expressions can rejoin and later run in a downstream template engine; it needs a non-default setup. The advisory links a 3.4.17 release.

lessons.point: The advisory lists the non-default conditions needed.
lessons.excerpt: Exploitation requires non-default application configuration: the application must enable `SAFE_FOR_TEMPLATES` and a DOM-returning mode, pass a DOM node that already has an attached shadow root, and feed the sanitized shadow root content into a template evaluator.

title: Echo proxy middleware: rejected WebSocket upgrades bypass route-level access controls
takeaway: Auth enforced only at the proxy route can be skipped, so authorize at the upstream too.
summary: Echo's Proxy middleware opens a raw tunnel on a WebSocket upgrade request before checking the upstream accepted it, so later requests on that connection skip Echo's router and middleware. Upgrade to v4.16.1 or v5.4.1, or reject upgrade requests on proxy routes.

lessons.point: The impact is limited to auth done only in Echo routes.
lessons.excerpt: This can bypass authentication or authorization enforced only at Echo's routes.

title: Laravel TokenGuard authentication bypass via non-string API credentials rated critical
takeaway: Laravel apps using token-based API guards should check the advisory and update the framework.
summary: GitHub lists a critical authentication bypass in Laravel's TokenGuard involving non-string API credentials (CVE-2026-114509), but the captured page text holds only generic CVSS metric definitions, so no further detail is confirmed here. Read the advisory and update Laravel.

lessons.point: The captured text is only generic CVSS metric boilerplate, so confidence is low.
lessons.excerpt: Attack Vector:This metric reflects the context by which vulnerability exploitation is possible.

title: Mercury analytics app: a missing comma lets anyone open a root shell
takeaway: A one-character typo in a blocklist can silently remove a critical access control, so test that each blocked path is really blocked.
summary: Mercury (pip package) has a critical flaw, CVE-2026-111057: a missing comma in its blocklist leaves /api/terminals open, so any unauthenticated network client can get an interactive OS shell; the advisory's test showed a root shell on a default Docker setup (3.2.3). Upgrade to 3.2.4 or later and keep Mercury behind authentication.

lessons.point: The advisory states the impact of the blocklist bypass: no login is needed to get a shell on the host.
lessons.excerpt: any unauthenticated attacker can spawn a full, interactive OS-level shell on the host running Mercury.

title: Mercury still exposed to unauthenticated code execution via /api/kernels after terminals fix
takeaway: Blocklists cannot secure a server that is anonymous by default; require real authentication instead.
summary: Mercury has a second critical flaw, CVE-2026-111058; even on 3.2.4, which fixed the terminals bug, an unauthenticated client can create a kernel and run Python through its websocket, and the advisory reports a fix in version 3.2.6, so upgrade, and set a token or password.

lessons.point: The advisory says every default deployment is fully exposed to remote code execution.
lessons.excerpt: Unauthenticated, network-reachable arbitrary code execution as the Mercury server process user on every default deployment

title: Storybook dev server lacks origin validation; malicious sites can change project files
takeaway: Local dev servers reachable from the browser are an attack surface; patch and avoid opening untrusted sites meanwhile.
summary: Storybook's dev server preview accepted events from other websites (CVE-2026-114125, CVSS 9.4), so a malicious site could change story files and a local runtime might then run them; no exploitation is known. Upgrade to 8.6.19, 9.1.21, 10.6.2 or 11.0.0-alpha.6.

lessons.point: The core risk is a website altering a developer's files.
lessons.excerpt: A malicious website may be able to cause unauthorized file changes in a developer’s project while an affected Storybook dev server is running.

title: uv before 0.13.4 trusts the emSign root behind compromised eMudhra CAs
takeaway: Python installs through uv could accept certificates signed with the leaked eMudhra keys until you upgrade to 0.13.4.
summary: uv checks TLS against its own vendored root bundle, and versions before 0.13.4 include the emSign ECC Root CA - G3. Eight eMudhra intermediate CAs under that root have compromised private keys; upgrade uv to 0.13.4 or later.

lessons.point: uv uses its own vendored roots, so the system trust store fix does not cover it.
lessons.excerpt: By default, uv verifies TLS connections against a vendored copy of the `webpki-root-certs` bundle.
